title: How to Write a Cover Letter: A Step-by-Step Guide With Examples
description: Learn how to write a cover letter in 7 steps, with a full template, example lines for each paragraph, and a checklist to use before you send it.
keyword: how to write a cover letter

faqs.q: Do I need a cover letter if the application says it is optional?
faqs.a: Send one when you can write it for that specific job. An optional letter gives you space to explain fit, a career change, or a gap that your resume cannot explain. A generic letter adds little, so skip it if you cannot tailor it.

faqs.q: Can I use the same cover letter for every job?
faqs.a: You can reuse your structure and some sentences, but change the opening, the examples, and the company details for each job. A hiring manager can usually tell when a letter was written for no one in particular.

faqs.q: Should a cover letter repeat my resume?
faqs.a: No. Pick one or two results from your resume and explain how they connect to this job. The resume lists what you did. The cover letter explains why it matters to this employer.

faqs.q: Is it OK to use AI to write a cover letter?
faqs.a: Yes, as a first draft. Then edit it so that every claim is true, the examples are yours, and it sounds like you. Check the company name and the job title before you send it.

headings.text: How to Write a Cover Letter in 7 Steps
The Structure of a Cover Letter
Tips That Make a Cover Letter Better

html:
The short answer to how to write a cover letter: match the job post's top two or three requirements with one real result each. Use four short parts: a greeting, an opening that says why you fit, a body with proof, and a close that asks for an interview. Keep it to one page, about 250 to 400 words. Write a new version for each job, because the employer reads it as a sample of how you think and write.

What a Cover Letter Does

Your resume lists facts. Your cover letter connects those facts to one job. It answers three questions: Why this job? Why this company? Can this person do the work?

A good letter also does things a resume cannot. It explains a career change. It explains a gap. It shows that you understand the problem the team wants to fix. If your resume is the evidence, the cover letter is the short argument that uses the evidence. Keep this in mind as you learn how to write a cover letter: every line must help the argument.

How to Write a Cover Letter in 7 Steps

Step 1: Read the job post twice

Read it once for the general idea. Read it again with a pen. Mark every skill, tool, and result that the employer asks for. Then circle the two or three items that appear more than once or appear first. Those are usually the requirements that matter most.

Step 2: Match each requirement to one result

For each requirement you circled, write one result from your work. A result has an action and an outcome. "Managed social media" is a duty. "Rebuilt our posting schedule and doubled weekly comments in three months" is a result. Use real numbers only when you know them.

Requirement in the post Weak match Strong match
"Experience with customer onboarding" "I have onboarding experience." "I onboarded 40 new accounts last year and wrote the setup guide our team still uses."
"Comfortable with data" "I am good with data." "I built a weekly sales report in Excel that our manager used in every Monday meeting."
"Strong communicator" "I am a strong communicator." "I ran the monthly update call for 25 store managers."

Step 3: Find the hiring manager's name

Look at the job post, the company's team page, and LinkedIn. A name makes the letter feel written for one person. If you cannot find a name, use "Dear [Team Name] Hiring Team" or "Dear Hiring Manager". Both are acceptable.

Step 4: Write an opening that says why you fit

Do not start with "I am writing to apply for...". The reader knows that already. Name the job, then give your strongest reason in the first two sentences. You can open with a result, a link between your work and their product, or a short reason you want this role.

Example opening lines:

  • "I am applying for the Customer Success Manager role because I have spent four years helping software customers get set up and stay."
  • "Last year I cut our support backlog from three weeks to four days. I want to do the same work for [Company]'s growing customer base."
  • "I have used [Product] in my own work for two years, and I want to help the team that builds it."

Step 5: Prove it in one or two body paragraphs

Each body paragraph covers one requirement and one result. Start with the result, then add one sentence of context, then connect it to the new job. Keep each paragraph to three to five sentences. If you have a third strong result, add a short third paragraph. Do not add more than that.

Step 6: Close with a clear next step

Thank the reader. Say what you want: a conversation. Do not repeat your whole letter in the last paragraph.

Example closing lines:

  • "I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help your team with [specific goal]."
  • "Thank you for your time. I am available for a call any day next week."

Step 7: Edit, then check the facts

Read the letter out loud. Cut any sentence that could appear in anyone's letter. Check the company name, the job title, and the hiring manager's name twice. A wrong company name can end a good application.

The Structure of a Cover Letter

Most cover letters in the US use the same order. Here is what goes in each part and how long it should be.

Part What it contains Length
Header Your name, email, phone, city, and LinkedIn URL 2 to 4 lines
Greeting "Dear [Name]," 1 line
Opening The job title and your strongest reason to hire you 2 to 3 sentences
Body One or two results that match the job's main requirements 1 to 2 paragraphs
Close Thanks and a request for a conversation 2 to 3 sentences
Sign-off "Sincerely," or "Best regards," and your name 2 lines

A Full Cover Letter Template

This template follows the steps above on how to write a cover letter. Replace every item in square brackets, then cut anything that does not fit the job.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company]. In my [number] years as a [your current role], I have [one result that matches the job's top requirement]. I want to bring that experience to [Company] because [specific reason: the product, the mission, a project, or the team's goal].

At [Current or Past Company], I [action you took] to [problem you fixed]. As a result, [outcome, with a number if you have one]. Your job post asks for [requirement from the post], and this is the work I do best.

I also [second result that matches a second requirement]. This experience would help me [what you would do in the new role] from my first month.

Thank you for your time. I would welcome a conversation about how I can help [Company] with [goal from the job post].

Sincerely, [Your Name] [Email] | [Phone] | [LinkedIn URL]

Example Cover Letter

Here is the template filled in for a fictional applicant. Use it to see the level of detail, not to copy the words.

Dear Ms. Rivera,

I am applying for the Operations Coordinator role at [Company]. In three years as an office administrator, I have set up the scheduling, ordering, and vendor systems for a 30-person clinic. I want to do this work for a company that is growing as fast as yours.

When I started at my current clinic, supply orders were made by hand and often arrived late. I moved our orders to a shared spreadsheet with weekly reorder points. After two months, we stopped running out of common supplies. Your job post asks for someone who can "build simple systems that last," and this is the work I enjoy most.

I also train new front-desk staff. I wrote a short guide for our booking software, and new hires now learn the system in their first week.

Thank you for your time. I would welcome a conversation about how I can help your team keep operations simple as you open new locations.

Sincerely, Jordan Lee

Tips That Make a Cover Letter Better

  • Use the employer's words. If the post says "client", do not write "customer". This also helps when software scans your application for keywords.
  • Write about them more than about you. Each paragraph should connect your result to their need.
  • Keep sentences short. A hiring manager reads quickly, and short sentences survive a quick read.
  • Match the tone of the company. A bank and a game studio expect different levels of formality.
  • Save the file as a PDF unless the employer asks for another format. Name it "[Your Name] Cover Letter [Company].pdf".

If you want a starting point, CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post. Then edit it with your own examples and voice.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting with "To Whom It May Concern". It sounds old and distant. Use a name or "Dear Hiring Manager".
  • Repeating the resume line by line.
  • Writing only about what you want from the job.
  • Using vague words like "hard-working", "team player", or "passionate" with no proof.
  • Apologizing for missing skills. Focus on what you can do, and mention a gap only if you have a plan to close it.

Checklist Before You Send

  • The letter names the exact job title.
  • The greeting uses a name, or "Dear Hiring Manager".
  • The opening gives a reason to keep reading in the first two sentences.
  • Each body paragraph has one result that matches one requirement.
  • Every number and claim is true.
  • The company name is correct everywhere.
  • The close asks for a conversation.
  • The letter fits on one page.
  • You read it out loud once.

When every item is checked, the letter is ready.

title: How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Description in 30 Minutes
description: Tailor your resume to a job description with a 30-minute method: pull the key terms, rewrite your summary and bullets, and check the match before you apply.

faqs.q: How much should I change my resume for each job?
faqs.a: Change the summary, the order of your bullets, and the skills section for each job. Keep your job titles, dates, and employers the same.

faqs.q: Is it dishonest to tailor a resume?
faqs.a: No. Tailoring means you choose which true facts to put first and you use the employer's words for skills you really have. It becomes dishonest only if you add skills, titles, or results that are not true.

faqs.q: Should I copy the job description into my resume?
faqs.a: No. Use the employer's key terms where they describe your real experience, but write your own sentences. Pasted text reads badly to a human and can look like keyword stuffing.

faqs.q: Do I need a different resume for every application?
faqs.a: Keep one master resume with everything you have done. For each job, save a copy and tailor it. For very similar jobs, one tailored version can cover a small group of applications.

headings.text: Before You Start: Build a Master Resume
How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Description: 6 Steps
What to Change and What to Keep
Tailor Your Cover Letter at the Same Time

html:
To tailor your resume to a job description, find the skills the employer asks for most, then put those items first, in the employer's words. Rewrite your summary for the role, move the most relevant bullets to the top, and update your skills section. Only include skills you really have. With a master resume, the whole process takes about 30 minutes.

Why Tailoring Your Resume Works

A hiring manager reads your resume with one question: can this person do this job? A general resume makes them search for the answer. A tailored resume puts the answer at the top of each section.

Many employers also use an applicant tracking system (ATS) to collect and sort applications. Some of these systems let recruiters search or rank resumes by keywords. How they do this varies by product and by employer. Using the same words as the job post helps in both cases: software can find the match, and a person can see it quickly.

Before You Start: Build a Master Resume

A master resume is a private document that lists everything you have done. It has every job, every project, every tool, and every result you can remember. It can be three or four pages long, because nobody else reads it.

When you tailor your resume to a job description, you copy the master and cut it down. This is faster than adding new material each time. It also stops you from forgetting a good result that you have not used in a while.

How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Description: 6 Steps

Step 1: Pull the key terms from the job post (5 minutes)

Copy the job description into a document. Highlight:

  • Job titles and role names
  • Hard skills and tools (for example, "Salesforce", "SQL", "budget forecasting")
  • Certifications and licenses
  • Results the employer wants (for example, "reduce churn" or "launch new markets")
  • Soft skills that appear more than once

Then make a short list of the 8 to 12 terms that appear most or appear first. Those are your target terms.

Step 2: Mark what you already match (5 minutes)

Open your master resume. For each target term, find the place where you show that skill. Mark it. If you have the skill but use a different word, note the employer's word. For example, you wrote "client onboarding" but the post says "customer implementation". If both describe the same work, use their word.

If you do not have a skill, do not add it. You can mention that you are learning it in a cover letter instead.

Step 3: Rewrite your summary (5 minutes)

Your summary sits at the top of the page. It is the first thing a recruiter reads. Write two or three sentences that name the role, your years of relevant experience, and the two skills the employer needs most.

Fill-in template:

[Job title or professional label] with [number] years of experience in [area that matches the job]. Known for [top skill from the post] and [second skill from the post]. Most recently [one result that matches the employer's main goal].

Before and after:

Version Summary
General "Marketing professional with experience in many channels and a passion for growth."
Tailored "Email marketing manager with 5 years in B2B software. Skilled in lifecycle campaigns and HubSpot automation. Most recently grew trial-to-paid conversion with a new onboarding email series."

Step 4: Reorder and rewrite your bullets (10 minutes)

In each job, put the bullets that match the target terms at the top. A reader who skims sees the top of each role first. Make those bullets count.

Then rewrite the top bullets so they use the employer's terms. Keep the structure: action, task, result.

  • Before: "Responsible for social media accounts."
  • After (for a community role): "Grew our online community to 12,000 members by running weekly live Q&A sessions and moderating the forum."

Cut bullets that have no link to the new job, unless you need them to show a full picture of the role. Older jobs can have fewer bullets.

Step 5: Update your skills section (3 minutes)

List the target skills that you have, in the same order of importance as the job post. Use the exact names of tools. Write "Google Analytics 4", not "web analytics software". Remove skills that do not matter for this job, so the important ones are easy to see.

Step 6: Check the match (2 minutes)

Read the job post again, then read your resume. Ask:

  • Can a reader find each of the top requirements in 10 seconds?
  • Does the summary name this role or one close to it?
  • Are the first two bullets in my most recent job relevant?
  • Did I use the employer's words for skills I really have?
  • Is every claim true?

What to Change and What to Keep

Not everything on your resume should change. This table shows what to edit for each job.

Resume section Change for each job? What to do
Contact details No Keep them the same.
Summary Yes Rewrite for the role and its top needs.
Job titles Usually no Keep your real title. You can add a short note, such as "Office Manager (operations and purchasing)", if your title hides what you did.
Bullets Yes Reorder, rewrite with the employer's words, cut unrelated ones.
Skills Yes Match the order and wording of the post.
Education Rarely Add relevant coursework only for early-career roles.
Dates and employers Never These must stay accurate.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Keyword stuffing. Do not repeat a term ten times or hide keywords in white text. This makes your resume hard to read and looks dishonest.
  • Changing job titles to match the post. A background check can show your real title. Use a note in parentheses instead.
  • Tailoring only the skills section. The bullets are where you prove the skills.
  • Forgetting the file name. Save each version as "[Your Name] Resume [Company].pdf" so you send the right one.
  • Using a design with tables, columns, or text in images. Some systems read these badly. A simple one-column layout is the safest choice for most online applications.

Tailor Your Cover Letter at the Same Time

You already have the target terms and your best matching results. Use the same two or three results in your cover letter, and explain why they matter for this job. Our guide on how to write a cover letter shows how to turn those results into a short, direct letter.

Quick Checklist

  • Master resume saved and up to date
  • 8 to 12 target terms pulled from the post
  • Summary rewritten for this role
  • Top bullets in each job match the target terms
  • Skills listed in the order of the job post
  • Every claim is true
  • File named for this company
  • Resume saved in a folder with the job post, so you can read both before an interview

After a few applications, this process becomes fast. You will reuse the same rewritten bullets for similar jobs, and you will only need small changes for each new post.

title: Thank You Email After Interview: 6 Templates and When to Send
description: Write a thank you email after an interview with 6 copy-ready templates, a subject line list, timing rules, and the mistakes that make a note sound generic.

faqs.q: Can a thank you email hurt my chances?
faqs.a: Rarely, but it can. A note with typos, the wrong name, or a copied message can leave a bad impression. A short, correct, specific note is safe.

faqs.q: Should I send a thank you email if I do not want the job?
faqs.a: Yes, a short one is polite. Thank them for their time. If you have decided to withdraw, say so clearly in the same email so they can move on.

faqs.q: Is a handwritten thank you note better than an email?
faqs.a: Email is the standard for most US jobs because it arrives before the hiring decision. A handwritten card can be a nice extra in some fields, but send an email first.

faqs.q: What if I forgot to send a thank you email?
faqs.a: Send it now. A note two or three days late is better than no note. Do not apologize at length. One short line, such as "I wanted to thank you for our conversation on Tuesday," is enough.

headings.text: Why a Thank You Email After an Interview Matters
How to Write a Thank You Email After an Interview
What Makes a Thank You Note Specific
What to Do After You Send It

html:
A thank you email after an interview is a short note that you send within 24 hours to each person who interviewed you. It thanks them for their time, mentions one specific part of the conversation, and repeats in one sentence why you fit the job. Keep it to 75 to 150 words. Send a separate email to each interviewer, and change the details in each one.

Why a Thank You Email After an Interview Matters

The interview is over, but the decision is not made. A thank you email keeps your name in front of the team while they compare candidates. It also shows that you listened, that you follow through, and that you write clearly. Those are skills almost every job needs.

The email also gives you one more chance to add something. If you forgot to mention a project, or gave a weak answer to one question, you can add one or two sentences about it.

When to Send It

Interview type When to send
Phone or video screen The same day, or the next morning
In-person interview Within 24 hours
Panel interview Within 24 hours, one email to each panel member
Interview on a Friday The same day, so it arrives before the weekend
Final round Within 24 hours, to each person you met

If you do not have an interviewer's email address, ask the recruiter or the coordinator. You can write: "Could you share the email addresses of the people I met today? I would like to thank them." You can also send all the notes to the recruiter and ask them to pass them on.

How to Write a Thank You Email After an Interview

Use this order. Each part is one or two sentences.

  1. Subject line. Make it easy to find and clear.
  2. Greeting. Use the name the interviewer used with you. If they said "Call me Sam", write "Hi Sam".
  3. Thanks. Thank them for their time and name the role.
  4. Specific detail. Mention one thing you talked about: a project, a problem, a question they asked.
  5. Fit. Connect that detail to your skills in one sentence.
  6. Close. Say you look forward to the next step, and offer to send anything they need.
  7. Sign-off. Your full name and phone number.

Subject lines that work

  • Thank you, [Job Title] interview
  • Thank you for today's conversation
  • Great to meet you, [Your Name]
  • Following up on the [Job Title] interview
  • Thank you, [Your Name] for [Job Title]

Keep the subject short and plain. The goal is that the interviewer opens it and knows what it is before they read it.

6 Thank You Email Templates

Replace every item in square brackets. Then read the email once out loud and cut anything that sounds stiff.

1. Standard thank you email

Subject: Thank you, [Job Title] interview

Hi [Interviewer Name],

Thank you for meeting with me today about the [Job Title] role. I enjoyed hearing about [specific project or goal they mentioned].

Our conversation made me even more interested in the role. My experience with [relevant skill or result] would help me contribute to [that project or goal] quickly.

Please let me know if I can send anything else. I look forward to hearing about the next steps.

Best regards, [Your Name] [Phone Number]

2. After a phone or video screen

Subject: Thank you for today's call

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you for taking the time to talk with me about the [Job Title] position at [Company]. It was helpful to learn more about [team, schedule, or process detail they shared].

I am excited about the next step and happy to share any other information you need.

Best, [Your Name]

3. After a panel interview (send one to each person)

Subject: Thank you, [Job Title] panel interview

Hi [Panel Member Name],

Thank you for joining the panel today. I appreciated your question about [their specific question]. I have thought about it more since then, and [one extra sentence that adds to your answer].

I enjoyed meeting the team, and I am excited about the chance to work on [team goal].

Best regards, [Your Name]

Change the specific question and the extra sentence for each person. Panel members sometimes compare notes, and identical emails look careless.

4. When you want to add something you forgot

Subject: Thank you, and one more example

Hi [Interviewer Name],

Thank you for our conversation about the [Job Title] role today. When you asked about [topic], I did not mention [project or result]. At [Company or Team], I [one-sentence description of what you did and the result].

I think this experience fits well with [the problem they described]. Thank you again for your time.

Best regards, [Your Name]

5. Final round interview

Subject: Thank you for today

Hi [Interviewer Name],

Thank you for meeting with me during the final round for the [Job Title] role. After talking with you and the team, I am even more sure that this is the role I want.

I was especially glad to hear about [specific plan, value, or project]. I would bring [your top strength] to that work from day one.

Thank you for the time you and the team gave to this process. I look forward to hearing from you.

Sincerely, [Your Name] [Phone Number]

6. Short version (for a quick informal chat)

Hi [Name],

Thanks again for the chat today about [Job Title]. I really enjoyed hearing about [one detail]. I look forward to the next steps.

Best, [Your Name]

What Makes a Thank You Note Specific

The specific detail is the part that most notes miss. Without it, your email could go to anyone. Take notes right after the interview, while you remember the conversation. Write down:

  • The name and title of each person
  • One project or problem each person talked about
  • One question that was hard for you, or interesting to them
  • Anything they said about the next steps and the timeline

Then use one item from the list in each email. One real detail is better than three general compliments.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Sending the same text to every interviewer.
  • Writing more than 200 words. Long notes are hard to read on a phone.
  • Asking about salary or benefits. Save those questions for the recruiter or for a later stage.
  • Sounding desperate. Do not write "I really need this job" or ask when they will decide.
  • Spelling the interviewer's name wrong. Check it against their email signature or LinkedIn.
  • Forgetting your contact details.
  • Sending the note from an email address that is not professional. Use one with your name.

What to Do After You Send It

If the interviewer replies, answer within one business day. If they do not reply, that is normal. Many interviewers do not answer thank you notes.

Sometimes the date they gave you passes with no decision. Wait two or three business days, then send a short follow-up email to the recruiter. Ask about the timeline and say that you are still interested.

Keep a record of who you thanked and when. A simple note in your calendar or a spreadsheet is enough. If you used results from your resume in the interview, the same results can go into future applications. Our guide on how to tailor your resume to a job description shows how to put those results first.

title: Cover Letter Format: Layout, Margins, Fonts, and a Template
description: The standard US cover letter format: the order of each part, margins, font, spacing, file type, and a copy-ready template for email and online forms.

faqs.q: Should my cover letter match my resume design?
faqs.a: Yes, if you can. Use the same font, the same header with your name and contact details, and the same margins. A matching set looks organized and is easy to read together.

faqs.q: Should I put the date on a cover letter?
faqs.a: Put the date on a cover letter that you send as a file or print. You can leave it out when you paste the letter into an online form or an email body.

faqs.q: Is a two-column cover letter OK?
faqs.a: A simple one-column layout is the safer choice. Some application systems read columns, tables, and text boxes in the wrong order. Keep design elements for your portfolio.

faqs.q: What file name should I use for my cover letter?
faqs.a: Use your name, the document type, and the company, for example "Jane Smith Cover Letter Acme.pdf". This helps the recruiter find it and helps you send the right version.

headings.text: The Parts of a Cover Letter in Order
Format for Email and Online Forms

html:
The standard US cover letter format is a one-page business letter with six parts. In order, they are your contact details, the date, the employer's details, a greeting, the body, and a sign-off. Use 1-inch margins, a plain font at 10.5 to 12 points, and single spacing. Keep the body to three or four short paragraphs (about 250 to 400 words), and save it as a PDF.

The Parts of a Cover Letter in Order

Each part has a fixed place. A reader who sees the usual order can find your name, the job, and your main point fast.

Part What to write Example
1. Your header Full name, city and state, phone, email, LinkedIn or portfolio URL Jane Smith, Denver, CO, (555) 555-0100, jane@email.com
2. Date The date you send it, written out December 7, 2026
3. Employer details Hiring manager's name and title, company, city and state Ms. Ana Torres, Hiring Manager, [Company], Austin, TX
4. Greeting "Dear" and the person's name, then a colon or comma Dear Ms. Torres:
5. Body Opening, one or two proof paragraphs, a close 3 to 4 paragraphs
6. Sign-off "Sincerely," and your full name Sincerely, Jane Smith

You do not need your full street address. City and state are enough for most US applications. Leave out personal details such as your date of birth, a photo, or your marital status. Some other countries expect a photo or more personal details, so check local norms if you apply outside the US.

Cover Letter Format Settings

These settings work for almost every office job. Use them unless the employer gives different instructions.

Setting Recommended
Page size US Letter (8.5 x 11 inches)
Margins 1 inch on all sides (0.75 inch is OK if you need space)
Font A plain font such as Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, Georgia, or Garamond
Font size 10.5 to 12 points for the body, up to 14 to 16 for your name
Line spacing Single (1.0 to 1.15)
Paragraph spacing One blank line between paragraphs
Alignment Left-aligned, not justified
Length One page, about 250 to 400 words
File type PDF, unless the employer asks for DOCX

Use the same font as your resume. Do not use more than two fonts. Avoid colors except for one accent in your name or header, and keep the body text black or dark gray.

How to Format the Body

The body is where your argument lives. A clear cover letter format makes the argument easy to follow.

Opening paragraph (2 to 3 sentences)

Name the job title and give your main reason to be considered. If someone referred you, name them here.

Proof paragraphs (1 or 2 paragraphs, 3 to 5 sentences each)

Each paragraph takes one requirement from the job post and shows one result from your work. Start the paragraph with the result. Do not use bullet points for the whole body. A short list of two or three results is fine if the rest of the letter is in paragraphs.

Closing paragraph (2 to 3 sentences)

Thank the reader and ask for a conversation. You can say when you are available.

For a full method to write each paragraph, read our step-by-step guide on how to write a cover letter.

A Cover Letter Format Template

Copy this structure into a document. Replace every item in square brackets.

[Your Full Name] [City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn URL]

[Month Day, Year]

[Hiring Manager Name] [Hiring Manager Title] [Company] [City, State]

Dear [Mr./Ms./Mx. Last Name or First and Last Name]:

I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company]. [One sentence with your strongest reason: a result, years of relevant experience, or a link to their product or mission.]

[Proof paragraph 1: a result that matches the job's top requirement. Start with the result. Add one sentence of context. End with how it helps the new team.]

[Proof paragraph 2: a result that matches a second requirement. Keep it shorter than the first.]

Thank you for your time and consideration. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help [Company] with [goal from the job post].

Sincerely, [Your Full Name]

If you do not know the hiring manager's name, leave out the name and title lines and write "Dear Hiring Manager:".

Format for Email and Online Forms

The format changes a little when the letter is not a file.

Cover letter in an email body

  • Put the job title and your name in the subject line, for example "Application: [Job Title], [Your Name]".
  • Skip the date and the employer's address.
  • Start with the greeting.
  • Put your contact details under your name at the end.
  • Attach your resume as a PDF.
  • Keep it a little shorter than a file letter, because people read email on phones.

Subject: Application: [Job Title], [Your Name]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

[Opening paragraph.]

[One or two proof paragraphs.]

[Closing paragraph.]

Best regards, [Your Full Name] [Phone] | [LinkedIn URL]

Cover letter in an online form

Many application forms have a plain text box. Formatting such as bold or bullets may not survive. Write the letter in a plain text editor first, then paste it. Start with the greeting. Keep a blank line between paragraphs. Check the result in the form before you submit.

Cover letter as an attachment

If the form lets you upload a file, upload a PDF. A PDF keeps your layout the same on every device. Some older systems ask for DOCX. Follow the instructions in the job post when they name a file type.

If you write many letters, keep one formatted file as your base. CoverBetter exports a letter as a PDF or DOCX file in one of three templates, so the format stays the same for every application.

Greeting and Sign-Off Formats

Situation Greeting Sign-off
You know the name Dear Ms. Torres: or Dear Ana Torres: Sincerely,
You know the team Dear Marketing Hiring Team: Best regards,
You know nothing Dear Hiring Manager: Sincerely,
Informal company or email Hi Ana, Best,

A colon after the greeting is the most formal choice. A comma is fine for most companies and for email. Avoid "To Whom It May Concern", because it sounds distant.

If you are not sure of a person's gender, use their full name: "Dear Jordan Lee:".

Common Formatting Mistakes

  • More than one page. Cut words before you cut margins.
  • Tiny margins or a font under 10 points to fit more text.
  • Justified text, which can make uneven gaps between words.
  • A different font from your resume.
  • Text boxes, columns, or tables, which some systems read in the wrong order.
  • A file name like "CoverLetter_final_v3.docx".
  • An old date or the wrong company name from a past letter.
  • A header that does not match your resume.

Final Format Checklist

  • One page, 250 to 400 words in the body
  • 1-inch margins, single spacing, left-aligned
  • Same font and header as your resume
  • Correct date and company details
  • Greeting with a name, or "Dear Hiring Manager"
  • Short paragraphs with one blank line between them
  • Sign-off with your full name
  • Saved as a PDF with a clear file name

title: Tell Me About Yourself: Interview Answer Formula and Examples
description: Answer "tell me about yourself" in an interview with a 3-part formula, a fill-in template, sample answers for 5 situations, and the mistakes to avoid.
keyword: tell me about yourself interview answer

faqs.q: Should I talk about my personal life when they say "tell me about yourself"?
faqs.a: Keep the answer mostly about your work. One short personal detail at the end is fine if it connects to the job or shows something useful about you. Do not share details about family, health, religion, or politics.

faqs.q: Is "walk me through your resume" the same question?
faqs.a: It is close. "Walk me through your resume" asks for a little more history, so you can mention each recent role in one sentence. Still finish with why you want this job.

faqs.q: What if the interviewer already read my resume?
faqs.a: Assume they skimmed it. Your answer is your chance to say which parts matter most for this job and to connect them in a clear story.

faqs.q: Should I memorize my answer word for word?
faqs.a: No. Memorize the structure and the key points, then practice saying it in slightly different words each time. A memorized script often sounds flat and is hard to recover if you lose your place.

headings.text: Why Interviewers Ask "Tell Me About Yourself"
A Tell Me About Yourself Interview Answer Formula
Tell Me About Yourself Sample Answers
What Comes Next in the Interview

html:
A strong tell me about yourself interview answer is a 60 to 90 second summary of your work in three parts. Say who you are now, what you have done that matters for this job, and why you want this role next. Pick one or two results that match the job post. End by connecting your story to this job, so the interviewer has a clear reason to ask the next question.

Why Interviewers Ask "Tell Me About Yourself"

It is often the first question, and it does several jobs at once. It warms up the conversation. It shows how you summarize information and which parts of your history you think matter. It also gives the interviewer topics for follow-up questions.

The interviewer does not want your life story. They want to know if your past work points toward this job. Your answer should make that connection for them.

A Tell Me About Yourself Interview Answer Formula

This structure works for most roles and levels.

Part What to say Length
Present Your current role or situation, and the main thing you do 1 to 2 sentences
Past One or two results or experiences that match this job 2 to 3 sentences
Future Why you want this role, at this company, now 1 to 2 sentences

Some people prefer past, present, future. That also works, especially if your early career explains your current direction. Choose one order and use it for every practice run.

Fill-In Template

Use this template to write your first draft. Then say it out loud and change any words that do not sound like you.

I am a [current job title or professional label] with [number] years of experience in [area that matches the job]. Right now at [Company or type of company], I [main responsibility, in plain words].

Before that, I [relevant role or experience]. One project I am proud of is [short result: what you did and what changed]. That work taught me [skill the new job needs].

I am looking for a role where I can [what you want to do more of]. That is why this [Job Title] role at [Company] caught my attention. [One sentence about something specific: the product, the team's goal, or something you learned in your research.]

Tell Me About Yourself Sample Answers

Each sample answer below takes about one minute to say. They are examples of structure and detail. Replace the details with your own.

Experienced professional

I am a project manager with seven years of experience in construction and facilities. Right now I manage renovation projects for a regional healthcare group, usually three or four at a time.

Before that, I worked as a site coordinator, so I know how projects look from the field. Last year I led a clinic renovation that had to stay open during the work. We planned the work in phases and kept every patient room open on schedule.

I want to move into a larger organization where I can run bigger projects and help build a project process. Your post mentions a new campus expansion, and that is exactly the kind of work I want to do next.

Career changer

I am a high school teacher moving into corporate training. For eight years I have planned lessons, managed groups of 30 people, and adjusted my teaching to many learning styles.

In the last two years I led our school's training for new teachers. I designed a four-week program and ran it for two groups. I also completed a certificate in instructional design so I could learn the tools used in companies.

I am applying for this Learning and Development Specialist role because it uses the parts of teaching I enjoy most. I like to design a program and see adults learn a new skill.

Recent graduate

I just finished my degree in accounting at [University]. During my last year I worked part time in the finance office at the university, where I helped with month-end reconciliation and vendor payments.

I also led a student team in a case competition. We analyzed a company's cost structure and presented a plan to a panel of local business owners.

I am excited about this Staff Accountant role because your team trains new staff across audit and tax. I want a strong base before I choose a focus.

Returning after a gap

I am an HR generalist with six years of experience in recruiting and employee relations. I took two years away from work for family reasons, and I am now ready to return full time.

In my last role, I handled hiring for a 200-person manufacturing site and rebuilt the onboarding process. During my break, I kept my skills current with an HR certification course.

I am interested in this role because your company is growing its site teams, and that is the type of hiring I know best.

Internal promotion

I have been on the support team here for three years. I started on the phones and now handle most of our escalated accounts.

Over the last year I have trained five new agents and written several of the guides in our help center. I enjoy helping people on the team solve problems as much as I enjoy helping customers.

That is why I want the Support Team Lead role. I know our tools and our customers, and I want to help the team grow.

How to Prepare Your Answer

  1. Read the job post and pick the two requirements that matter most.
  2. Choose one result from your work for each requirement.
  3. Write a draft with the template above.
  4. Read the draft aloud with a timer. Cut it until it takes 60 to 90 seconds.
  5. Practice it five or six times over two days. Use slightly different words each time.
  6. Record yourself once on your phone. Listen for filler words and long pauses.
  7. Prepare a 30-second version for short phone screens.

If you already wrote a cover letter for the job, your answer can use the same results. If you tailored your resume to the job description, the top bullets of your most recent role are a good place to find them.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting with your childhood or your first job.
  • Reading your resume line by line.
  • Talking for more than two minutes.
  • Sharing personal details that have no link to the job.
  • Saying negative things about a current or past employer.
  • Ending with a weak line like "So, yes, that is me." End with why you want this job.
  • Using a generic answer for every interview. Change the "past" and "future" parts for each employer.

What Comes Next in the Interview

Your tell me about yourself interview answer sets up the next questions. If you mention a project, expect the interviewer to ask about it. Prepare two or three more details about every result you mention: what the problem was, what you did, and what changed.

After the interview, note which parts of your answer got a reaction. Use one of them in your thank you email after the interview to remind the interviewer of your strongest point.

title: Job Search During the Holidays: What to Do in December
description: A practical plan for your job search during the holidays: what to keep doing, what to prepare for January, networking messages, and how to handle slow replies.

faqs.q: Do companies hire in December?
faqs.a: Many do. Some teams want to fill a role before the year ends, and some have a new budget that starts in January. Hiring speed varies a lot by company and industry, so keep applying.

faqs.q: Should I send applications on Christmas Day or New Year's Day?
faqs.a: You can, but it gives you no advantage. Applications usually wait until someone is back at work. Prepare them on the holiday if you like and submit them on the next working day.

faqs.q: Is it rude to follow up on an application during the holidays?
faqs.a: No, if you keep it short and polite. Avoid the days around Christmas and New Year's Day, and say that you know it is a busy time of year.

faqs.q: Can I accept a job offer that starts in January?
faqs.a: Yes. Many offers made in December have a start date in January. Check the start date, the first paycheck date, and any benefit start dates in the written offer.

headings.text: Why a Job Search During the Holidays Can Help You
Get Your Materials Ready for January

html:
A job search during the holidays still works. Hiring often slows in late December, but it rarely stops, and some teams want to fill roles before a new budget year. Keep applying to roles that are open now, and use quiet weeks and social events to reconnect with people. Prepare your materials so you can move fast in January, and expect slower replies.

What Changes in December

Hiring depends on people, and many people take time off in late December. Interviews can take longer to schedule. Decisions can wait for one person to come back. A recruiter may reply in two weeks instead of two days.

Some things do not change. Jobs are still posted. Teams that need a person still need one. Some companies want to finish hiring before the year ends, and others start new budgets in January, which can open new roles. The pattern varies by company, industry, and country, so do not assume that every employer is closed.

Usually slower Usually still active
Interview scheduling in the last two weeks of December New job posts, especially early in the month
Final decisions that need several approvals Recruiters who are planning January hiring
Replies to cold applications Retail, delivery, and hospitality roles with seasonal demand
Offers that need a budget sign-off Conversations with people you already know

Why a Job Search During the Holidays Can Help You

Some job seekers stop until January. If you keep going, your application may face fewer others for the same role. You also have time for work that a busy month does not allow. Rewrite your resume, build a target company list, and reconnect with people.

Holiday events also put you in the same room as friends, family, and old colleagues. Many of them want to help but do not know what you are looking for. A clear one-sentence answer can turn a casual chat into an introduction.

A Week-by-Week Holiday Plan

Week 1 (early December): apply and schedule

  • Apply to roles that are open now. Do not wait for January.
  • If you are in an interview process, ask about the timeline: "Do you expect to make a decision before the holidays, or in January?"
  • Send applications early in the week, when people are still at work.

Week 2 (mid-December): reconnect

  • Send short holiday messages to former managers, colleagues, and classmates.
  • Update your LinkedIn profile and your headline.
  • Ask two or three people for a short call in early January.

Week 3 (around Christmas): prepare

  • Update your master resume with every result from this year.
  • Write a base cover letter that you can adapt quickly.
  • Build a list of 20 to 30 target companies.
  • Practice your answer to "tell me about yourself" and two or three common questions.

Week 4 (between Christmas and New Year's Day): plan

  • Check which of your target companies posted new roles.
  • Write a job search plan for January: how many applications, how many conversations, and which days.
  • Rest. A short break helps you start January with energy.

Holiday Networking Messages

A holiday message is a good reason to contact someone you have not spoken to in a while. Keep it short, warm, and easy to answer. Do not attach your resume to the first message.

Message to a former colleague

Hi [Name],

I hope you are well and have a good break planned. I was thinking about our time on [project or team] at [Company], and I wanted to say hello.

I am now looking for a [type of role] role in [industry or city]. If you hear of anything, or know someone I should talk to, I would be grateful. Either way, I hope we can catch up in the new year.

Best, [Your Name]

Message to someone at a target company

Hi [Name],

I hope your December is going well. I have followed [Company]'s work on [product, project, or announcement] for some time, and I am interested in roles on the [team name] team.

Would you be open to a 15-minute call in early January? I would like to learn what the team values in new hires.

Thank you, [Your Name]

What to say at a holiday party

When someone asks what you do, give one clear sentence:

I am a [job title] with [number] years in [area], and I am looking for my next role in [type of company or industry]. If you know anyone at [company or type of company], I would love an introduction.

How to Handle Slow Replies

Silence in December usually means people are away. It does not always mean no.

  • Write down the date of each application and each interview.
  • If an interviewer gave you a date, wait two or three working days after it before you follow up.
  • If you had an interview, send a thank you email after the interview within 24 hours, even if the office closes the next day.
  • For applications with no response, wait until the second week of January to follow up.

Here is a short follow-up for an interview process:

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I hope you had a good holiday. I wanted to check in on the [Job Title] role. I am still very interested and happy to share anything else you need.

Best regards, [Your Name]

Get Your Materials Ready for January

January can bring a wave of new postings and new applicants. Use the quiet days of your job search during the holidays to make your materials fast to adapt.

  • Update your master resume with every project and result from the year.
  • Write three or four strong bullets for each role that you can reorder for each job. Our guide to tailor your resume to a job description shows the method.
  • Draft a base cover letter, so each new letter takes minutes instead of an hour. Use the structure in how to write a cover letter.
  • Collect work samples, references, and certificates in one folder.
  • Check that your email address, voicemail, and LinkedIn profile look professional.

Take Care of Yourself

A job search during the holidays can feel lonely when people around you are celebrating. Questions from family about your search can also be hard. Prepare a short, calm answer, such as: "I am looking for a role in [area]. I have some conversations going." Then change the subject if you want to.

Set a small daily goal, such as one application or one message. Small, steady steps are easier to keep during a busy month than big plans. Count the work you control: messages sent, applications finished, materials improved. Replies are not in your control, especially in December.

Holiday Job Search Checklist

  • Applications sent for roles that are open now
  • Interview timelines confirmed before the break
  • Holiday messages sent to 5 to 10 people
  • LinkedIn profile and headline updated
  • Master resume updated with this year's results
  • Base cover letter ready
  • Target company list started
  • January plan written with weekly goals

title: How to Address a Cover Letter (With and Without a Name)
description: How to address a cover letter when you know the name, when you do not, and when the gender or title is unclear. Includes greetings to use and ones to avoid.
keyword: how to address a cover letter

faqs.q: Is "Dear Sir or Madam" acceptable on a cover letter?
faqs.a: It is acceptable in some countries, but in the US it sounds old and assumes a gender. "Dear Hiring Manager" is a better choice when you do not know the name.

faqs.q: Can I address a cover letter to the recruiter?
faqs.a: Yes. If the job post or LinkedIn shows that a recruiter manages the role, address the letter to them. Recruiters often read applications first and pass strong ones to the hiring manager.

faqs.q: Should I use the hiring manager's first name only?
faqs.a: Use the full name or a title with the last name in a formal letter, such as "Dear Ana Torres" or "Dear Ms. Torres". Use the first name only in a short email to a startup or after the person used their first name with you.

faqs.q: What if the job post says not to contact the company?
faqs.a: Do not call or email to ask for the name. Use what you can find on the company website or LinkedIn, or write "Dear Hiring Manager".

headings.text: How to Address a Cover Letter: The Options in Order
How to Find the Hiring Manager's Name
Using Titles: Mr., Ms., Mx., and Dr.
Colon or Comma After the Greeting

html:
Here is how to address a cover letter: use "Dear" and the hiring manager's full name, such as "Dear Ana Torres,". A title and last name, such as "Dear Ms. Torres,", is also correct. If you cannot find a name, address the team, such as "Dear Marketing Hiring Team,", or write "Dear Hiring Manager,". Avoid "To Whom It May Concern" and "Dear Sir or Madam", because they sound old and distant.

How to Address a Cover Letter: The Options in Order

Use the first option that you can. Each one is a little less personal than the one before it.

Order What you know Greeting
1 The hiring manager's name Dear Ana Torres, or Dear Ms. Torres,
2 The recruiter's name Dear Sam Patel,
3 The name of the team or department Dear Customer Success Hiring Team,
4 The job title of the person you report to Dear Head of Engineering,
5 Nothing Dear Hiring Manager,

All five are correct and professional. A name is best because it shows that you did some research. If you spent ten minutes and found nothing, use a general greeting and spend your time on the letter itself.

How to Find the Hiring Manager's Name

Try these places in order. Give the search about 15 minutes, then stop.

  1. Read the whole job post. Some posts name the manager or say "You will report to [Name], our [Title]".
  2. Check the email address in the post. An address such as "ana.torres@company.com" gives you a name.
  3. Search LinkedIn for the company and the team. Use terms such as "[Company] head of marketing" or "[Company] engineering manager".
  4. Look at the company's About or Team page.
  5. Check the recruiter who posted the job on LinkedIn. If you cannot find the manager, the recruiter is a good second choice.
  6. Ask someone you know at the company.
  7. If the post allows it, call the front desk and ask: "Could you tell me who manages the [Team Name] team? I would like to address my application correctly."

If two people could be the manager, pick the one whose title is closest to the role, or use the team greeting instead. A wrong name is worse than no name.

Using Titles: Mr., Ms., Mx., and Dr.

In the US, a full name with no title is now common and safe: "Dear Jordan Lee,". It avoids guessing gender. Use a title when you are sure it is correct.

Title When to use it
Ms. For a woman, when you do not know her marital status. Use Ms., not Miss or Mrs., unless she uses one of those.
Mr. For a man.
Mx. For a person who uses this title. Check their profile or email signature.
Dr. For a person with a doctorate who uses the title at work, for example in medicine, research, or universities.
Professor For a faculty member, when you apply for an academic role.

If a person lists pronouns or a title on LinkedIn or in their email signature, follow what they use.

Colon or Comma After the Greeting

Both are correct. A colon is the most formal choice and is common in traditional business letters. A comma is more common in email and at most companies today. Use the same punctuation in every letter you send to one employer.

  • Formal: "Dear Ms. Torres:"
  • Standard: "Dear Ms. Torres,"
  • Informal email: "Hi Ana,"

Use "Hi" only when the company is informal, or when the person has already written to you in an informal way.

Greetings to Avoid

Greeting Why to avoid it Use instead
To Whom It May Concern Sounds distant and old Dear Hiring Manager,
Dear Sir or Madam Assumes a gender and sounds old in the US Dear Hiring Manager,
Dear Sirs Assumes all readers are men Dear Hiring Team,
Hey there, Too casual for most applications Hi [First Name],
Dear Ana, (first name only, formal letter) Can sound too familiar to a stranger Dear Ana Torres,
Dear Mrs. Torres, (guessing) You may guess wrong Dear Ana Torres,
No greeting at all Looks unfinished Dear Hiring Manager,

Customs differ outside the US. In some countries, "Dear Sir or Madam" is still standard, so check local practice if you apply abroad.

Addressing the Employer Block

When you send a cover letter as a file, put the employer's details above the greeting. Our cover letter format guide shows the full layout.

[Hiring Manager Name] [Hiring Manager Title] [Company] [City, State]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

If you do not know the name, start the block with the company name:

[Company] [City, State]

Dear Hiring Manager,

When you paste the letter into an online form or an email, skip the block and start with the greeting.

Special Cases

Two hiring managers

Name both: "Dear Ms. Torres and Mr. Patel,". Put them in the order the job post uses, or alphabetically.

A whole panel or committee

Use the group name: "Dear Search Committee," or "Dear Members of the Hiring Committee,". This is common for academic and public sector roles.

A referral

If someone referred you, address the letter to the hiring manager, then name your contact in the first sentence:

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

[Referrer Name], who works on your [Team Name] team, suggested that I apply for the [Job Title] role.

A gender-neutral or unfamiliar name

Use the full name with no title: "Dear Taylor Morgan,". This is correct for every reader.

A recruitment agency

Address the letter to the agency recruiter by name. If you know the client company, mention the role and the client in the first line.

Check Before You Send

  • The name is spelled exactly as it appears on LinkedIn or the company site.
  • The title (Ms., Mr., Mx., Dr.) is correct, or you used the full name with no title.
  • The greeting matches the company's tone.
  • The punctuation after the greeting is a comma or a colon, and it is the same in all your letters to this employer.
  • The name in the employer block matches the name in the greeting.
  • You did not copy the greeting from a letter to another company.

Learning how to address a cover letter takes a few minutes, and the greeting is the first line the reader sees. After the greeting, your opening line has to name the job and give a reason to read on. Our step-by-step guide on how to write a cover letter covers that next part.

title: Job Search Plan: A Weekly Template You Can Start Today
description: Build a job search plan in one afternoon: set your target, choose weekly goals, block time on your calendar, and track results with a free weekly template.

faqs.q: How many hours a week should I spend on a job search?
faqs.a: It depends on your situation. If you are not working, many people treat it like a part-time or full-time job. If you are employed, 5 to 10 focused hours a week can be enough when you spend them on targeted applications and conversations.

faqs.q: How many jobs should I apply to each week?
faqs.a: There is no correct number. Choose a number of tailored applications that you can finish well, often 5 to 15 a week, and add networking conversations. Change the number after four weeks if you get no interviews.

faqs.q: Should I tell my current employer that I am looking?
faqs.a: Usually not, until you have an offer. Do your search outside work hours, use your personal email and phone, and do not use company devices.

faqs.q: What should I do if my plan is not working after a month?
faqs.a: Look at where people drop off. No replies usually points to your resume or your targets. Interviews with no offers usually points to interview preparation. Change one thing at a time and measure again.

headings.text: Why You Need a Job Search Plan
Step 2: Build a Target Company List
Step 4: Block Time on Your Calendar
Step 7: Review Every Week and Fix One Thing

html:
A job search plan is a written list of the roles you want, the companies you target, and the weekly actions that get you interviews. Start with a clear target role, then set weekly goals for applications, networking messages, and interview practice. Block fixed time on your calendar for each activity. Track your numbers every Friday, and change one thing when a step is not working.

Why You Need a Job Search Plan

Without a plan, a search turns into random scrolling and applying. You can spend hours and still not know what is working. A plan gives each week a clear finish line. It also gives you data, so you can fix the weak step instead of guessing.

A plan also helps with motivation. Replies are not in your control. Your actions are. When you measure the actions, you can see progress even in a slow week.

Step 1: Define Your Target

Write one or two sentences that describe the job you want. Be specific enough that a friend could forward you a job post.

I am looking for a [job title] role at a [type or size of company] in [industry]. I want to work [remote, hybrid, or in-office in City]. My minimum salary is [amount], and I can start [date or notice period].

If you have two different targets, such as "project manager" and "operations manager", write one sentence for each. Use a separate version of your resume for each target.

Step 2: Build a Target Company List

List 20 to 40 companies where you want to work. Include:

  • Companies whose products or services you know
  • Companies in your industry that are growing
  • Companies where you already know someone
  • Local employers, if you want to work in-office

For each company, note the careers page, one or two contacts, and any open roles. This list keeps you from applying only to whatever appears on job boards that day.

Step 3: Set Weekly Goals

Weekly goals are better than daily goals, because some days are full and some are empty. Choose numbers you can reach with quality work.

Activity Starter weekly goal Why it matters
Tailored applications 5 to 10 Each one has a resume and a letter for that job.
Networking messages 5 to 10 Conversations can lead to referrals and roles that are not posted.
Informational calls 1 to 3 You learn about teams and get known before a role opens.
Follow-ups All that are due A polite follow-up can bring a reply.
Interview practice 1 to 2 hours Practice makes your answers shorter and clearer.
Skill work 1 to 3 hours A course or project can close a gap you see in job posts.

These are starting points, not rules. If you are not working, you may do more. If you work full time, start smaller and stay steady.

Step 4: Block Time on Your Calendar

A goal without a time slot often does not happen. Put each activity on your calendar like a meeting.

Sample week for someone not working

Day Morning (9:00 to 12:00) Afternoon (1:00 to 3:00)
Monday Find roles, update target list 2 tailored applications
Tuesday 2 tailored applications Networking messages
Wednesday Informational call, follow-ups Skill work
Thursday 2 tailored applications Interview practice
Friday Follow-ups, weekly review Free time

Sample week for someone working full time

Day Time Activity
Monday 7:00 to 8:00 pm Find roles and save 3 to 5 posts
Tuesday 7:00 to 8:30 pm 2 tailored applications
Wednesday Lunch break 3 networking messages from your phone
Thursday 7:00 to 8:30 pm 1 or 2 tailored applications
Saturday 9:00 to 11:00 am Interview practice and weekly review

Keep at least one day a week free of job search work. Rest helps you stay consistent for a longer search.

Step 5: Prepare Your Materials Once

Before you start sending applications, prepare the parts you will reuse:

  • A master resume with all your results
  • A base cover letter with your strongest examples
  • A LinkedIn profile that matches your target role
  • A 60 to 90 second answer to "tell me about yourself"
  • A list of three references who have agreed to help

Then adapt them for each job. Our guides on how to tailor your resume to a job description and how to write a cover letter show the steps. Tailoring takes longer than sending the same file everywhere, but a tailored application gives the reader a clear reason to call you.

Step 6: Track Your Numbers

Use a simple spreadsheet. Add one row for each application, with the company, role, date, source, contact, status, and next follow-up date. Then, every Friday, count these numbers:

  • Applications sent
  • Networking messages sent
  • Replies received
  • First interviews
  • Later-stage interviews
  • Offers

Step 7: Review Every Week and Fix One Thing

Each Friday, spend 20 minutes on a review. Use the numbers to find the weak step.

What you see after 3 to 4 weeks Likely cause What to change
Many applications, no replies Resume not tailored, or the target is too senior or too junior Rewrite your summary and top bullets for the target role. Check the level of jobs you apply for.
Replies from recruiters, but few interviews The first screen does not go well Practice your short answers and your salary answer.
Interviews, but no offers Answers lack proof, or weak follow-up Prepare stories with results, and send thank you notes.
Few roles to apply for The target is too narrow Add a close job title, a new city, or remote roles.
Low energy, missed goals Goals are too high Reduce the goals, and keep them steady for two weeks.

Change one thing at a time. If you change everything at once, you will not know what helped.

A One-Page Weekly Template

Copy this job search plan template into a note or document, and fill it in every Monday.

Week of [Date]

Target role: [Job title], [location or remote]

Goals this week:

  • Tailored applications: [number]
  • Networking messages: [number]
  • Informational calls: [number]
  • Interview practice: [hours]

Top 5 companies this week: [Company 1], [Company 2], [Company 3], [Company 4], [Company 5]

Follow-ups due: [Names and dates]

Friday review:

  • What worked: [notes]
  • What did not: [notes]
  • One change for next week: [change]

Plan for a Long Search

Some searches take a few weeks. Others take many months. The length depends on your field, your level, your location, and the economy. Plan your money and your energy for a longer search than you hope for. If you need income, a part-time or contract role can support you while you keep looking. For questions about unemployment benefits, check your state's official labor department website.

Keep your job search plan simple enough that you follow it in a bad week. A small plan that you follow every week is better than a large plan that you drop after ten days.

title: Resume Keywords: How to Find and Use the Right Ones for Each Job
description: Find the resume keywords each job post asks for, choose the ones you can prove, and place them in your summary, skills, and bullets without stuffing.

faqs.q: How many keywords should a resume have?
faqs.a: There is no fixed number. Aim to include most of the 8 to 15 most important terms from the job post, each in a place where you prove it. Quality of placement matters more than the count.

faqs.q: Should I use acronyms or full terms?
faqs.a: Use both the first time, for example "Search Engine Optimization (SEO)". Then use the form the job post uses most. A recruiter may search for either one.

faqs.q: Are soft skills good resume keywords?
faqs.a: They can be, if the job post repeats them. Show them in a bullet with a result, such as "Led weekly calls with 12 client teams", instead of listing "communication" alone.

faqs.q: Do keyword scanning tools tell me if my resume will pass?
faqs.a: They can show which terms from a post are missing. They cannot tell you how a specific employer's system or recruiter will rank you, because each employer sets it up differently.

headings.text: The Main Types of Resume Keywords
How to Find Resume Keywords in a Job Post
Where to Put Keywords on Your Resume
Keyword Stuffing: What Not to Do
Format So Keywords Can Be Read
A Fast Keyword Routine for Each Application

html:
Resume keywords are the specific skills, tools, job titles, and qualifications that an employer lists in a job post. To use them, mark the terms that appear most often or first in the post. Add the ones you really have to your summary, skills, and bullets, in the employer's words. Put each keyword in a sentence that proves it.

Why Resume Keywords Matter

Keywords help two kinds of readers. Many employers use an applicant tracking system (ATS) to store applications. Some of these systems let a recruiter search resumes for terms such as "Salesforce" or "RN license". Some show how well a resume matches a post. How each system works depends on the product and on how the employer sets it up.

The second reader is a person. A recruiter scans a resume quickly to check the main requirements. When your resume uses the same words as the post, the recruiter can see the match without effort.

The Main Types of Resume Keywords

Type Examples Where to find them in a post
Hard skills Financial modeling, Python, inventory control, wound care Requirements and responsibilities
Tools and software Excel, Salesforce, Figma, QuickBooks, Epic Requirements, "nice to have"
Job titles Account Executive, Staff Accountant, Charge Nurse The title, and "experience as a..."
Certifications and licenses PMP, CPA, RN, CDL Class A Requirements
Industry terms B2B SaaS, HIPAA, lean manufacturing About the company, responsibilities
Soft skills Stakeholder management, cross-functional collaboration Responsibilities, "you are..."
Education Bachelor's degree in accounting Requirements

Hard skills, tools, titles, and certifications usually carry the most weight, because they are specific and easy to check. Soft skills matter too, but you must show them with results.

How to Find Resume Keywords in a Job Post

Step 1: Copy the full post

Paste the full job post into a document. Include the title, the summary, the responsibilities, and the requirements.

Step 2: Highlight specific terms

Mark every skill, tool, title, certification, and industry term. Skip general words such as "fast-paced" or "dynamic".

Step 3: Rank the terms

Give more weight to a term when:

  • It appears in the job title
  • It appears more than once
  • It is in the "requirements" list, not the "nice to have" list
  • It appears near the top of the post

Pick the 8 to 15 terms with the most weight. These are your target keywords.

Step 4: Compare two or three similar posts

If you apply for many similar roles, look at three posts for the same title. Terms that appear in all three are core keywords for that role. Put them in your master resume, so each new version starts close to the target.

Step 5: Check your match honestly

For each target keyword, ask: "Can I prove this with something I did?" If yes, use it. If you have a little experience, describe what you did with care. If no, leave it out.

Where to Put Keywords on Your Resume

Use each important keyword in at least one place where you prove it. The best resumes use the top keywords in two or three sections.

Summary

Put your target job title and the two or three top skills in the summary.

[Target Job Title] with [number] years of experience in [industry keyword]. Skilled in [hard skill keyword] and [tool keyword]. Most recently [result that uses a third keyword].

Skills section

List hard skills and tools in a short section. Use the exact names from the post, with the correct spelling and capital letters: "QuickBooks Online", not "Quickbooks".

Bullet points

This is where keywords do the most work, because the bullet shows proof.

Keyword in the post Weak bullet Strong bullet
Stakeholder management "Good with stakeholders." "Ran monthly reviews with finance, sales, and product leads to agree on the launch plan."
Inventory control "Did inventory." "Ran weekly inventory counts for a 4,000-item warehouse and fixed the reorder points."
SQL "SQL" (in skills only) "Wrote SQL queries to build a weekly churn report for the customer team."

Job titles

Keep your real job titles. If your title is unusual, add a common title in parentheses, such as "Customer Champion (Customer Success Manager)". This helps both people and search tools understand your role.

Keyword Stuffing: What Not to Do

Stuffing means adding keywords where they do not belong, to try to beat the software. It usually hurts you when a person reads the resume.

Avoid:

  • Repeating one keyword many times
  • Hiding keywords in white text or tiny font
  • Pasting the job post into your resume
  • Listing skills you do not have
  • A skills section with 40 items and no proof anywhere else

If a recruiter calls you about a skill, they will ask about it. Every keyword on your resume is a topic for the interview.

Format So Keywords Can Be Read

Some systems read complex layouts badly. To make sure your keywords are read:

  • Use a simple one-column layout
  • Use standard section names: Summary, Experience, Skills, Education
  • Do not put text in images, headers, footers, or text boxes
  • Save as a PDF or DOCX, following the employer's instructions
  • Use common fonts

These rules matter more for some systems than for others. A simple format is a safe choice for all of them.

A Fast Keyword Routine for Each Application

  1. Copy the job post.
  2. Highlight specific terms and pick the top 8 to 15.
  3. Check each one against your master resume.
  4. Put the job title and top skills in your summary.
  5. Rewrite your top two or three bullets to use the employer's words.
  6. Update the skills list to match the post's order.
  7. Read the resume once as a person. Remove any sentence that sounds forced.

For the full process of adapting a resume to one job, read how to tailor your resume to a job description. Use the same keywords in your cover letter, in sentences that show results. Add the routine to the weekly hours in your job search plan. With practice, it takes about 15 to 30 minutes per job.

Keyword Checklist

  • The target job title appears in your summary or as a title in your experience
  • The top hard skills appear in the skills section and in at least one bullet
  • Tool names use the exact spelling from the post
  • Acronyms appear once in full
  • Every keyword describes something you can talk about in an interview
  • The layout is simple, and no text is inside images or text boxes
  • The resume still reads naturally to a person

title: How Long Should a Cover Letter Be? Word Count by Situation
description: How long should a cover letter be? See the ideal word count, paragraph count, and page length for each type of application, plus how to cut a long letter.
keyword: how long should a cover letter be

faqs.q: Is a half-page cover letter too short?
faqs.a: Not if it does its job. A half page is about 200 to 250 words. That is enough to name the role, give one or two strong results, and ask for a conversation.

faqs.q: Can a cover letter be two pages?
faqs.a: For most US jobs, no. Keep it to one page. Some academic, research, and senior public sector roles expect longer letters, so follow the instructions in the post.

faqs.q: Does the length limit include the header and sign-off?
faqs.a: Word counts in this guide refer to the body: from the greeting to the sign-off. If a form gives a character limit, it usually counts everything you paste into the box, including spaces.

faqs.q: How long should a cover letter email be?
faqs.a: Shorter than a letter you attach. Aim for 150 to 250 words, because many people read email on a phone. Attach your resume and, if you want, a full cover letter as a PDF.

headings.text: How Long Should a Cover Letter Be for Each Situation?
How to Cut a Long Cover Letter
How to Lengthen a Short Cover Letter

html:
How long should a cover letter be? For most jobs, 250 to 400 words in three or four paragraphs, which fits on less than one page. Go shorter, about 150 to 250 words, for an email or an online form. Go longer only when the employer asks for more detail, as some academic and senior roles do.

How Long Should a Cover Letter Be for Each Situation?

The best length depends on where the letter goes and who reads it.

Situation Word count (body) Paragraphs
Standard application with an uploaded letter 250 to 400 3 to 4
Online form with a text box 150 to 300 3
Cover letter in an email 150 to 250 2 to 3
Entry-level or internship 200 to 300 3
Senior or executive role 300 to 450 4 to 5
Career change 300 to 400 4
Academic or research role Often 1 to 2 pages; follow the post Varies
Internal transfer 150 to 250 2 to 3

If the job post gives a limit, follow it. Some posts ask for "a short note" or "a few sentences about why you want this role". That means 100 to 150 words, not a full letter.

If you draft with CoverBetter, you can choose the length to match the situation. The options are Short (about 200 words), Standard (about 300 words), and Detailed (about 400 words).

Why Shorter Usually Works Better

A hiring manager often reads many applications for one role. A short letter is easier to read in full. Each extra paragraph is one more chance for the reader to stop before your best point.

A short letter also forces you to choose. When you can only include two results, you pick the two that match the job best. That choice is the main skill a good cover letter shows.

Too short is also a problem. A letter of three sentences with no example tells the reader nothing new. The goal is the shortest letter that still gives real proof.

Length of Each Part

Once you know how long a cover letter should be, use this table as a budget when you write.

Part Sentences Words
Greeting 1 line 2 to 5
Opening paragraph 2 to 3 40 to 70
Body paragraph 1 3 to 5 60 to 110
Body paragraph 2 (optional) 2 to 4 50 to 90
Closing paragraph 2 to 3 30 to 60
Sign-off 2 lines 3 to 6

If one part goes over budget, look there first when you cut.

Example: A 250-Word Cover Letter

This example shows how much fits in about 250 words. Replace the items in square brackets.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company]. For [number] years I have [main type of work], and your post's focus on [requirement from the post] matches the work I do best.

At [Current Company], I [action you took] to fix [problem]. Within [time period], [measurable or clear outcome]. I did this by [one or two specific steps], and I worked with [team or partners] to keep it going. Your team wants to [goal from the job post], and I would bring the same approach to that work.

I have also [second relevant result in one or two sentences]. This gives me a practical base for [another part of the new job].

I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help [Company] with [goal]. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

When you fill in the brackets with real details, this template lands between 200 and 280 words. For the full method to write each part, read our guide on how to write a cover letter.

Page Length and Layout

Your cover letter should fit on one page with normal settings: 1-inch margins, a font size of 10.5 to 12 points, and single spacing. If you need smaller margins or a tiny font to fit, the letter is too long. Our cover letter format guide lists the full settings.

A letter of 250 to 400 words on one page leaves white space. White space is good. It makes the letter easy to read.

How to Cut a Long Cover Letter

Most first drafts are too long. Use these steps to cut a draft down to size.

  1. Delete the first sentence if it says "I am writing to apply for...". Start with the second sentence.
  2. Remove any sentence that repeats a line from your resume with no new context.
  3. Keep only the two results that match the job's top requirements. Save the others for the interview.
  4. Cut general claims such as "I am a hard-working team player." Keep claims with proof.
  5. Combine short sentences that say the same thing.
  6. Remove filler phrases: "I believe that", "I feel that", "in order to", "the fact that".
  7. Shorten the close to two sentences.
  8. Read it again. If a paragraph has more than five sentences, split it or cut it.

Before and after

Before After
"I am writing to express my strong interest in the open position of Marketing Coordinator at your company." "I am applying for the Marketing Coordinator role at [Company]."
