"I believe that I would be a great fit for this role due to the fact that I have experience in social media." "I ran social media for a local retailer for two years and grew our email list by running monthly giveaways."
"I would be very grateful if you would consider my application and I look forward to hopefully hearing from you soon." "Thank you for your time. I would welcome a conversation about the role."

How to Lengthen a Short Cover Letter

If your letter is under 150 words for a standard application, it probably lacks proof. Add one of these:

  • One specific result with a number or a clear outcome
  • One sentence on why you want this company, based on something real (a product, a project, a value they state)
  • One sentence that explains a career change or a gap, if your resume raises the question

Do not add length with general praise for the company or a list of soft skills.

Character Limits in Online Forms

In an online form, the answer to how long should a cover letter be often comes from the form itself. Some forms limit the cover letter box to a number of characters, not words. A rough guide is that one word in English averages about five to six characters with the space. So:

Character limit Approximate words
1,000 150 to 180
2,000 300 to 370
3,000 450 to 550

Write in a document first, check the character count, then paste it. If the form cuts your text, the reader sees a letter that stops in the middle of a sentence.

Quick Length Check

  • Body is 250 to 400 words for a standard letter
  • 150 to 250 words for an email or a short form
  • Three or four paragraphs
  • No paragraph over five sentences
  • Fits on one page with 1-inch margins and an 11-point font
  • Every paragraph has a clear job: open, prove, or close

title: STAR Method Interview Guide: Answer Format, Template, Examples
description: Use the STAR method in an interview to answer behavioral questions with a clear story. Get a fill-in template, 4 sample answers, and a story bank to prepare.

faqs.q: How long should a STAR answer be?
faqs.a: Aim for about 1.5 to 2 minutes. Spend most of the time on the Action and the Result. If the interviewer wants more detail, they will ask.

faqs.q: Can I use the same story for more than one question?
faqs.a: Yes, but not in the same interview if you can avoid it. One project can give you several stories if you focus on a different part each time, such as a conflict, a deadline, or a mistake.

faqs.q: What if my story did not have a good result?
faqs.a: You can still use it. Say what happened, then say what you learned and what you did differently next time. Interviewers often ask about failure on purpose.

faqs.q: Can I use a story from school, volunteering, or a part-time job?
faqs.a: Yes, especially early in your career. Choose the story that shows the skill best, and be clear about your role in it.

headings.text: When to Use the STAR Method in an Interview
Build a Story Bank Before the Interview

html:
The STAR method is a way to answer behavioral interview questions with a short story in four parts: Situation, Task, Action, and Result. Describe the situation and task briefly, then spend most of your answer on your actions and the result. Use it for any question that starts with "Tell me about a time..." or "Give me an example of...". A good STAR method interview answer takes about two minutes.

What STAR Stands For

Letter Meaning What to say Share of the answer
S Situation Where you were and what was happening About 15%
T Task What you had to do, or the problem you owned About 10%
A Action The specific steps you took About 50%
R Result What changed, with numbers if you have them, and what you learned About 25%

The Action is the most important part. A common mistake is to spend too long on the Situation and run out of time. The interviewer wants to know what you did, so say "I", not "we", when you describe your own steps.

When to Use the STAR Method in an Interview

Behavioral questions ask about your past, because past behavior shows how you work. Listen for these openings:

  • "Tell me about a time when..."
  • "Give me an example of..."
  • "Describe a situation where..."
  • "What did you do when..."
  • "Have you ever..."

Common topics include conflict with a coworker, a missed deadline, a mistake, and a difficult customer. Others are leading without authority and having too much work.

You do not need STAR for every question. For "Why do you want this job?" or "Tell me about yourself", use a different structure. Our guide on the tell me about yourself interview answer covers that one.

STAR Method Template

Use this template to draft each story. Write it in notes, not as a script.

Situation: At [Company or team], [one or two sentences about the context and the problem].

Task: I was responsible for [your specific goal or duty]. [Optional: the deadline, the stakes, or the limit you had.]

Action: First, I [step 1]. Then I [step 2]. I also [step 3, such as how you worked with others or handled a problem along the way].

Result: As a result, [outcome, with a number or a clear change]. [What you learned, or what the team still uses today.]

STAR Method Examples

Each example below shows the structure. Replace the details with your own true stories.

Example 1: "Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer."

Situation: I worked on the support team for a software company. A long-time customer emailed our CEO because a billing error had charged them twice for three months.

Task: My manager asked me to own the case, fix the billing, and keep the account.

Action: I called the customer the same day, apologized, and told them exactly what I would do and by when. I worked with our finance team to issue the refund within two days. Then I found the cause: a setting in our billing system that affected a small group of accounts. I wrote up the issue and checked the other affected accounts before they noticed.

Result: The customer renewed their contract that quarter. We fixed the setting, and the double charges stopped for every affected account. I still use the same approach: call fast, give a date, and look for the root cause.

Example 2: "Give me an example of a time you missed a deadline."

Situation: In my first year as a marketing coordinator, I was building a product launch email series with a fixed launch date.

Task: I had to write five emails, get approval, and schedule them.

Action: I underestimated the approval time. With two days left, three emails were still in review. I told my manager the same day, suggested we launch with the first two emails, and asked reviewers for a 24-hour turnaround on the rest.

Result: The launch went out on time with two emails, and the rest went out a week later. Since then I build review time into every plan and share a schedule with reviewers on day one.

Example 3: "Describe a time you disagreed with a coworker."

Situation: Our team was choosing a new project tool. A senior colleague wanted to keep our spreadsheets. I thought a project tool would save time.

Task: I needed to make my case without damaging the working relationship.

Action: I asked to meet one to one and listened to her concerns first. Her main worry was training time. I suggested a two-week trial on one small project, and I offered to write a one-page guide for the team.

Result: After the trial, she agreed to switch, and she suggested two changes that made the setup better. We now work well together, and she often reviews my plans.

Example 4: "Tell me about a time you took initiative."

Situation: At the clinic where I worked, new front-desk staff took a long time to learn our booking system.

Task: Nobody owned training. I decided to fix it, with my manager's approval.

Action: I wrote down the 15 most common booking tasks, made a short guide with screenshots, and recorded three short videos. I asked two new hires to test the guide and changed it based on their feedback.

Result: New staff now learn the system in their first week. My manager added the guide to our onboarding checklist.

Build a Story Bank Before the Interview

You cannot predict every question, but you can prepare stories that fit many of them. A story bank is a list of 6 to 10 short stories from your work.

  1. Read the job post. List the skills it asks for.
  2. For each skill, write down one story from your work that shows it.
  3. Write each story in STAR notes, not full sentences.
  4. Mark which questions each story can answer.
  5. Practice each story aloud until it takes about two minutes.
Story Skills it shows Questions it can answer
[Billing error customer] Customer care, problem solving Difficult customer, a time you fixed a problem, pressure
[Missed email deadline] Ownership, planning Mistake, missed deadline, what you learned
[Project tool trial] Influence, teamwork Disagreement, change, persuading others
[Onboarding guide] Initiative, training Initiative, improving a process, helping others

Use the results from your story bank in other places too. The best ones belong on your resume as bullets and in your cover letter.

Common STAR Method Interview Mistakes

  • A long Situation. Keep it to two sentences.
  • Saying "we" for everything. The interviewer needs to know your part.
  • No result. Always finish the story, even if the result was mixed.
  • An invented or exaggerated story. Follow-up questions often expose it.
  • A story with no link to the job. Choose stories that match the skills in the post.
  • Choosing a "weakness" story where the real problem is serious misconduct. Pick a real, fixable mistake.
  • Reading a script. Know the points, then speak naturally.

After the Interview

Write down which questions you were asked and which stories you used. That helps you prepare for the next round and keeps you from repeating a story to the same team. If a story made the interviewer react, mention it in one sentence in your thank you email after the interview.

title: Job Application Tracker: Free Template and How to Use It
description: Set up a job application tracker in 15 minutes: the columns to include, status stages, a weekly routine, and follow-up rules. Copy the free template.

faqs.q: What is the best app to track job applications?
faqs.a: The best tracker is the one you will update every day. A spreadsheet in Google Sheets or Excel works for most people. Notion, Trello, and job search apps add boards and reminders if you prefer them.

faqs.q: How long should I keep records of my job applications?
faqs.a: Keep them until you start a new job, and then for a few months after. If you claim unemployment benefits, your state may ask you to keep a record of your job search for a set time. Check your state's rules.

faqs.q: Should I track jobs I saved but did not apply to?
faqs.a: Yes, with a status such as "Saved". It stops you from losing a good post and shows you which roles you keep putting off.

faqs.q: When should I mark an application as closed?
faqs.a: Mark it closed when you get a rejection, when the post is removed, or about four to six weeks after your last follow-up with no reply. You can still reopen it if they contact you.

headings.text: Why Use a Job Application Tracker
A Free Job Application Tracker Template
Follow-Up Rules to Put in Your Tracker
Use the Tracker to Improve Your Search

html:
A job application tracker is a simple list, usually a spreadsheet, where you record every job you apply for. Each row has the company, role, date, status, contact, and next step, and you update it the same day something changes. A tracker stops you from missing follow-ups and shows which parts of your search work. You can set one up in about 15 minutes.

Why Use a Job Application Tracker

After a few weeks of applying, it is hard to remember every role. A recruiter calls, and you cannot remember the job post. You apply twice to the same company. You forget to follow up after an interview. A tracker fixes all of these problems.

It also gives you data. When you can see how many applications led to replies, you can tell if the problem is your resume, your targets, or your interviews. That turns a stressful search into a set of small, clear tasks.

The Columns to Include

Start with the columns in the first table. Add the optional columns only if you will use them.

Core columns

Column What to enter Example
Company The employer's name [Company]
Role The exact job title from the post Operations Coordinator
Link The URL of the job post [URL]
Date applied The day you submitted 2027-02-01
Source Where you found it Company site, LinkedIn, referral
Status The current stage (see below) Applied
Contact Recruiter or hiring manager name and email [Name], [Email]
Next step What you will do next Follow up
Next step date When you will do it 2027-02-11
Notes Anything useful Referred by [Name]; asks for SQL

Optional columns

  • Salary range from the post
  • Location and work type (remote, hybrid, in-office)
  • Resume version and cover letter file name
  • Interview dates and interviewer names
  • Priority (high, medium, low)
  • Date closed and reason

Save a copy of each job post as a PDF or in a document, and note where you saved it. Employers often remove posts when the role closes, sometimes before your interview.

Status Stages

Use a short, fixed list of statuses. A drop-down menu in your spreadsheet keeps the words the same, which makes counting easy.

Status Meaning
Saved You found the role and plan to apply.
Applied You submitted the application.
Followed up You sent a follow-up and are waiting.
Screen You have a recruiter or phone screen scheduled or done.
Interview You are in interviews with the team.
Final You are in the final round.
Offer You received an offer.
Accepted You accepted an offer.
Rejected The employer said no.
Withdrawn You took yourself out of the process.
Closed No reply after your follow-ups, or the post was removed.

A Free Job Application Tracker Template

Copy this header row into the first row of a new spreadsheet. Then add one row for each job.

Company | Role | Link | Date applied | Source | Status | Contact | Next step | Next step date | Resume version | Cover letter file | Notes

Here is an example row, with placeholders:

[Company] | [Job Title] | [URL] | [Date] | [Source] | Applied | [Recruiter Name], [Email] | Follow up | [Date + 7 to 10 days] | [Resume file name] | [Cover letter file name] | [Key requirements from the post]

Useful spreadsheet settings

  • Freeze the first row so the headers stay visible.
  • Add a drop-down list to the Status column.
  • Use conditional formatting to color rows with a next step date of today or earlier.
  • Sort by next step date each morning.
  • Add a second tab for networking contacts, with name, company, date of last contact, and next step.

Spreadsheet, Board, or App?

Option Good for Limits
Spreadsheet (Google Sheets, Excel) Full control, easy counting, free No reminders unless you set them up
Board (Trello, Notion) Seeing stages as columns, dragging cards Harder to count and filter
Job search app Reminders, saving posts from your browser Your data sits in one product; features vary
Paper notebook People who think better on paper Hard to search and sort

Pick one and keep all applications in it. Two trackers lead to gaps.

A Daily and Weekly Routine

Every day (5 minutes)

  1. Add every application you sent today.
  2. Update the status of anything that changed.
  3. Check the rows where the next step date is today, and do those steps.

Every week (20 minutes)

  1. Count applications, replies, screens, interviews, and offers for the week.
  2. Mark old applications as Closed if you have followed up and heard nothing.
  3. Look for patterns. Which sources lead to replies? Which roles lead to interviews?
  4. Set the goals for next week in your job search plan.

Follow-Up Rules to Put in Your Tracker

Set the next step date at the moment you add a row. These are common time frames, but every company is different, and a date given by the employer always wins.

After this Follow up after
Applying online with no contact 7 to 10 business days, if you can find a contact
Applying through a referral 5 to 7 business days, through the referrer or the recruiter
A phone screen 5 business days, or the day after the date they gave you
An interview Send a thank you email within 24 hours, then follow up after the date they gave
A final round 2 to 3 business days after the date they gave

Our guide to the thank you email after an interview has templates for the step after each interview.

A short follow-up for an application:

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I applied for the [Job Title] role on [Date] and wanted to confirm that my application arrived. I am very interested in [specific part of the role], and I would be glad to share more about my experience with [relevant skill].

Best regards, [Your Name]

Use the Tracker to Improve Your Search

After three or four weeks, your job application tracker can answer these questions:

  • Which sources lead to the most replies? Spend more time there.
  • Which job titles lead to interviews? Focus on those.
  • Which resume version gets more replies? Use it as your new base.
  • How long does each company take to reply? Use this to set realistic follow-up dates.

If many applications get no reply, look at how you tailor your resume to the job description and check that your targets match your level.

Before a Recruiter Calls

When a company calls you, open the row first. Read the saved job post, your notes, and the resume version you sent. Then you can talk about the exact role and the results you used to apply for it.

title: Cover Letter Opening Lines: 25 Examples and a Formula
description: Write cover letter opening lines that make the reader keep going. Get a simple formula, 25 examples by situation, and openers to avoid.

faqs.q: Should my first sentence say which job I am applying for?
faqs.a: Yes, in the first or second sentence. The reader may be hiring for several roles. Name the exact job title so they do not have to search for it.

faqs.q: Is it OK to start a cover letter with a question?
faqs.a: It is risky. A question such as "Are you looking for a hard-working marketer?" sounds like an advertisement. A direct statement with a result usually works better.

faqs.q: Can I start with a quote?
faqs.a: Avoid it. A famous quote uses the reader's first seconds on someone else's words. Start with your own result or your link to the company.

faqs.q: How formal should my opening be?
faqs.a: Match the company. A law firm or a bank expects a formal opening. A small startup accepts a more relaxed one. In both cases, be clear and specific.

headings.text: A Formula for Cover Letter Opening Lines
25 Cover Letter Opening Lines by Situation
Where the Opening Fits in the Letter

html:
Good cover letter opening lines name the job you want and give the reader one specific reason to keep reading, in one or two sentences. The strongest openings start with a relevant result, a real connection to the company, or a referral. Avoid "I am writing to apply for..." on its own, because it tells the reader nothing new. Write a new opening for each job, because it is the part the reader is most likely to read.

Why the Opening Matters

A hiring manager often reads many letters for one role. The first lines decide how carefully they read the rest. An opening that sounds like every other letter gives them a reason to skim. An opening with a real detail gives them a reason to slow down.

The opening also sets your tone. A clear, specific first sentence shows that you can write clearly at work.

A Formula for Cover Letter Opening Lines

Use this formula for almost any job:

[Hook: a result, a connection, or a referral] + [the exact job title and company] + [why you fit, in a few words]

Fill-in version:

[Result or connection that matches the job]. That is why I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company], where I can [what you would do for them].

You can change the order. Some people prefer to name the role first, then add the hook. Both work if the hook is specific.

You may start from a draft, for example one that CoverBetter writes from your resume and the job post. Rewrite its opening line with your own strongest result. That line deserves the most care.

25 Cover Letter Opening Lines by Situation

Each example below uses square brackets for details that you replace. Do not copy any line exactly. Use the structure and add your own facts.

Start with a result

  1. "Last year I cut our customer response time from two days to four hours. I want to bring that focus on speed to the Support Lead role at [Company]."
  2. "In three years as a sales rep, I grew my territory from [number] to [number] accounts. I am applying for the Account Executive role at [Company] to do the same for your [region] team."
  3. "I built the scheduling system that my clinic still uses for 30 staff. I would like to do that kind of work as an Operations Coordinator at [Company]."
  4. "My last campaign brought [number] new sign-ups in one month with a budget of [amount]. I am applying for the Growth Marketing role at [Company] because your post asks for exactly this kind of work."
  5. "I have closed every month-end on time for [number] years in a row. I am applying for the Senior Accountant role at [Company]."

Start with a connection to the company

  1. "I have used [Product] every day for two years to plan my team's work, and I want to help build it as a Product Designer."
  2. "Your team's recent launch of [project] solves a problem I have worked on for years: [problem]. I am applying for the [Job Title] role to help with the next phase."
  3. "I first heard about [Company] when your team [specific public action]. Since then I have followed your work, and the [Job Title] role is the first one that matches my skills."
  4. "As a long-time customer of [Company], I know how much your support team affects the experience. I am applying for the Customer Success Manager role."

Start with a referral

  1. "[Referrer Name] on your [Team Name] team suggested that I apply for the [Job Title] role. We worked together at [Company], where I [short result]."
  2. "When I told [Referrer Name] about my work in [area], she said your team needed someone with that background. I am applying for the [Job Title] role."
  3. "I met [Name] at [event], and our conversation about [topic] led me to this [Job Title] opening."

Start with your expertise

  1. "I am a registered nurse with six years in emergency care, and I am applying for the Charge Nurse role at [Hospital]."
  2. "I am a data analyst who turns messy sales data into weekly reports that managers use. I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company]."
  3. "For [number] years I have managed warehouse teams of up to [number] people. I am applying for the Warehouse Manager role at [Company]."
  4. "I write technical documentation that engineers actually read. That is the skill your Technical Writer post asks for."

Career change

  1. "After eight years of teaching, I am moving into corporate training, and the Learning Specialist role at [Company] fits the skills I use every day."
  2. "I have spent five years in hospitality solving guest problems in real time. I am now applying those skills to the Customer Success role at [Company]."
  3. "My background in nursing gives me a patient's view of health software. That is why I am applying for the Clinical Product Specialist role at [Company]."

Entry-level or recent graduate

  1. "I just finished my degree in [field], where my final project was [short description]. I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company] to use those skills full time."
  2. "During my internship at [Company], I [short result]. I want to continue that work as a [Job Title] on your team."
  3. "I have worked part time in retail through college, and I learned how to handle busy days and difficult customers. I am applying for the Store Supervisor role."

Returning to work or internal move

  1. "After two years away from work for family reasons, I am ready to return to project management. The [Job Title] role at [Company] matches my experience."
  2. "I have been on the [Team Name] team for three years. I am applying for the [Job Title] role so I can help the team in a bigger way."
  3. "I am applying for the [Job Title] role because it combines the two parts of my job I enjoy most: [task 1] and [task 2]."

A Full Opening Paragraph Example

The opening line is one or two sentences. The full opening paragraph adds one more sentence that leads into your proof.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Last year I cut our customer response time from two days to four hours by changing how our team sorted incoming tickets. I am applying for the Support Lead role at [Company] because your post asks for someone who can build simple, fast support processes. I would bring the same approach to your growing team.

If you are not sure what goes above that paragraph, read how to address a cover letter.

Openings to Avoid

Weak opening Why it is weak Better approach
"To Whom It May Concern, I am writing to apply for..." Distant greeting and no new information Use a name, then start with a result
"My name is [Name] and I am applying for..." Your name is already at the top Start with the job or a result
"I am the perfect candidate for this job." A claim with no proof Give the proof and let them decide
"I have always dreamed of working at [Company]." Hard to believe without a reason Name the real reason you like the company
"Are you looking for a passionate team player?" Sounds like an advertisement Make a direct statement
"Although I do not have all the qualifications..." Starts with a weakness Start with what you can do
"I saw your job post on [job board]." Only useful if a person referred you Name the role and give a hook

How to Test Your Opening

Read your cover letter opening lines and ask:

  • Does it name the job title?
  • Does it include one specific fact: a number, a project, a product, or a name?
  • Could someone else send the same sentence to another company? If yes, rewrite it.
  • Does it connect to a need in the job post?
  • Is it short enough to read in one breath?

Where the Opening Fits in the Letter

The opening is only the start. After it, you need one or two paragraphs of proof and a short close. Our step-by-step guide on how to write a cover letter covers each part. For the right total length, see how long should a cover letter be.

title: What Is an Applicant Tracking System? How ATS Reads Your Resume
description: Learn what an applicant tracking system does with your application and what it does not do. Then format a resume that it can read without errors.

faqs.q: Can an applicant tracking system read a PDF resume?
faqs.a: Most modern systems can read a text-based PDF. A PDF made from a scanned image or a design tool can fail. If the job post asks for DOCX, send DOCX.

faqs.q: How do I know which ATS a company uses?
faqs.a: Look at the web address of the application page. It often contains the name of the system, for example a Workday, Greenhouse, or Lever domain.

faqs.q: Does an ATS reject resumes automatically?
faqs.a: Some employers set knockout questions, such as work authorization or a required license, that can screen out an application. Many other decisions are made by a person who reads or searches the applications.

faqs.q: Should I put white text with keywords on my resume?
faqs.a: No. The system often shows the parsed text to the recruiter, so hidden words become visible. It looks like a trick and can end your chance at that company.

headings.text: What an Applicant Tracking System Does
What an ATS Usually Does Not Do
How to Write a Resume for an Applicant Tracking System
A Quick ATS Checklist Before You Apply
What to Do After You Apply

html:
An applicant tracking system (ATS) is software that employers use to collect, store, and sort job applications. When you apply online, the system reads your resume and pulls out details such as your name, job titles, and skills. Then it puts your application in a list for the recruiter. A person usually decides who moves forward, but the ATS controls what that person sees and how they search.

This guide explains what an applicant tracking system does, what it does not do, and how to prepare a resume that it can read correctly.

What an Applicant Tracking System Does

Think of an ATS as a database with a front door. The front door is the application form on the company's careers page. The database is where your resume, your answers, and your status live.

Most systems do some or all of these tasks:

  • Post the job to the company careers page and to job boards.
  • Collect resumes, cover letters, and answers to application questions.
  • Parse the resume, which means it copies the text into fields such as "Work experience" and "Education".
  • Let recruiters search all applicants by keyword, job title, location, or other filters.
  • Track each applicant through stages, such as "Applied", "Phone screen", "Interview", and "Offer".
  • Send emails, such as the automatic confirmation you get after you apply.
  • Keep records that the employer may need for reporting.

Common names include Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, iCIMS, SmartRecruiters, and Taleo. Small companies sometimes use the hiring tools inside their payroll or HR software. The features and the settings differ from one system to the next, and from one employer to the next.

What an ATS Usually Does Not Do

You may have read that a robot rejects most resumes before a human sees them. Be careful with that idea. The behavior depends on how each employer sets up its system.

Here is what is commonly true:

  • A recruiter often searches or filters the applicant list. If your resume does not contain the words they search for, you may not appear in the results.
  • Some employers add knockout questions. For example, "Are you authorized to work in the US?" or "Do you have a current RN license?" A "no" can move the application out of the main list.
  • Some systems give each applicant a match score. Recruiters can choose to use it or ignore it.
  • Many recruiters read applications in the order they arrive, or they sort by date.

So the main risk is not a secret robot. The main risks are a resume that the system parses badly, and a resume that does not use the words of the job.

How ATS Parsing Works

When you upload a resume, the system tries to find the parts. It looks for headings it knows, such as "Experience", "Education", and "Skills". It looks for dates next to job titles. It reads the text from top to bottom and left to right.

Parsing errors happen when the layout confuses that reading order. After a bad parse, the recruiter may see your job titles in the wrong place, or your dates in the skills field. Some application forms then ask you to fix the fields by hand. That takes your time and is a warning sign that the file is hard to read.

Formatting that parses well

Usually safe Often causes problems
One column Two or three columns
Standard headings ("Experience", "Education", "Skills") Creative headings ("Where I've Been")
Text in the body of the document Text in headers, footers, or text boxes
Common fonts, such as Arial, Calibri, or Georgia Icons, charts, and skill bars
Dates in one format, such as "Mar 2023 to Present" Dates in several formats
DOCX or a text-based PDF Scanned PDFs and image files

A two-column resume can parse correctly in some systems. But you do not know which system a company uses until you apply. A simple one-column layout removes that risk.

Test your resume in 2 minutes

  1. Open your PDF and select all the text. Copy it.
  2. Paste it into a plain text editor.
  3. Read the result from top to bottom.
  4. Check that each job title, company, and date appears in the correct order.
  5. Fix anything that is missing, mixed up, or shown as strange symbols.

If the text comes out clean, most systems can read it. If it comes out mixed up, change the layout before you apply.

How to Write a Resume for an Applicant Tracking System

A resume that works well in an ATS is also a resume that works well for a person. The goal is clear text and the right words.

Use the words from the job post

Recruiters search with the words they know. Those words are usually in the job post. If the post says "project management" and your resume says "ran projects", a search can miss you.

Read the post and mark the skills, tools, and titles that appear more than once. Then use the same terms in your resume where they are true for you. The guide on resume keywords shows how to find and place them.

Match your title where it is honest

If the job is "Customer Success Manager" and your title was "Client Relations Lead", you can add a short line under your title. For example: "Client Relations Lead (customer success, 40 accounts)". Do not change your real title. A background check can show the real one.

Spell out acronyms once

Write "search engine optimization (SEO)" the first time. A recruiter may search for either form.

Keep skills in plain text

Put a skills section near the top or bottom with simple comma-separated items. Do not use a chart or a star rating. A system cannot read a bar that shows "80% Excel".

Tailor each application

One resume for every job rarely matches the search terms of each post. Change your summary, your skills, and the order of your bullets for each job. The steps are in how to tailor your resume to a job description.

The Application Form Matters Too

Many people focus on the resume and rush the form. In many systems, the form answers go into fields that recruiters filter on.

  • Answer every required question with care, especially work authorization, location, and years of experience.
  • If a field asks for salary, read the guidance from your local rules and the post. Some US states require employers to show a pay range in the job post.
  • Upload a cover letter if there is a field for it. Some recruiters read it, and it gives you one more place to use the words of the job.
  • Check the confirmation email. Save it, and record the date you applied.

A Quick ATS Checklist Before You Apply

  • One-column layout with standard headings.
  • No important text in headers, footers, tables, or text boxes.
  • File type that the post asks for, or DOCX or a text-based PDF.
  • File name with your name, such as "Jordan-Lee-Resume.pdf".
  • Skills and tools from the job post, used where they are true.
  • Acronyms spelled out once.
  • Dates in one format.
  • Copy-and-paste test passed.
  • All form questions answered and checked.

What to Do After You Apply

The ATS changes your status as the recruiter moves you through the process. Some systems send an email at each step. Many do not. A quiet application does not always mean a rejection, because some teams review in batches.

Keep your own record of each job, the date, the contact, and the next step. A simple sheet works well, and the guide on a job application tracker gives you a template. Your own record is the only one you control.

title: Follow Up Email After Interview: When to Send It and 5 Templates
description: Know when to send a follow up email after an interview, what to write, and how often. Copy 5 templates for each stage, from first check-in to final note.

faqs.q: Is it OK to follow up after an interview by phone?
faqs.a: Email is the safer default because the recruiter can answer when they have time. Call only if the recruiter gave you a phone number and said calls are fine.

faqs.q: Should I follow up with the hiring manager or the recruiter?
faqs.a: Follow up with the person who manages your process, which is usually the recruiter or coordinator. Write to the hiring manager only if they were your main contact.

faqs.q: What if the recruiter said they would get back to me by a date that has passed?
faqs.a: Wait one or two business days after that date, then send a short check-in. Delays are common and are often caused by schedules, not by a decision about you.

faqs.q: Can a follow up email hurt my chances?
faqs.a: A short, polite email rarely hurts. Too many emails in a short time, or a tone that sounds impatient, can.

headings.text: When to Send a Follow Up Email After an Interview
What to Put in the Email
How Many Times Should You Follow Up?

html:
A follow up email after an interview is a short message. You send it when you have not heard back by the date the employer gave you. Send it one or two business days after that date, or about one week after the interview if they gave no date. Keep it to three or four sentences: thank them, restate your interest, and ask about the timeline.

The follow up email is different from the thank-you email. You send the thank-you within 24 hours of the interview. If you have not sent one yet, start with the guide on the thank you email after an interview. This post covers what to do after that, while you wait.

When to Send a Follow Up Email After an Interview

Timing is the most common question. Use the information the employer gave you.

Situation When to send your first follow-up
They gave you a date ("by Friday") 1 to 2 business days after that date
They gave a range ("in two weeks") The day after the range ends
They gave no timeline About 5 to 7 business days after the interview
You have another offer with a deadline Now, with a clear and polite note about the deadline
They asked you for something (references, a work sample) Send it within 1 business day, then wait for their date

At the end of each interview, ask: "What are the next steps, and when can I expect to hear back?" The answer gives you a fair date for your follow-up. It also saves you from guessing.

What to Put in the Email

A good follow-up has four parts. Each part is one or two sentences.

  1. A clear subject line with the job title.
  2. A thank-you and a reminder of who you are and when you met.
  3. One line that shows you still want the job.
  4. A direct, polite question about the timeline or next steps.

Do not repeat your whole interview. Do not list everything you forgot to say. The recruiter needs to see your name, the job, and your question in a few seconds.

Subject lines that work

  • "Following up: [Job Title] interview on [Date]"
  • "[Your Name], [Job Title] interview follow-up"
  • "Checking in on [Job Title] next steps"

5 Follow Up Email Templates

Change the words in brackets. Then read the email aloud once before you send it.

1. First follow-up after the expected date

Subject: Following up: [Job Title] interview on [Date]

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I hope your week is going well. I interviewed for the [Job Title] role with [Interviewer Name] on [Date], and I am still very interested in joining [Company].

You mentioned that the team planned to decide by [Date]. Is there an update on the timeline, or anything else I can send you?

Thank you, [Your Name] [Phone Number]

2. Follow-up when they gave no timeline

Subject: [Your Name], [Job Title] interview follow-up

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you again for the time on [Date] to talk about the [Job Title] role. I enjoyed learning about [specific project or goal from the interview], and the role is a strong fit for my experience in [your skill].

Could you share what the next steps are and when I might hear back?

Best regards, [Your Name]

3. Second follow-up after no reply

Send this about one week after the first follow-up.

Subject: Checking in on [Job Title] next steps

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I wanted to check in once more about the [Job Title] position. I know hiring decisions can take time, and I am still interested in the role.

If there is any news on the timeline, I would be glad to hear it.

Thank you, [Your Name]

4. Follow-up when you have another offer

Be honest and calm. Do not use the offer as a threat.

Subject: Timeline question: [Job Title] at [Company]

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you again for the interviews for the [Job Title] role. [Company] is my first choice, and I want to keep you informed.

I have received another offer, and I need to give an answer by [Date]. Is it possible to learn where I stand in your process before then?

I understand if the timeline cannot change. Thank you for your help.

Best, [Your Name]

5. Final follow-up

Use this when you have sent two follow-ups and heard nothing. It closes the loop in a friendly way.

Subject: [Job Title] at [Company]

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I have not heard back about the [Job Title] role, so I will assume the team has moved forward with other candidates. Thank you for your time and for the chance to meet [Interviewer Name].

If anything changes, or if a similar role opens, I would be glad to talk again.

Best regards, [Your Name]

How Many Times Should You Follow Up?

Two or three emails in total is a reasonable limit after one interview round. Space them about one week apart. After the final note, stop writing and put your energy into other applications.

Some companies never send a rejection. That is frustrating, but it is common. Silence after three polite emails is an answer, even if it is not a clear one.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Writing the day after the interview to ask for a decision.
  • Sending the same email to several people at the company on the same day.
  • Adding a long list of new reasons why you are the best person for the job.
  • A tone that blames the company for the delay ("I still have not heard anything").
  • Following up on LinkedIn and by email and by phone in the same week.
  • Forgetting the job title. Recruiters often hire for many roles at once.

Add Value When You Can

A follow-up is stronger when it gives the reader something useful. You do not need it every time, but it helps when it is natural.

  • A short link to a work sample you mentioned in the interview.
  • An answer to a question you did not answer well, in two or three sentences.
  • A relevant certificate or result you completed since the interview.

Keep the addition to one or two sentences. Then ask your timeline question.

Keep Track of Each Follow-Up

When you interview with several companies, the dates mix together fast. Write down the interview date, the person's name, the date they gave you, and each follow-up you send. A simple sheet is enough. The guide on how to build a job application tracker has columns you can copy.

Set a reminder for the date of your next follow-up. Then stop checking your inbox every hour. The email you send is short, but the process behind it can take weeks, and other applications need your time while you wait.

title: How to End a Cover Letter: Closing Lines, Sign-Offs, and Examples
description: Learn how to end a cover letter with a strong last paragraph, the right sign-off, and a clean signature. Includes example closing lines and a template.
keyword: how to end a cover letter

faqs.q: Should I say "I look forward to hearing from you" in a cover letter?
faqs.a: You can, and it is polite. It is also very common, so add one specific sentence before it that gives the reader a reason to call you.

faqs.q: Is "Best" too casual to end a cover letter?
faqs.a: "Best" alone is fine for an email application in many industries. In a formal letter, or a conservative field such as law or finance, "Best regards" or "Sincerely" is safer.

faqs.q: Do I need a handwritten signature on a cover letter?
faqs.a: No. For an online application, your typed name is enough. Add a scanned signature only if the employer asks for a signed letter.

faqs.q: Should I mention salary in the closing paragraph?
faqs.a: No, unless the job post asks you to include your salary requirements. If it does, give a range in one sentence and keep the rest of the close about the job.

headings.text: The Three Parts of a Strong Close
How to End a Cover Letter: Step by Step
Mistakes to Avoid at the End
Make the Ending Match the Opening

html:
To end a cover letter, write a short final paragraph that restates your fit in one sentence, asks for an interview, and thanks the reader. Then add a professional sign-off, such as "Sincerely" or "Best regards", and your full name. Keep the whole close to three or four sentences, and make the call to action clear.

The end of the letter is the part the hiring manager reads last, so it shapes what they remember. This guide gives you a structure, example closing lines, sign-offs to use and avoid, and a full template.

The Three Parts of a Strong Close

A good cover letter ending has three parts. Each is one or two sentences.

  1. A summary of your value. Connect your strongest skill to the main need of the job.
  2. A call to action. Say that you want to talk, and make it easy to reply.
  3. A thank-you. Thank the reader for their time.

After that comes the sign-off, then your name and contact details. The guide on cover letter format shows where each part goes on the page.

How to End a Cover Letter: Step by Step

Step 1: Restate your fit in one sentence

Do not repeat your whole letter. Pick the one skill or result that matters most for this job.

Weak: "I believe I would be a great fit for this role."

Better: "My five years running payroll for multi-state teams match the growth plans you described for [Company]."

The better line names a real skill and a real need. The reader can see the link without guessing.

Step 2: Ask for the next step

Say what you want: a conversation or an interview. You do not need to be pushy. You do need to be direct.

  • "I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help your team reach [goal]."
  • "Could we set up a call to talk about the [Job Title] role?"
  • "I am available for an interview at your convenience and can start [timeframe]."

Step 3: Thank the reader

One short sentence is enough. "Thank you for your time and consideration." works well. You can also make it specific: "Thank you for reading my application."

Step 4: Choose a sign-off

Pick a sign-off that fits the industry and the tone of your letter. Put a comma after it, then your full name on the next line.

Step 5: Add your contact details

If your contact details are not already in the header, add your phone number and email under your name. Add a LinkedIn or portfolio link if it helps the reader.

Example Closing Paragraphs

Change the bracketed parts so each line is about the real job.

Confident tone:

I have built the kind of [skill or system] that [Company] needs to [goal from the job post]. I would like to talk about how I can do the same for your team. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Friendly tone:

I would love to bring my experience in [skill] to the team at [Company], and I would be glad to share more in a conversation. Thank you for reading my application.

Career change:

My background in [old field] gives me a different view of [new field problem], and I am ready to apply it to the [Job Title] role. I would welcome the chance to explain how my skills transfer. Thank you for your consideration.

Entry level:

I am eager to learn from your team and contribute to [specific project or goal] from my first week. I would be grateful for the chance to interview. Thank you for your time.

Referral:

[Referrer Name] said that your team values [quality], and I would be glad to show you how I work. I am available to talk any time next week. Thank you for considering my application.

Sign-Offs: Which to Use

Sign-off When it fits
Sincerely Formal letters, conservative industries, any time you are unsure
Best regards Most professional settings, email and letter
Kind regards Professional and a little warmer; common in many countries
Respectfully Government, military, and very formal settings
Thank you Works well when your last sentence is not already a thank-you
Best Email applications in casual industries

Avoid these in a cover letter:

  • "Cheers", "Thanks!", or "Talk soon". They are too casual for most first contacts.
  • "Love" or "Warmly". They are too personal.
  • "Yours truly". It is not wrong, but it sounds old to many US readers.
  • No sign-off at all. The letter looks unfinished.

Conventions differ by country. In the UK, for example, many people use "Yours sincerely" when they know the name and "Yours faithfully" when they do not.

Full Cover Letter Ending Template

Copy this block and replace the brackets.

[One sentence that connects your top skill or result to the company's main need.] I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help [Company] [goal from the job post]. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

[Your Full Name] [Phone Number] | [Email Address] [LinkedIn or Portfolio URL]

Mistakes to Avoid at the End

  • Ending with a question about pay, benefits, or vacation.
  • Writing "I will call you next week to set up an interview." It can sound like pressure.
  • Apologizing for gaps or lack of experience in the last line. Address a gap earlier, once, and end on a strength.
  • Using "Hope to hear from you soon!" with an exclamation mark.
  • Repeating the first paragraph word for word.
  • Leaving a name or job title from another letter in the close. Check this every time.

Make the Ending Match the Opening

The best letters feel like one argument from start to end. If your first line is about a specific result, your last line can return to it. For example, open with how you cut onboarding time at your last job, and close by offering to do the same at the new company. The guide on cover letter opening lines has openers that pair well with the closes above.

Keep the length in check too. A close of three or four sentences fits the usual one-page letter. If your letter runs long, cut from the middle, not from the close. The guide on how long a cover letter should be explains the usual limits.

If you want a starting point, CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post. Then you edit the close to sound like you.

Final Check

Read the last paragraph alone. Ask yourself three questions:

  • Does it name a real skill and a real need of this company?
  • Does it ask for a conversation in a clear way?
  • Is the sign-off right for this industry, with your full name under it?

If the answer to each is yes, your cover letter ends well.

title: LinkedIn Headline Examples: 40 Headlines for Job Seekers by Role
description: Copy LinkedIn headline examples for job seekers, career changers, students, and 28 common roles, plus a simple formula to write your own headline today.

faqs.q: How long can a LinkedIn headline be?
faqs.a: LinkedIn allows up to 220 characters in the headline. Fewer words often show in search results and comments, so put the most important words first.

faqs.q: Should I write "Open to Work" or "Seeking opportunities" in my headline?
faqs.a: You can, but it uses space that could name your skills. LinkedIn has a separate Open to Work setting that you can show to everyone or only to recruiters.

faqs.q: Should my LinkedIn headline match my resume?
faqs.a: It should use the same job title and core skills, so a recruiter sees one clear story. The headline can be shorter and can name the role you want next.

faqs.q: How often should I change my LinkedIn headline?
faqs.a: Change it when your target role changes, when you learn a new key skill, or when you start a job search. There is no need to change it every week.

headings.text: A Simple Formula for Your Headline
LinkedIn Headline Examples for Job Seekers
Headlines for Students and New Graduates
How to Pick the Right Keywords

html:
A good LinkedIn headline says what you do, what you work on, and one proof point. It uses plain words that recruiters search for. For a job seeker, the simplest strong form is "[Job Title] | [Top Skill or Specialty] | [Result or Industry]". The LinkedIn headline examples below follow that formula for many roles and situations, so you can copy one and change the details.

Your headline appears under your name on your profile, in search results, in comments, and in connection requests. That makes it one of the most visible lines you write in a job search.

Why Your Headline Matters

Recruiters search LinkedIn with job titles and skills. Your headline is one of the fields that search reads. If it says only "Seeking new opportunities", a search for "Data Analyst" may not show you near the top.

LinkedIn often fills the headline with your current job title and company by default. That can be fine. But if your current title is unclear, or if you want a different role, write your own.

A Simple Formula for Your Headline

Use this structure and change it as you need:

[Job Title you want or have] | [Specialty or Top Skills] | [Proof point, industry, or audience]

Some tips for each part:

  • Job title: use the common title that appears in job posts, not an internal title. "Customer Success Manager" is better than "Client Happiness Hero".
  • Specialty or skills: name two or three skills or tools from the job posts you want.
  • Proof point: a short result, a certification, or the type of company you know best.

Use a vertical bar (|), a comma, or a bullet to separate the parts. Keep it easy to read.

LinkedIn Headline Examples by Role

Change the details so they are true for you.

Business and operations

  • Project Manager | PMP | Delivering Software Launches On Time for Fintech Teams
  • Operations Manager | Process Improvement, Vendor Management | Retail and E-commerce
  • Executive Assistant to C-Suite | Calendar, Travel, and Board Meeting Support
  • Business Analyst | SQL, Process Mapping, Requirements | Healthcare Systems

Sales and customer roles

  • Account Executive | B2B SaaS Sales | Mid-Market Deals From Discovery to Close
  • Customer Success Manager | Onboarding and Retention | 60+ Enterprise Accounts
  • Sales Development Representative | Outbound Prospecting | HubSpot and Salesforce
  • Customer Support Specialist | Zendesk | Clear Answers for Technical Products

Marketing and communications

  • Content Marketing Manager | SEO, Editorial Strategy | B2B Technology
  • Social Media Manager | Short-Form Video, Community Growth | Consumer Brands
  • Digital Marketing Specialist | Google Ads, Meta Ads, Analytics
  • Communications Specialist | Press Releases, Internal Comms | Nonprofit Sector

Technology and data

  • Software Engineer | React, TypeScript, Node.js | Building Fast Web Apps
  • Data Analyst | SQL, Python, Tableau | Turning Sales Data Into Decisions
  • IT Support Specialist | CompTIA A+ | Microsoft 365 and Help Desk
  • UX Designer | User Research, Figma, Accessibility | Mobile Apps
  • DevOps Engineer | AWS, Terraform, CI/CD | Reliable Cloud Infrastructure

Healthcare and education

  • Registered Nurse | ICU and Critical Care | BLS, ACLS Certified
  • Medical Assistant | Patient Intake, EHR, Phlebotomy
  • High School Math Teacher | Algebra and Statistics | Project-Based Learning
  • Instructional Designer | E-Learning, Articulate 360 | Corporate Training

Finance and HR

  • Staff Accountant | Month-End Close, Reconciliations | CPA Candidate
  • Financial Analyst | FP&A, Forecasting, Excel Modeling
  • HR Generalist | Employee Relations, Onboarding, HRIS
  • Recruiter | Technical Hiring | Engineering and Product Roles

Trades and skilled work

  • Licensed Electrician | Commercial and Residential | OSHA 30
  • Logistics Coordinator | Freight, Inventory, Carrier Relations
  • Maintenance Technician | HVAC, Preventive Maintenance | Manufacturing Plants

LinkedIn Headline Examples for Job Seekers

If you are between jobs, you can still lead with your title. A recruiter searches for the role, not for "unemployed".

  • Marketing Coordinator | Email, Social, Events | Open to Full-Time Roles in Austin
  • Senior Product Designer | Design Systems, Research | Seeking Remote Product Roles
  • Supply Chain Analyst | Forecasting, ERP | Available Immediately
  • Paralegal | Litigation Support, E-Discovery | Looking for Roles in Chicago

Add your location or "Remote" only if it helps your search. Use the Open to Work setting for the rest.

Headlines for Career Changers

Name the role you are moving toward, then connect it to your past.

  • Aspiring UX Designer | Former Teacher | Google UX Design Certificate
  • Data Analyst | Moving From Finance | SQL, Python, Excel
  • Project Coordinator | 8 Years in Hospitality Operations | CAPM
  • Customer Success | Former Nurse Who Explains Complex Things Simply

"Aspiring" is fine when you do not yet have experience in the new title. If you have done the work in projects or freelance jobs, use the title without "aspiring".

Headlines for Students and New Graduates

  • Computer Science Student at [University] | Python, Java | Seeking Summer 2027 Internship
  • Recent Accounting Graduate | Excel, QuickBooks | CPA Track
  • Marketing Graduate | Social Media and Content | Campus Ambassador for [Brand]
  • Nursing Student | Clinical Rotations in Pediatrics | Graduating May 2027

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Only words like "Passionate", "Motivated", or "Hardworking". They do not say what you do.
  • A clever title that no one searches for, such as "Spreadsheet Wizard".
  • A long list of every skill you have. Pick the ones that match your target jobs.
  • A headline that does not match your resume or your experience section.
  • All capital letters.
  • Emojis in a conservative industry. In some creative fields they are fine, but they add no search value.

How to Pick the Right Keywords

Open five job posts for the role you want. Note the job title they use and the skills that appear in most of them. Use those words in your headline, in your About section, and in your experience bullets. The method is the same one you use for your resume, and the guide on resume keywords walks through it.

Your headline is one part of a larger plan. If you are starting a search now, the guide on how to build a job search plan shows where LinkedIn fits each week.

How to Change Your Headline

LinkedIn changes its layout from time to time, but the steps are usually these:

  1. Go to your profile.
  2. Select the pencil icon in the top section, next to your name.
  3. Find the Headline field.
  4. Type your new headline and check the character count.
  5. Save.

LinkedIn may ask whether to share the profile change with your network. If you are job searching while employed, you can turn that off.

Check Your Headline

Read your headline as a recruiter would. Ask:

  • Does it include the job title I want?
  • Does it name skills from real job posts?
  • Is there one proof point, such as a certification, an industry, or a result?
  • Does the start of the line make sense alone, in case LinkedIn cuts it short?

If the answer is yes to each, your headline does its job.

title: Common Interview Questions: 20 Questions and How to Answer Each One
description: Prepare for the 20 most common interview questions with what the interviewer wants to learn, a simple structure for each answer, and sample lines.

faqs.q: How many interview questions should I prepare for?
faqs.a: Prepare full answers for about 10 core questions and short notes for 10 more. Many other questions are versions of these, so you can adapt a prepared story.

faqs.q: Should I memorize my interview answers?
faqs.a: Memorize the structure and the key facts, not every word. Answers that you recite word for word often sound stiff, and they break when the question is a little different.

faqs.q: What questions are illegal for an interviewer to ask in the US?
faqs.a: US employers should not base hiring decisions on protected traits, such as age, religion, national origin, disability, or pregnancy. Questions about these traits are a risk. Rules also differ by state, so check your state's guidance if a question concerns you.

faqs.q: How long should an interview answer be?
faqs.a: Aim for about one to two minutes for most answers. Behavioral stories can run a little longer. If you see the interviewer wants more detail, they will ask.

headings.text: How to Prepare for Common Interview Questions
Questions About the Job and the Company
A Quick Table: What Each Question Tests
Practice Plan for the Week Before

html:
Five of the most common interview questions are "Tell me about yourself", "Why do you want this job?", and "What are your strengths and weaknesses?". The other two are "Tell me about a challenge you solved" and "Why are you leaving your current job?". Most interviews use some version of these, plus a few role-specific questions. Prepare a short, true story for each one, and you can answer most of what you will hear.

This guide lists 20 common interview questions. For each one, you get what the interviewer wants to learn and a simple way to answer.

How to Prepare for Common Interview Questions

Do not write 20 separate scripts. Instead, prepare five to eight stories from your work, school, or volunteer life. Each story should show a skill the job needs. Then match stories to questions.

For each story, note four things:

  1. The situation and your role.
  2. The task or problem.
  3. The actions you took.
  4. The result, with a number if you have a true one.

That is the STAR structure. The guide on the STAR method interview technique shows how to build each story step by step.

Then practice aloud. Say each answer two or three times. Record yourself on your phone once and listen back. You will hear filler words and long parts that you can cut.

Questions About You

1. Tell me about yourself.

The interviewer wants a short summary that connects your past to this job. Use present, past, and future: what you do now, what you did before that matters, and why this role is the next step. Keep it to about one minute. The full guide on the tell me about yourself answer has examples.

2. What are your greatest strengths?

Name one or two strengths that the job post asks for. Give one short example for each. "I am good at explaining technical things to customers. At [Company], I rewrote our setup guide, and support tickets about setup dropped."

3. What is your greatest weakness?

Name a real weakness that does not block the core of the job. Then say what you do to improve it. Avoid fake weaknesses such as "I work too hard".

4. How would your coworkers describe you?

Pick two or three words and back each with a short proof. If you have a real quote from a review or a manager, you can use it.

5. What are you most proud of in your career?

Choose a result that is relevant to the new job. Tell it as a short STAR story, and say why it matters to you.

Questions About the Job and the Company

6. Why do you want to work here?

The interviewer wants to see that you did research and that you chose them on purpose. Name something specific: a product, a customer group, a value, or a project. Then link it to your skills.

7. Why are you interested in this role?

Talk about the work itself. Point to two or three tasks in the job post that you enjoy and do well.

8. What do you know about our company?

Know the basics: what they sell, who their customers are, and one recent piece of news from their website or press page. Say it in your own words.

9. Why should we hire you?

Summarize your fit in three or four sentences. Match their top needs from the job post with your proof. End with how you will help in the first months.

10. Where do you see yourself in five years?

They want to know if your goals fit the role. Talk about the skills you want to grow and the kind of work you want to own. You do not need a job title.

Questions About Your Experience

11. Walk me through your resume.

Go in time order, briefly. Spend the most time on the roles most like this one. Explain each move in one sentence.

12. Why are you leaving your current job?

Stay positive and short. Focus on what you want next, not what you dislike now. "I have learned a lot in support, and I want to move into a role with more product work."

13. Why is there a gap in your employment?

Give a short, honest reason. Then say what you did to stay current and why you are ready now. You do not need to share private details.

14. Tell me about a time you made a mistake.

Pick a real mistake with a clear lesson. Spend most of the answer on how you fixed it and what you changed after.

Behavioral Questions

Behavioral questions start with "Tell me about a time..." or "Give me an example of...". Use a STAR story for each.

15. Tell me about a challenge you solved.

Choose a problem with real stakes. Show your thinking, not only the result.

16. Tell me about a conflict with a coworker.

Show that you listened, stayed calm, and focused on the work. Do not blame the other person. End with how the relationship or the process improved.

17. Tell me about a time you led a project or a team.

Leadership can be informal. Training a new hire or running a small process change counts.

18. Tell me about a time you had a tight deadline.

Show how you set priorities, what you said no to, and how you kept people informed.

Questions About Logistics

19. What are your salary expectations?

Research the pay range for the role and the location first. Many US job posts now show a range, and some states require it. You can give a range based on your research, or ask what range they have budgeted. Check your local rules on salary history questions, because they differ by state and city.

20. Do you have any questions for us?

Always say yes. Prepare three to five questions about the work, the team, and how they measure success. Do not ask about anything that the job post already answers.

A Quick Table: What Each Question Tests

Question What the interviewer is checking
Tell me about yourself Can you summarize your fit clearly?
Why do you want to work here? Did you research us and choose us on purpose?
Greatest weakness Are you self-aware and willing to improve?
Why are you leaving? Is there a problem we should know about?
Tell me about a conflict Can you work with people when it is hard?
Salary expectations Are we in the same range?
Questions for us Are you seriously interested in the job?

Practice Plan for the Week Before

  • Day 1: Read the job post twice. List the top five skills it asks for.
  • Day 2: Write your five to eight stories in STAR notes.
  • Day 3: Match stories to the 20 questions above. Fill any gaps.
  • Day 4: Practice aloud. Time each answer.
  • Day 5: Do a mock interview with a friend, or record yourself.
  • Day before: Review your notes, prepare your questions, and plan your route or test your video setup.

After the Interview

Write down the questions you were asked while you still remember them. Note which answers went well and which did not. That list makes your next interview easier.

Then send a short thank-you within 24 hours. The guide on the thank you email after an interview has templates you can copy.

title: Cover Letter With No Experience: How to Write One, With a Template
description: Write a cover letter with no experience by using school, projects, volunteer work, and transferable skills. Includes a full template and example lines.

faqs.q: Should I say I have no experience in my cover letter?
faqs.a: No. Do not point out what you lack. Show what you have done that relates to the job, and let the reader see the fit.

faqs.q: Can I use a school project as experience in a cover letter?
faqs.a: Yes. A school project counts when it used skills the job needs. Describe what you did, the tools you used, and the result, the same way you would describe a job.

faqs.q: How long should a cover letter be when I have no experience?
faqs.a: Keep it to about 200 to 300 words. A short, specific letter reads better than a long letter filled with general claims.

faqs.q: Do I need a cover letter for an entry-level job?
faqs.a: If the application allows one, send it. For entry-level roles, the letter is a good place to show interest and skills that your resume cannot show yet.

headings.text: How to Write a Cover Letter With No Experience: 6 Steps
Cover Letter Template With No Experience

html:
To write a cover letter with no experience, focus on what you can do instead of what you have done in a paid job. Use examples from school, projects, volunteer work, part-time jobs, and clubs that show skills from the job post. Then explain why you want this specific role and close by asking for an interview.

Everyone starts somewhere, and hiring managers for entry-level roles know that. They do not expect a long work history. They look for signs that you can learn fast, work with people, and do the basic tasks of the job. Your letter gives them those signs.

What Counts as Experience

"No experience" usually means no full-time job in the field. You almost always have more to work with than you think.

Look at this list and note anything that fits:

  • Part-time or seasonal jobs (retail, food service, delivery, camp counselor).
  • Internships, even short or unpaid ones.
  • School projects, capstones, and lab work.
  • Volunteer work and community service.
  • Clubs, sports teams, and student government.
  • Freelance or gig work, including small jobs for family or neighbors.
  • Personal projects: a website, a small business, a social media account, a coding project.
  • Certificates and online courses.
  • Caring for a family member, if it built skills such as scheduling or problem solving.

A cashier job shows customer service, cash handling, and reliability. A group project shows teamwork and deadlines. A club role shows organization. Name the skill, then give the proof.

How to Write a Cover Letter With No Experience: 6 Steps

Step 1: Read the job post and list the skills

Read the post twice. Write down the skills and qualities it asks for, such as "attention to detail", "Excel", or "customer service". Circle the three or four that appear most.

Step 2: Match each skill to one example

For each skill, find one example from the list above. Write one sentence that shows what you did and, if you can, what happened.

Skill in the job post Example without a full-time job
Customer service Helped 50+ customers a shift at a busy coffee shop
Organization Planned a fundraiser for the robotics club and kept the budget
Data and Excel Cleaned and charted survey data for a statistics class project
Communication Wrote weekly updates for a volunteer group's email list
Reliability Worked every weekend for two years while in school

Use true numbers only. If you do not know the number, describe the work without one.

Step 3: Open with interest and a reason

Your first lines say which job you want and why you are a good match. Do not start with "My name is". The guide on cover letter opening lines has many options.

Step 4: Build the middle around two or three examples

Pick your strongest two or three examples. Give each a short paragraph or a few sentences. Connect each one to a need in the job post.

Step 5: Show you know the company

Add one or two sentences about why you want to work at this company. Mention something specific, such as a product you use, a community program, or the type of customers they serve.

Step 6: Close with a clear ask

Say that you want an interview, and thank the reader. Keep it short. The guide on how to end a cover letter has closing lines you can use.

Cover Letter Template With No Experience

Copy this template and replace every bracket. Remove any line that does not fit you.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I am applying for the [Job Title] position at [Company]. As a [recent graduate / student / career starter] in [field or major], I have built skills in [skill 1] and [skill 2] through [school, volunteer work, or part-time job], and I am excited to bring them to your team.

At [Place or Program], I [specific action that shows skill 1]. This taught me how to [what you learned that applies to the job]. In [another place or project], I [specific action that shows skill 2], which [result, if you have one].

I am drawn to [Company] because [specific reason: product, mission, customers, or team]. I am a fast learner, and I am ready to take on [main task from the job post] from my first week.

I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help your team. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely, [Your Full Name] [Phone Number] | [Email Address]

Example Lines You Can Adapt

For a retail or customer service role:

In two years at [Store Name], I learned to stay calm with long lines and upset customers. My manager asked me to train three new hires on the register and returns process.

For an office or administrative role:

As treasurer of the [Club Name], I tracked every expense in a shared spreadsheet and gave a monthly report to the club advisor.

For a tech role:

For my capstone project, I built a [type of app] in [language or tool] with two classmates. I wrote the [part you built] and fixed the bugs we found in testing.

For a healthcare support role:

As a volunteer at [Hospital or Clinic], I greeted patients, helped them check in, and kept the waiting area organized during busy afternoons.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Apologizing for your lack of experience. Lines such as "Although I have no experience" make the reader focus on the gap.
  • Only general claims, such as "I am hardworking and passionate". Back every claim with an example.
  • Repeating your resume line by line. Use the letter to explain one or two things in more detail.
  • Talking only about what the job will do for you. Show what you will do for them.
  • A long letter. Three or four short paragraphs are enough.
  • Sending the same letter to every job. Change the skills and the company reason each time.

Format and Length

Use a simple, professional layout: your contact details at the top, a greeting, three or four paragraphs, and a sign-off. The guide on cover letter format shows the layout. Aim for about 200 to 300 words.

If you find it hard to start, CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post. Then you edit it, add your own examples, and make it sound like you.

Before You Send It

  • Does the first paragraph name the job and give a reason you fit?
  • Does each example connect to a skill in the job post?
  • Did you name the company and give one real reason you want to work there?
  • Is every number true?
  • Did you check the spelling of the company name and the hiring manager's name?

If the answer to each question is yes, send the letter. Then move on to the next application.

title: How to Follow Up on a Job Application: Timing, Channels, Templates
description: Learn how to follow up on a job application: when to wait, who to contact, what to write, and how often. Includes email and LinkedIn templates.
keyword: how to follow up on a job application

faqs.q: Is it rude to follow up on a job application?
faqs.a: No. A short, polite message after a reasonable wait is normal. It becomes a problem only when you send many messages or use a demanding tone.

faqs.q: What if the job post says "no calls or emails, please"?
faqs.a: Respect the request. Do not contact the company directly about that application. Use your time to apply to other roles, and connect with people there in a general way later if it makes sense.

faqs.q: Should I follow up if I applied through a job board?
faqs.a: Yes, if you can find the right contact. Job boards usually send your application to the company's own system, so the person to contact is still at the company.

faqs.q: Can I follow up on an application more than once?
faqs.a: Two messages, about one to two weeks apart, is a reasonable limit. After that, move your attention to other applications.

headings.text: When to Follow Up on a Job Application
What to Say in a Follow-Up
Follow-Up Email Template After You Apply
What to Do Before You Follow Up

html:
To follow up on a job application, wait about one to two weeks after you apply. Then send a short, polite email or LinkedIn message to the recruiter or hiring manager. Say which job you applied for and when, add one line about why you fit, and ask whether they need anything else from you. If you hear nothing, send one more message about a week later, then stop.

A follow-up does not guarantee a reply. It does put your name in front of a person, which a submitted form cannot always do. This guide covers timing, who to contact, what to say, and templates you can copy.

When to Follow Up on a Job Application

Waiting too short a time looks impatient. Waiting too long means the role may already be filled. Use the job post and your own situation to choose a date.

Situation When to follow up
Standard online application About 1 to 2 weeks after you apply
The post shows a closing date A few business days after that date
You applied through a referral Ask your contact to check in after about 1 week
You already met someone from the company After about 1 week, to that person
The post says "no calls or emails" Do not follow up about that application

Apply early when you can. Many teams start to review applications while the post is still open, so an early application and a polite follow-up work well together.

Who to Contact

The best person is the one who will make or influence the decision. Try these in order:

  1. The recruiter or hiring contact named in the job post.
  2. The recruiter for that team. Search LinkedIn for "[Company] recruiter" or "talent acquisition".
  3. The hiring manager. The job post often names the team, which helps you guess the manager's title.
  4. A person you know at the company, who can pass your name along.

Do not message the CEO or five people at once. One or two well-chosen contacts are enough.

How to find an email address

Look at the job post, the careers page, and the contact's LinkedIn profile. Some people list an email there. If you cannot find an address, send a LinkedIn message instead. Do not guess email addresses and send to many versions.

What to Say in a Follow-Up

Keep the message short. Four parts are enough:

  1. The job title and the date you applied.
  2. One sentence about your strongest match for the role.
  3. A polite question: is there anything else they need, or what is the timeline?
  4. A thank-you.

Use a subject line that makes the purpose clear, such as "Application for [Job Title], [Your Name]".

Follow-Up Email Template After You Apply

Subject: Application for [Job Title], [Your Name]

Hi [Recruiter or Hiring Manager Name],

I applied for the [Job Title] role at [Company] on [Date], and I wanted to confirm my interest. My experience in [top skill from the job post], including [one short proof], fits what the team is looking for.

Is there anything else I can send to help with your review? I would also be glad to hear about the timeline when you have one.

Thank you for your time, [Your Name] [Phone Number] | [LinkedIn URL]

LinkedIn Message Template

LinkedIn connection notes have a short character limit, so keep this version brief.

Hi [Name], I recently applied for the [Job Title] role at [Company]. I have [number] years of experience in [skill], and I am very interested in the team's work on [project or product]. I would be glad to connect and answer any questions.

If you are already connected, you can send a longer direct message, similar to the email above.

Second Follow-Up Template

Send this about one week after the first message, only if you had no reply.

Subject: Re: Application for [Job Title], [Your Name]

Hi [Name],

I wanted to check in once more on my application for the [Job Title] role. I am still very interested and would welcome the chance to talk.

Thank you, [Your Name]

Reply in the same email thread as your first message, so the reader sees the history.

Should You Call Instead?
