In my [number] years as a [current or recent role], I have [main result that matches the top requirement in the job post]. At [Company or Project], I [second result, with a number or a clear outcome]. I also bring [skill from the job post], which I used to [short example].

Your post says that the team needs someone who can [requirement in the employer's words]. That is the work I do best, and I would like to do it for [Company].

Thank you for your time. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help with [team goal or project].

Sincerely, [Your Name] [Phone Number] | [Email]

For more detail on each part, read the full guide on how to write a cover letter.

Phrases to Remove From an AI Draft

These phrases appear often in AI drafts. They take up space and say little.

  • "I am excited to apply for..."
  • "proven track record"
  • "dynamic team" or "fast-paced environment"
  • "I am confident that I would be a valuable addition"
  • "passionate about" with no example
  • "In today's world..."
  • "I believe my skills and experience make me a perfect fit"

Replace each one with a fact or delete it. If a sentence still works without the phrase, the phrase was not needed.

Prompt Tips if You Use a General Chat Tool

A general chat tool does not know what a cover letter needs, so tell it.

  • Paste your resume and the job post, and label each one.
  • Ask for a letter of a fixed length, such as 300 words.
  • Tell it to use only facts from your resume and your notes.
  • Ask it to write in plain language, with no clichés.
  • Ask for two different first paragraphs, then pick the better one.

A cover letter tool does these steps for you. For example, CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post. You pick one of four tones and three lengths, and you make the changes above in its editor.

Is an AI Cover Letter Honest?

An AI cover letter is honest when every fact in it is true and you stand behind every sentence. The tool is a writing aid, like a template or a friend who reviews your draft. The facts and the final decisions are yours.

Rules differ by employer. Some job posts ask candidates not to use AI, and some roles test your writing directly. Read the application instructions and follow them. In the interview, you must be able to talk about every claim in your letter, so do not send anything that you cannot explain.

Final Checklist

  • Every fact, number, and project in the letter is true.
  • The letter names the company, the role, and one specific reason.
  • At least two requirements from the job post appear, with an example for each.
  • No phrase from the list above is left.
  • The letter sounds like you when you read it aloud.
  • The names and the company details are correct.

title: What Are Your Salary Expectations? How to Answer, With Examples
description: How to answer "What are your salary expectations?" in an interview or on a form: research a range, choose your number, and use these example answers.

faqs.q: Should I give a salary range or one number?
faqs.a: A range is usually better early in the process. Put your target number at or near the bottom of the range, because the employer will often focus on the low end.

faqs.q: What do I put in a required salary field on an application form?
faqs.a: Enter the bottom of your researched range, or a number that you would accept with confidence. If the form allows text, you can write "Negotiable", but many forms only accept numbers.

faqs.q: Can an employer ask about my current salary?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live. Some US states and cities ban employers from asking about salary history, so check your local rules. You can always answer with your expectations instead of your history.

faqs.q: Is it bad to ask about salary in the first interview?
faqs.a: No. It is reasonable to ask the recruiter for the range early, so that neither side wastes time. Ask politely and in a neutral tone.

headings.text: How to Answer "What Are Your Salary Expectations?"
How to Answer on an Application Form
How the Question Fits in the Interview

html:
To answer "What are your salary expectations?", give a researched range for the role, not your current pay, and connect it to the job's scope. For example: "Based on my research for this role and my experience, I am looking for $85,000 to $95,000 in base salary. I am open to talking about the full package." First ask what range the company has budgeted. If they share it, you can respond to their number instead of guessing.

Why Employers Ask This Question

The question is not a trap. Most employers ask it for practical reasons:

  • They want to know if your expectations fit the budget for the role.
  • They want to avoid a long process that ends with an offer that you will refuse.
  • They want to see if you understand the market value of the role.

Your goal is to give an answer that keeps you in the process and does not set your pay lower than it should be.

Step 1: Research the Market Range

Do this before your first call with a recruiter. You need a range for this role, at this level, in this location or remote market.

Use several sources and compare them:

  • The pay range in the job post. Some US states and cities require employers to publish a range, so many posts now include one.
  • Salary data on job sites and pay comparison sites.
  • The US Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook, which gives median pay by occupation.
  • People in your network who do similar work. Ask about ranges, not their exact pay.
  • Recruiters who contact you about similar roles.

Write down a low, middle, and high number for the role. Adjust for your experience, the company size, and the cost of living where the job is.

Step 2: Choose Your Numbers

You need three numbers before the interview:

  1. Your walk-away number: the lowest base salary you would accept.
  2. Your target number: the salary that you want and can support with research.
  3. Your stated range: the range that you will say out loud.

Make the bottom of your stated range equal to your target or a little above it. Employers often hear the low end of a range first. Do not make the range very wide. A range like "$70,000 to $110,000" looks like you have not done the research.

How to Answer "What Are Your Salary Expectations?"

Use one of these approaches. Choose the one that fits the stage of the process and how much you know.

Option 1: Ask for Their Range First

This works best in an early recruiter call.

"Before I give a number, could you share the range budgeted for this role? That will help me see if we are aligned."

Many recruiters will share it. If the range fits, you can say: "That range works for me, depending on the full package."

Option 2: Give a Researched Range

Use this when they ask again, or when you already know the market well.

"I researched [Job Title] roles in [location or remote], and I have [number] years of experience in [key skill]. Based on that, I am looking for a base salary between [$X] and [$Y]. I am flexible depending on the benefits and the full package."

Option 3: Delay Politely

Use this when you know very little about the role yet.

"I would like to learn more about the responsibilities and the team before I name a number. I am sure we can find a figure that is fair if we agree that I am the right person for the role."

Do not delay more than once or twice. If you refuse many times, the recruiter may think you are difficult to work with.

Option 4: Answer With the Full Package in Mind

Use this when the role has a large bonus, equity, or unusual benefits.

"For base salary, I am targeting [$X] to [$Y]. I am also interested in how the bonus and equity work for this role, because the total package matters to me."

Example Answers by Situation

Situation What to say
Early phone screen Ask for their range first, then confirm if it fits.
They insist on a number Give your researched range with a short reason.
You are changing careers Base the range on the new role, and mention transferable skills.
You earn far below the market now Talk about the market range for the role, not your current pay.
You earn more than the posted range Say what matters most to you, and ask if there is flexibility.

What Not to Say

These answers often hurt your result:

  • "Whatever you think is fair." This gives the employer all the control.
  • "I need $X because my rent is high." Your costs are not the employer's reason to pay more. Talk about the value of the role.
  • A number with no research. If you guess low, you may get an offer at that low number.
  • Your current salary, when you do not have to share it. It can anchor the offer to your old pay.
  • A number far above the market without a reason. It can end the process early.

How to Answer on an Application Form

Many online forms have a required field for desired salary. You cannot ask a question there, so you must enter something.

  1. Read the job post for a posted range. If there is one, enter a number inside it that matches your target.
  2. If there is no posted range, enter the bottom of your researched range.
  3. If the field accepts text, you may write "Negotiable" or "Open to discussion", but expect the recruiter to ask again.

Do not leave a required field blank or enter "0" or "1". Some systems filter on this field, so a fake number can remove you from the list.

How the Question Fits in the Interview

The salary question often comes near the end of a first call, after questions like "Tell me about yourself". Prepare it like other common interview questions. Write it down, say it aloud, and practice it until it sounds calm.

Practice the number itself. Many people know their range but say it in a weak voice, or add "but I am flexible" too fast. Say the range, give one reason, and then stop talking.

After You Give Your Range

Your answer is not a final agreement. The real negotiation happens when you get an offer. At that time, you know more about the role, and the employer has already decided that they want you.

If the recruiter says your range is above their budget, ask: "What is the range for this role?" Then decide if it still makes sense for you. You can also ask about other parts of the package. Examples are a signing bonus, extra paid time off, or a salary review after six months.

Pay rules, salary history rules, and pay range disclosure rules differ by state and city. Check your local rules if you are not sure what an employer may ask.

title: Employment Gap on Resume: How to Explain It Honestly and Briefly
description: How to show an employment gap on your resume, explain it in a cover letter and an interview, and use example lines for common reasons.

faqs.q: How long is too long for an employment gap?
faqs.a: There is no fixed limit. A gap of a few months often needs no explanation. A longer gap needs a short, honest line, and the length matters less than what you say about it.

faqs.q: Do I have to give the reason for a gap?
faqs.a: No. You can give a short, general reason such as "family responsibilities" or "a health matter, now resolved". You do not need to share private details.

faqs.q: Should I use only years for dates to hide a gap?
faqs.a: Using only years is a common format, and it is fine for older roles. Do not use it to mislead. If an interviewer asks about exact dates, give them.

faqs.q: Can a background check show an employment gap?
faqs.a: An employment verification can confirm your dates at past employers, so any gap between them becomes visible. That is one more reason to be accurate on your resume.

headings.text: Why Gaps Matter Less Than You Fear
How to Show an Employment Gap on a Resume
Show That Your Skills Are Current
How to Explain the Gap in a Cover Letter
How to Explain an Employment Gap in an Interview

html:
An employment gap on a resume is a period when you were not in paid work. Many people have one, for reasons such as caregiving, health, a layoff, study, or travel. The best way to handle it is to be honest and brief. Show accurate dates, add a one-line reason if the gap is long, and focus on what you can do now. Hiring managers usually care more about your current skills than about the gap itself.

Why Gaps Matter Less Than You Fear

A gap feels large to you because you lived it. To a reader, it is one line on a page. Most hiring managers have seen many gaps, and many have one on their own resume.

A gap becomes a problem in only a few cases:

  • The resume hides it badly, and the reader feels misled.
  • The skills for the role changed a lot during the gap, and the resume does not show that you kept up.
  • The candidate gets nervous or defensive when someone asks about it.

You can prevent all of these. The rest of this guide shows how.

How to Show an Employment Gap on a Resume

Choose the method that fits the length of your gap and what you did during it.

Option 1: Leave It as It Is

For a gap of a few months, do nothing. Use accurate dates and let the gap be. Many readers will not ask.

Option 2: Add a One-Line Entry

For a longer gap, add an entry in your work history with the dates and a short reason. This answers the question before the reader asks it.

Career break, [Month Year] to [Month Year] Full-time caregiver for a family member. Completed [course or certification] in [skill].

Planned career break, [Month Year] to [Month Year] Travel and study. Completed [course] and built [project].

Option 3: List What You Did During the Gap

If you did freelance work, volunteer work, part-time work, or study, list it like a job. Real work is real experience, even if it was unpaid or short.

Freelance [Your Role], [Month Year] to [Month Year]

  • Built [project] for [type of client].
  • [Result with a number or a clear outcome].

Option 4: Use Year-Only Dates for Older Roles

Year-only dates are common for roles from many years ago. They can make a short old gap less visible. Do not use this method to hide a recent or long gap. It looks misleading when the interviewer asks for months.

Example Lines for Common Reasons

Keep your reason short and neutral. You do not need to share private details.

Reason Example line
Caregiving "Full-time caregiver for a family member."
Health "Took time off for a health matter, now fully resolved."
Layoff "Position eliminated in a company restructuring. Used the time to complete [certification]."
Parenting "Full-time parent. Returned to work as children started school."
Study "Completed [degree or program] at [school]."
Relocation "Moved to [city] and handled the family relocation."
Travel "Planned career break for travel. Completed [course] during this time."
Starting a business "Founded [Business], a [type] business. [One result]."

Each line is true, short, and closed. It does not invite more questions about private matters.

Show That Your Skills Are Current

The biggest real worry about a gap is skill decay. Answer it on the page.

  • Add recent courses or certifications to an "Education and Training" section.
  • Add projects you built during the gap, with links if they are public.
  • Use current tools and terms from the job post in your skills section.
  • Start the resume with a summary that names your role and your strongest recent skills. These resume summary examples include lines for people who return to work.

If you are moving to a new field after the gap, read this guide on the career change cover letter too.

How to Explain the Gap in a Cover Letter

A cover letter is a good place for one or two sentences about a long gap. Put them near the end, not in the first paragraph. Lead with your fit for the job.

After [number] years as a [Previous Role], I took a planned break from [Month Year] to [Month Year] to [short reason]. During that time, I [completed a course, kept a skill current, or did related work]. I am now ready to return full time, and the [Job Title] role at [Company] fits both my experience and my plans.

Do not apologize for the gap. State it as a fact, and move on to what you offer.

How to Explain an Employment Gap in an Interview

Interviewers may ask, "Can you tell me about this gap?" Prepare a short answer in three parts:

  1. The reason, in one sentence.
  2. What you did to stay ready, in one or two sentences.
  3. Why you are ready for this role now, in one sentence.

Here is an example:

"I took a year off to care for a parent who was ill. During that time, I completed a certificate in [skill] and kept up with [industry topic]. My family situation is stable now, and I am ready to commit full time to a role like this one."

Practice the answer aloud until it sounds calm and short. Then stop talking and let the interviewer move on. This answer often connects to "Tell me about yourself", so make the two answers fit together.

What Not to Do

  • Do not change dates to hide the gap. Employers can verify dates, and a false date can cost you the offer.
  • Do not invent a job or a title.
  • Do not give long details about health or family matters. A general reason is enough.
  • Do not speak badly about a past employer, even after a layoff.
  • Do not let the gap become the main topic of your resume or your letter.

Note on Rules That Differ

Some questions about health, family status, or similar topics may be limited by law in an interview. The rules differ by state and by country. If an interviewer asks something that seems improper, you can answer only the part that is about your ability to do the job.

Checklist for Your Resume

  • All dates are accurate.
  • Any gap longer than a few months has a short, neutral line or an entry.
  • Courses, projects, or volunteer work during the gap are listed.
  • The summary and skills section show current skills that match the job post.
  • You have a short, practiced answer for the interview.

An employment gap on your resume is common and manageable. Show the facts, explain briefly, and spend your words on what you can do for the next employer.

title: Why Do You Want to Work Here? How to Answer With Sample Answers
description: Answer "Why do you want to work here?" with a simple 3-part formula, research steps, and sample answers for different roles and companies.
keyword: why do you want to work here

faqs.q: How long should my answer to "Why do you want to work here?" be?
faqs.a: Aim for about 45 to 90 seconds. That is enough for one specific reason about the company, one link to your skills, and one sentence about your goals.

faqs.q: Is it OK to mention salary or benefits in my answer?
faqs.a: Do not lead with them. Pay and benefits matter, but they do not tell the interviewer what you will add. Talk about pay when the employer raises it or at the offer stage.

faqs.q: What if I applied to many jobs and do not know much about this company?
faqs.a: Do 20 minutes of research before the interview. Read the company website, a recent news item, and the job post again, and pick one real detail that interests you.

faqs.q: How is this different from "Why do you want this job?"
faqs.a: "Why this job" is about the role and its tasks. "Why here" is about the company. A strong answer covers both, but this question puts the company first.

headings.text: What the Interviewer Wants to Learn
Research to Do Before the Interview
The 3-Part Formula to Answer "Why Do You Want to Work Here?"
How This Answer Connects to Other Questions
Use the Same Research at the End of the Interview

html:
To answer "Why do you want to work here?", give one specific reason about the company. Then connect it to your skills, and say how the role fits your goals. For example: "I want to work here because your team builds [product] for [customer group]. I have spent four years on that same problem at [Company]. This role lets me go deeper into [skill], which is where I want to grow." A specific answer shows that you did research and that you chose this company on purpose.

What the Interviewer Wants to Learn

The question looks simple, but it tests several things at once:

  • Did you research the company, or did you apply without reading?
  • Do you understand what the company does and who it serves?
  • Do your goals match what the role offers, so you will stay?
  • Will you bring energy to the work, or is this only a paycheck?

A general answer such as "It is a great company with a great culture" fails every one of these tests. A specific answer passes them.

Research to Do Before the Interview

You need two or three real details about the company. Spend 20 to 30 minutes on these sources:

  1. The company website, especially the "About", "Products", and "Careers" pages.
  2. The job post. Read it again and mark what the team wants to achieve.
  3. A recent news item, press release, or company blog post.
  4. The LinkedIn pages of the company and of the people who will interview you.
  5. The product itself, if you can use it or see it.
  6. Reviews from customers, if the company sells to the public.

Write down what interests you. Look for a product, a customer group, a mission, a way of working, or a recent change. Choose the detail that connects best to your own experience.

The 3-Part Formula to Answer "Why Do You Want to Work Here?"

Use this structure for your answer:

  1. The company: one specific thing that draws you to them.
  2. The fit: how your skills or experience match that thing.
  3. The future: what you want to learn or achieve in this role.

Here is the formula as a fill-in template:

"I want to work at [Company] because [specific detail about the company, product, mission, or team]. In my [number] years as a [role], I have [relevant experience or result], so I can help with [goal from the job post]. This role also lets me [grow in a skill or reach a goal], which is the next step I want in my career."

Each part is one or two sentences. The whole answer takes about one minute.

Sample Answers

Use these as models, and change every detail to your real facts.

Software Engineer at a Product Company

"I want to work here because your app solves a real problem for small business owners. I use it for my own side business, so I know the product from the customer side. In my current role, I build payment features in React and Node, and your post says the team is expanding payments. I want to work on a product I believe in, and I want to grow toward technical leadership on a team like this one."

Nurse at a Hospital

"I want to work at [Hospital] because of your focus on patient education after discharge. I have seen how much better patients do when they understand their care plan. In my six years in cardiac care, I created teaching materials for patients with heart failure. I want to bring that experience to a team that shares this focus."

Marketing Coordinator at a Nonprofit

"I have followed [Organization]'s work on [cause] since I volunteered at your [event] in [year]. I want my daily work to support a mission like this one. In my current role, I run email campaigns and social media for a retail brand, and I can bring that skill to your donor campaigns. I also want to learn how nonprofit fundraising works from the inside."

Entry-Level Candidate

"I want to start my career at [Company] because of your training program for new analysts, which I read about on your careers page. I want to learn from experienced people in a structured way. In my final year, I completed a project on [topic] using Excel and SQL, and I enjoyed turning data into clear recommendations. This role is the work I want to do."

Mistakes to Avoid

  • A general compliment. "You are a leader in the industry" could describe many companies.
  • Only what you get. "The benefits are great and the office is close to my home" says nothing about what you give.
  • Facts copied from the homepage without any personal link. Connect the fact to you.
  • Wrong or old facts. Check that the product or the news you mention is current.
  • Too much praise. One clear reason sounds more real than five big compliments.
  • A rehearsed speech that sounds memorized. Know the three parts, but say them in your own natural words.

How This Answer Connects to Other Questions

Your answer here should match what you say in other parts of the interview. Your answer to "Tell me about yourself" sets up your background. This answer explains why that background points to this company. Your answer to "Where do you see yourself in five years?" should fit the future part of this answer.

Prepare these answers together, along with other common interview questions. When the answers fit together, you sound focused and honest.

Use the Same Research at the End of the Interview

The details you find also help you at the end of the interview, when the interviewer asks if you have questions. Turn one detail into a question. For example: "I read that you launched [product] last quarter. How does this role support that work?" This guide to questions to ask in an interview has more ideas.

Practice Checklist

  • You have one specific reason about the company, based on research.
  • You connect that reason to a skill or a result of your own.
  • You say what you want to learn or achieve in this role.
  • Your answer takes about one minute.
  • Your facts are current and correct.
  • You practiced the answer aloud at least three times.

The interviewer asks "Why do you want to work here?" to learn if you chose them on purpose. A short answer with one true detail, one link to your skills, and one goal gives them that proof.

title: How to Ask for a Referral: Message Templates for Every Situation
description: Learn how to ask for a referral from a friend, a former coworker, or a new contact, with message templates and the details to send with your request.
keyword: how to ask for a referral

faqs.q: Should I apply before or after I ask for a referral?
faqs.a: Ask first, and wait for an answer before you apply, if you can. At many companies, the referral must be submitted before or with your application to count. Ask your contact how their company does it.

faqs.q: Is it OK to ask a stranger for a referral?
faqs.a: It is OK, but the success rate is lower. Start a short conversation first, ask about their work, and ask for the referral only when they know enough about you to say yes.

faqs.q: What if my contact says no?
faqs.a: Thank them and do not push. They may not know your work well enough, or their company may have rules. You can still ask if they have advice about the role or the team.

faqs.q: Should I thank someone after a referral if I do not get the job?
faqs.a: Yes. Send a short thank-you after they submit the referral, and a short update when the process ends. That keeps the relationship good for the future.

headings.text: Who to Ask for a Referral
What to Prepare Before You Ask
How to Ask for a Referral: The Message Structure
Template 1: A Former Coworker or Friend
Template 2: A Contact You Do Not Know Well
Template 3: A Request Through a Mutual Friend
What to Send After They Say Yes

html:
To ask for a referral, send a short, direct message to someone at the company. Name the exact role, say in one or two sentences why you fit, and make it easy to say yes or no. Attach your resume and a link to the job post so your contact does not have to search. The best referrals come from people who know your work, so start with former coworkers, classmates, and friends before you contact strangers.

Why a Referral Helps

A referral puts your application in front of a recruiter with a note from someone the company trusts. Many companies have a formal referral program, and some pay employees a bonus when a referred candidate is hired. That means many employees are glad to refer good candidates.

A referral does not guarantee an interview. It gives your application more attention, and it often gets you a faster answer. You still need a resume that fits the job.

Who to Ask for a Referral

Ask people in this order. The closer they are to your work, the stronger the referral.

  1. Former managers and coworkers who saw your work directly.
  2. Friends and classmates who know you well.
  3. Second-degree contacts, introduced by a friend.
  4. People you met at events, in online groups, or in alumni networks.
  5. Strangers at the company, after a short conversation.

Search LinkedIn for "[Company]" and filter by your connections. You may find more contacts than you expect.

What to Prepare Before You Ask

Make the request easy for your contact. Prepare these items first:

  • The link to the job post and the job ID.
  • Your resume, tailored to the role. This guide shows how to tailor your resume to a job description.
  • Two or three sentences about why you fit, which your contact can copy into the referral form.
  • Your LinkedIn profile, with a clear headline. See these LinkedIn headline examples if you need to update it.

How to Ask for a Referral: The Message Structure

Every good referral request has the same parts:

  1. A personal greeting that reminds them how you know each other.
  2. The role, with a link.
  3. Your fit, in one or two sentences.
  4. The direct request.
  5. An easy way to say no.
  6. Your thanks.

The easy way to say no matters. People feel more comfortable when they do not feel trapped, and you protect the relationship.

Template 1: A Former Coworker or Friend

Hi [Name],

I hope things are going well at [Company]. I saw that your team is hiring a [Job Title] ([link to job post]), and I think I am a strong fit. In my current role at [Current Company], I [one result that matches the job post].

Would you be comfortable referring me for this role? I attached my resume, and here is a short summary you can use: "[Two sentences about your experience and fit]."

If it is not a good time, or if you do not feel you know my work well enough, no problem at all. Thank you for considering it.

[Your Name]

Template 2: A Contact You Do Not Know Well

Start with a question about their work. Ask for the referral in a second message, after they reply.

First message:

Hi [Name], I am a [your role] interested in the [Job Title] role on your team at [Company]. I saw your post about [topic] and found it useful. Could I ask you two quick questions about what the team works on? Thanks, [Your Name]

Second message, after a short conversation:

Thanks again for your time, [Name]. Your answers made me even more interested in the role. If you are comfortable with it, would you be willing to refer me? I can send my resume and a short summary to make it easy. If not, I understand completely.

Template 3: A Request Through a Mutual Friend

Hi [Friend's Name], I am applying for a [Job Title] role at [Company], and I see that you know [Contact Name] there. Would you be willing to introduce us? I would like to ask [Contact Name] a few questions about the team. I can send you a short note to forward if that helps. Thanks, [Your Name]

Template 4: A Former Manager

A former manager's referral is often the strongest one. Be direct and specific.

Hi [Manager Name],

I am applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company], where you now work. You saw my work on [project] at [Old Company], and that work is close to what this team needs.

Would you be willing to refer me? I attached my resume. I am also happy to talk for 10 minutes if you want an update on what I have done since we worked together.

Thank you, [Your Name]

What to Send After They Say Yes

Send everything in one message so your contact can submit the referral in a few minutes:

  • The job post link and the job ID.
  • Your resume as a PDF.
  • Your full name and email, exactly as they should appear in the form.
  • A two-sentence summary of your fit.

Ask them to tell you when they submit it, so you can apply at the right time if your application is a separate step.

Follow-Up and Thanks

If your contact does not answer within about a week, send one short reminder in the same thread. Do not send more than one.

Hi [Name], I am following up on my note about the [Job Title] role. No pressure if now is not a good time. Thanks, [Your Name]

After they submit the referral, thank them. When the process ends, tell them the result, whether you got the job or not. People like to know how their help turned out.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Asking for a referral with no specific role. "Can you refer me for anything?" is hard to act on.
  • Sending a long message about your whole career.
  • Asking a stranger for a referral in the first message.
  • Asking someone who cannot judge your work to say that you are excellent. Let them describe what they know.
  • Applying through the normal portal before the referral, when the company only counts referrals submitted first.
  • Forgetting to thank them.

Rules for referrals differ by company. Some companies limit how many referrals one person can submit. Some ask the referrer how well they know you. Ask your contact about the process if you are not sure.

When you are not connected to anyone at the company, a message to the recruiter can be the next best step. This guide on how to message a recruiter on LinkedIn has templates for that.

title: Cover Letter Mistakes: 15 Errors to Fix Before You Hit Send
description: The most common cover letter mistakes, with a fix and an example for each, plus a corrected template and a final checklist before you apply.

faqs.q: What is the worst cover letter mistake?
faqs.a: The wrong company name or job title is the most damaging, because it shows that you reused a letter without reading it. Check both before you send every letter.

faqs.q: Can a cover letter hurt my application?
faqs.a: Yes. A letter with errors, false claims, or a generic tone can hurt more than no letter. If the letter is optional and you cannot write a good one, a strong resume alone may be better.

faqs.q: Is it a mistake to use the same cover letter for every job?
faqs.a: Yes, if you send it without changes. You can reuse a base letter, but change the opening, the main example, and the closing for each job post.

faqs.q: Should a cover letter repeat my resume?
faqs.a: No. The letter should pick one or two results from the resume and explain why they matter for this job. Do not list everything again.

html:
The most common cover letter mistakes are a generic letter, the wrong company name, a copy of the resume, a focus on what you want, and typos. Each one tells the reader that you did not take time with this application. The fix for most of them is the same: write for one job post, use specific examples, and check every detail before you send.

Why Small Mistakes Matter

A cover letter is a writing sample. The reader judges your care and your communication skills from it, not only your experience. A small error can make a reader doubt the whole application.

The good news: every mistake below is easy to fix once you know it. Use this list as an edit checklist for your next letter.

Content Mistakes

1. A Generic Letter

A letter that could go to any company tells the reader nothing. It also shows that you did not read their job post.

Fix: Name the company, the role, and one specific reason you want this job. Mention at least two requirements from the job post.

2. Repeating the Resume

Many letters list every job in order. The reader already has your resume.

Fix: Pick one or two results that match the job post best. Explain what you did and why it matters for this role.

3. Talking About What You Want

"This role would be a great step for my career" is about you. The employer wants to know what you give them.

Fix: Rewrite each "I want" sentence as a "you need, and I can do it" sentence.

Before After
"This role would help me grow my design skills." "Your post asks for someone who can redesign the checkout flow. I led a checkout redesign at [Company]."
"I am looking for a company with a good culture." "Your focus on [value] matches how I work. At [Company], I [example]."

4. No Proof

Words like "hardworking", "detail-oriented", and "team player" are claims without proof.

Fix: Replace each claim with a short example. Show, with a fact, that you are detail-oriented.

5. False or Exaggerated Claims

An inflated title or an invented number can end your application at the reference check or in the interview.

Fix: Use only facts that you can explain in detail. If you are not sure of a number, describe the result without it.

6. Apologizing for What You Lack

"Although I do not have experience in X..." points the reader to your weakest point.

Fix: Lead with what you have. If you must address a gap, do it briefly and connect it to a related skill.

7. Too Much Personal Information

Your age, family status, health, or reasons for leaving a past job are rarely needed.

Fix: Keep the letter about the job. Mention a personal detail only if it explains a clear fit, such as a move to the job's city.

Detail Mistakes

8. The Wrong Company Name or Job Title

This happens when you reuse a letter. It is the fastest way to lose a reader.

Fix: Search the letter for every company name and job title before you send it.

9. "To Whom It May Concern"

This greeting feels old and distant. It suggests that you did not try to find a name.

Fix: Search the job post, the company website, and LinkedIn for the hiring manager's name. If you cannot find one, use "Dear [Team Name] Hiring Team". This guide on how to address a cover letter covers every case.

10. Typos and Grammar Errors

Spelling errors are the most avoidable of all cover letter mistakes.

Fix: Run a spell check. Then read the letter aloud, slowly. Read it once more on your phone, because a new screen helps you see errors.

11. A Weak First Line

"I am writing to apply for the position of..." wastes the most important line.

Fix: Name the role and give a reason to read on in the same sentence. For example: "Your post for a [Job Title] asks for someone who can [requirement], and I have done that work for [number] years at [Company]."

Format Mistakes

12. Too Long

A letter longer than one page asks too much of a busy reader.

Fix: Keep it to about 250 to 400 words and three or four paragraphs. Follow a clean cover letter format with clear spacing.

13. A Hard-to-Read Layout

Small fonts, narrow margins, and long blocks of text make the letter hard to read.

Fix: Use a common font at 10 to 12 points, margins of about one inch, and short paragraphs.

14. The Wrong File Type or File Name

A file called "letter_final_v3.docx" looks careless.

Fix: Send a PDF unless the employer asks for another format. Name it "[First Name] [Last Name] Cover Letter [Company].pdf".

15. A Weak Ending

"I hope to hear from you" ends the letter on a passive note.

Fix: End with a clear next step and a thank you. For example: "I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help [team] with [goal]. Thank you for your time." See more ways to end a cover letter.

A Corrected Cover Letter Template

This template avoids every mistake above. Replace each item in square brackets.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Your post for a [Job Title] asks for someone who can [top requirement]. That is the work I have done for [number] years at [Current Company], and it is why I am applying.

At [Current Company], I [specific result that matches the top requirement]. I also [second result that matches another requirement]. Both projects needed [skill from the job post], which I use every day.

I am drawn to [Company] because of [specific detail: a product, a mission, or a team goal]. I would like to bring my experience in [skill] to help your team [goal from the job post].

I would welcome the chance to talk about the role. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely, [Your Name] [Phone Number] | [Email]

If you want a faster start, CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post. You still edit the draft with this checklist.

Final Checklist Before You Send

  • The company name and the job title are correct everywhere.
  • The greeting uses a name or a specific team.
  • The first line names the role and gives a reason to read on.
  • The letter mentions at least two requirements from the job post, with an example for each.
  • Every claim is true, and you can explain it in an interview.
  • The letter is one page or less, with short paragraphs.
  • Spelling and grammar are correct. You read it aloud.
  • The file is a PDF with a clear name, unless the employer asked for another format.

Fix these cover letter mistakes once, and your letters get better each time you write one.

title: How to Negotiate Salary: Steps, Scripts, and an Email Template
description: Learn how to negotiate salary after a job offer: research your number, make a counteroffer, use word-for-word scripts, and decide when to accept.

faqs.q: Can a company take back a job offer if I negotiate?
faqs.a: It can happen. You lower the risk when you ask politely, give reasons, and stay near the market range. Demands and very high numbers raise the risk.

faqs.q: How much more should I ask for in a counteroffer?
faqs.a: There is no fixed percentage. Base your number on your market research and the value of the role. Ask for a specific figure that you can support with reasons.

faqs.q: Should I negotiate by phone or by email?
faqs.a: Both work. A call lets you hear the recruiter's reaction and build rapport. An email gives you time to choose your words. Many people talk by phone and then confirm the details by email.

faqs.q: Can I negotiate an internal promotion or a raise the same way?
faqs.a: The same principles apply: research, a specific number, and reasons based on value. The timing differs, so tie a raise request to a review cycle or a clear new responsibility.

headings.text: How to Negotiate Salary in 7 Steps
Email Template for a Salary Counteroffer
A Note on Contracts and Rules

html:
To negotiate salary, wait for an offer and thank the employer. Then ask for a specific higher number, and support it with market research and the value you bring. Say it clearly, once, and then wait for their answer. If base salary cannot move, ask about other parts of the package. Examples are a signing bonus, extra paid time off, or an earlier salary review. Many employers expect a counteroffer, so a polite, specific request is a normal part of the offer stage.

When to Negotiate

The best time to negotiate is after you receive an offer and before you accept it. At that point, the employer has decided that they want you. They have spent time and money on interviews, and they want to close the process.

Before the offer, you only share your expectations. This guide explains how to answer "What are your salary expectations?" in the early stages. The real negotiation starts with the offer.

How to Negotiate Salary in 7 Steps

Step 1: Get the Full Offer in Writing

Ask for the details of the whole package: base salary, bonus, equity, benefits, paid time off, start date, and any other terms. You cannot judge an offer from the base salary alone.

Step 2: Thank Them and Ask for Time

You do not need to answer on the spot. Say thank you and ask for a day or two to review.

"Thank you, I am very happy to receive this offer. Could I have until [day] to review the details? I will come back to you then."

Most employers expect this and agree.

Step 3: Research Your Number

Compare the offer with the market range for the role, the level, and the location. Use the pay range in the job post, salary data sites, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook, and people in your network.

Then choose two numbers:

  • Your target: the salary you will ask for.
  • Your walk-away number: the lowest offer you would accept.

Step 4: List Your Reasons

A counteroffer is stronger when you give reasons. Good reasons are about value and the market, not about your personal costs.

  • The market range for the role is higher than the offer.
  • You bring a skill or a certification that the job post asked for.
  • Your experience is above the level the role requires.
  • You have another offer or a strong current position.

Step 5: Make the Counteroffer

Ask for one specific number. A specific figure, such as $92,000, sounds more researched than a round range. Say it once and then stop talking. The silence after your number is normal. Do not fill it with "but I am flexible".

Step 6: Listen and Respond

The employer may say yes, offer a number between theirs and yours, or say no. Each answer gives you information.

  • If they say yes, thank them and ask for the updated offer in writing.
  • If they meet you partway, decide if the new number is above your walk-away number.
  • If they say no to more base salary, ask about other parts of the package.

Step 7: Get the Final Offer in Writing

Do not resign from your current job or decline other offers until you have the final, signed offer in writing.

Scripts for Each Situation

Phone Script for a Counteroffer

"Thank you again for the offer. I am excited about the role and the team. Based on my research for [Job Title] roles in [location], and my experience with [key skill], I was hoping for a base salary of [$X]. Is there flexibility to get closer to that number?"

When You Have Another Offer

Use this only if it is true.

"[Company] is my first choice. I have another offer at [$X] base salary. If you can match it, I am ready to accept."

When Base Salary Is Fixed

"I understand that the base salary is set. Could we look at other parts of the package? A signing bonus of [$X] or [number] extra days of paid time off would help close the gap."

When the Offer Is Already Good

You can still ask, even when you like the offer.

"This is a strong offer, and I am ready to say yes. Is there any room for a small increase in base salary, or for a signing bonus?"

Email Template for a Salary Counteroffer

Subject: [Your Name], offer for [Job Title]

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you again for the offer for the [Job Title] role. I am excited about the chance to join [Company] and to work on [team goal or project].

I reviewed the details and the market range for this role in [location]. With my [number] years of experience in [key skill], I would like to ask for a base salary of [$X].

I am confident that I can deliver [specific value, for example a result from your past work that matches the role]. If we can agree on this number, I am ready to accept.

Thank you for considering it. I am happy to talk by phone if that is easier.

Best regards, [Your Name]

What Else You Can Negotiate

Item When it helps most
Signing bonus The base salary is fixed, or you lose a bonus at your current job
Paid time off You already have more time off at your current employer
Start date You need time to give notice or to rest between jobs
Remote or hybrid days Your commute or your family situation needs flexibility
Title The title affects your next job search
Salary review date The company wants to see results before a larger raise
Training budget You want a certification or a course that helps the role
Equity The company is private and equity is part of total pay

Choose the two or three items that matter most to you. A long list of requests can make the conversation harder.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Accepting on the spot when you wanted to negotiate.
  • Giving a range when the employer asks for your counteroffer. They will hear the low end.
  • Making personal reasons the main argument, such as rent or debt.
  • Lying about another offer.
  • Making many rounds of requests. Ask for everything that matters in one conversation.
  • Negotiating with an angry or demanding tone.
  • Resigning from your current job before you have the final offer in writing.

Know When to Stop

Negotiation has a natural end. When the employer says that this is their best and final offer, decide: accept, or decline politely. Do not keep pushing after that point.

Compare the final offer with your walk-away number, not with your target. If it is above your walk-away number and the role fits your goals, it is often a good offer to accept.

A Note on Contracts and Rules

Some offers include terms such as non-compete clauses, notice periods, or bonus repayment rules. These terms can matter as much as salary. Read the contract carefully, and check local rules or ask a qualified adviser if a term is unclear. Rules differ by state and country.

Learning how to negotiate salary takes one or two practice runs. Write your script, say it aloud to a friend, and use it on your next offer.

title: How to Look for a Job While Employed Without Your Boss Finding Out
description: How to look for a job while employed: keep your search private, schedule interviews, handle references, and resign the right way when you get an offer.
keyword: how to look for a job while employed

faqs.q: Can I be fired for looking for another job?
faqs.a: In much of the US, employment is "at will", so an employer may end it for many reasons. Rules differ by state and by contract, so check your contract and local rules if you are worried.

faqs.q: Should I tell my manager that I am looking for a new job?
faqs.a: Usually not, until you have a signed offer. Some people with a very trusting manager do share it, but it carries risk. Decide based on your own workplace.

faqs.q: What do I say if a coworker asks why I am dressed up?
faqs.a: Give a short, true answer that does not invite questions, such as "I have an appointment after work." You do not need to explain more.

faqs.q: Is it OK to job search on LinkedIn while employed?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the private setting that shows recruiters you are open to work without a public banner. No setting fully guarantees privacy, so assume that someone at your company could see your activity.

headings.text: Why Search While You Still Have a Job
Rules to Keep Your Search Private
How to Look for a Job While Employed: Step by Step
What to Say in Interviews About Your Current Job

html:
To look for a job while employed, keep the search private and separate from your current work. Use your personal phone, email, and laptop. Schedule interviews outside your core hours or take personal time for them. Do not tell coworkers until you have a signed offer. A quiet, steady search lets you choose your next role without pressure, because you still have income.

Why Search While You Still Have a Job

A job search while employed has real advantages. You have income, so you can say no to roles that do not fit. You can negotiate from a stronger position, because you do not need the job.

The challenge is time and privacy. You must do the search in a few hours each week, and you must protect your current job while you do it.

Rules to Keep Your Search Private

Follow these rules from the first day:

  1. Use only personal devices. Your employer may be able to monitor company laptops, phones, and networks.
  2. Use a personal email address and a personal phone number on your resume.
  3. Do not search, apply, or take calls on company time or at your desk.
  4. Do not store your resume or cover letters on company systems or cloud drives.
  5. Do not tell coworkers, even close ones. News travels.
  6. Do not post about your search in public.
  7. Keep your current work at the same level. A drop in performance gets attention.

How to Look for a Job While Employed: Step by Step

Step 1: Decide What You Want

Write down why you want to leave and what your next job must have. Name the role, the pay range, the location or remote setup, and two or three must-haves. This keeps your search focused and saves time.

Step 2: Make a Weekly Plan

You have limited hours, so plan them. For example, you might use two weekday evenings and one weekend morning. Set a small weekly goal, such as five strong applications and two networking messages. This guide on how to build a job search plan shows a full method.

Step 3: Update Your Materials Quietly

Update your resume and cover letter on your personal computer. Update your LinkedIn profile in small steps over several days. Many sudden changes at once can look like a signal. If LinkedIn lets you turn off notifications to your network about profile changes, turn them off first.

Step 4: Use Your Network With Care

Referrals are a strong channel when you have little time. Ask people you trust outside your company. This guide on how to ask for a referral has message templates. Ask each contact to keep your search confidential.

Step 5: Track Everything

With a full-time job, it is easy to forget which roles you applied to. Keep a simple job application tracker with the company, the role, the date, the contact, and the next step.

Step 6: Ask Recruiters for Confidentiality

When you talk to a recruiter, say that your search is confidential. This is a normal request.

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you for your message about the [Job Title] role. I am interested. I am currently employed at [Current Company], so I ask that you keep my application confidential and do not contact my current employer.

I am available for a call on [day] before [time] or after [time] [time zone], or during my lunch break from [time] to [time].

Best regards, [Your Name]

How to Schedule Interviews

Interviews are the hardest part of a search while employed. Use these options:

  • Ask for early morning, lunchtime, or late afternoon slots.
  • Ask if the first rounds can be by phone or video.
  • Take a call from your car, a quiet room outside the office, or your home.
  • Take a personal day or a half day for a final round that needs many hours.
  • Group interviews from different companies on the same day off, if you can.

When you take time off, you do not need to give a detailed reason. "I have a personal appointment" is enough. Do not invent a story, such as a fake illness. A lie is hard to keep up and can hurt your reputation.

For a video interview from home, check the background and the light, and keep your current company's logo off the screen.

How to Handle References

Employers usually ask for references near the end of the process. Do not list your current manager unless you want them to know.

Use these references instead:

  • A former manager from a previous job.
  • A former coworker who has left your current company.
  • A client or a partner who knows your work, if that is normal in your field.

Tell the hiring company that they may contact your current employer only after you accept an offer. This is a common request.

What to Say in Interviews About Your Current Job

Interviewers will ask why you want to leave. Keep your answer positive and about the future.

"I have learned a lot at [Current Company], especially in [skill]. I want a role where I can [goal, such as lead a team], and this role offers that."

Do not criticize your current employer. Do not share confidential information about your current company, its clients, or its plans.

When You Get an Offer

Do not resign until you have the final offer in writing and you have accepted it. If the offer depends on a background check or references, wait until those are complete if you can.

Then resign in a professional way:

  1. Read your contract for your notice period and any terms about leaving.
  2. Tell your manager first, in person or by video if you can.
  3. Follow with a short written resignation that gives your last day.
  4. Offer to help with the handover.
  5. Work well until your last day.

Your current employer may make a counteroffer. Think about why you started your search. Often the reasons you wanted to leave do not change with a higher salary.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Applying from your work email or computer.
  • Taking interview calls in the open office.
  • Leaving a printed resume on the office printer.
  • Telling a coworker "in secret".
  • Taking many sudden days off in a row.
  • Letting your current work slip.
  • Resigning before the offer is final and in writing.

Rules about notice periods, contracts, and at-will employment differ by state and by country. Check your contract and local rules before you resign.

When you know how to look for a job while employed, the search becomes a calm, steady process. You protect your income, you keep your reputation, and you choose your next role with care.

title: Behavioral Interview Questions: 30 Examples and How to Answer
description: Common behavioral interview questions grouped by skill, with a simple answer structure, sample answers, and a story bank you can prepare in one evening.

faqs.q: How many stories should I prepare for a behavioral interview?
faqs.a: Prepare six to eight strong stories. One story can often answer several questions if you change which part you stress.

faqs.q: Can I use the same story twice in one interview?
faqs.a: Try not to. If you have no other example, use it again but stress a different skill, and say that it is the same project.

faqs.q: What if I do not have work experience for a behavioral question?
faqs.a: Use an example from school, volunteer work, a part-time job, a sports team, or a personal project. The interviewer wants to see how you act, not only where.

faqs.q: How long should a behavioral answer be?
faqs.a: Aim for about one to two minutes. Spend most of the time on what you did and the result, not on the background.

headings.text: How to Spot a Behavioral Question
Build Your Story Bank in One Evening

html:
Behavioral interview questions ask you to describe how you handled a real situation in the past, such as "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a coworker." The interviewer uses your past actions to predict how you will act in the new job. Answer each one with a specific story: the situation, what you did, and the result. Prepare six to eight stories before the interview, and you can answer most behavioral questions with confidence.

How to Spot a Behavioral Question

Behavioral questions usually start with one of these phrases:

  • "Tell me about a time when..."
  • "Give me an example of..."
  • "Describe a situation where..."
  • "Have you ever...?"
  • "What did you do when...?"

They differ from hypothetical questions, such as "What would you do if...?" A behavioral question asks what you did. A hypothetical question asks what you would do. For a behavioral question, always tell a real story.

The Answer Structure

The most common structure for behavioral answers is the STAR method:

  1. Situation: the context, in one or two sentences.
  2. Task: your goal or your responsibility.
  3. Action: the specific steps that you took.
  4. Result: what happened, with a number or a clear outcome if you can.

Spend the most time on the action and the result. Use "I", not "we", so the interviewer knows what you did. This full guide to the STAR method interview has more examples.

Behavioral Interview Questions by Skill

Interviewers choose questions that match the skills in the job post. Read the post and expect questions about its main skills.

Teamwork

  1. Tell me about a time you worked on a team to reach a difficult goal.
  2. Describe a time you disagreed with a coworker. What did you do?
  3. Give me an example of how you helped a teammate who was struggling.
  4. Tell me about a time you worked with someone whose style was very different from yours.

Problem Solving

  1. Tell me about a difficult problem you solved at work.
  2. Describe a time you found a better way to do a task.
  3. Give me an example of a decision you made with incomplete information.
  4. Tell me about a time you had to learn something new quickly.

Leadership and Initiative

  1. Tell me about a time you led a project.
  2. Describe a time you took the lead without being asked.
  3. Give me an example of how you motivated others.
  4. Tell me about a time you had to give difficult feedback.

Conflict and Pressure

  1. Describe a time you worked under a tight deadline.
  2. Tell me about a time you dealt with an unhappy customer.
  3. Give me an example of a time you had too much work. How did you prioritize?
  4. Tell me about a time you had a conflict with your manager.

Failure and Growth

  1. Tell me about a time you made a mistake. What did you learn?
  2. Describe a project that did not go as planned.
  3. Give me an example of feedback that changed how you work.
  4. Tell me about a goal you did not reach.

Communication

  1. Tell me about a time you explained a complex idea to someone outside your field.
  2. Describe a time you had to persuade someone to change their mind.
  3. Give me an example of a time you had to deliver bad news.
  4. Tell me about a presentation that went well or badly.

Adaptability

  1. Tell me about a time your priorities changed suddenly.
  2. Describe how you handled a major change at work.
  3. Give me an example of a time you worked outside your comfort zone.

Values and Ethics

  1. Tell me about a time you saw someone break a rule. What did you do?
  2. Describe a time you put the customer's needs first.
  3. Give me an example of a time you admitted a mistake to your manager.

Sample Answers

Use these as models. Replace every detail with your own true story.

"Tell me about a time you disagreed with a coworker."

"On my last team, a coworker and I disagreed about the launch date for a new feature. She wanted to launch on time, and I thought we needed one more week of testing. My task was to find a way forward without delaying the whole team. I asked for a 30-minute meeting and showed her the three bugs I had found. We agreed to launch on time with the feature hidden for most users, and to fix the bugs that week. The launch went well, and we used the same approach for the next two releases."

"Tell me about a time you made a mistake."

"In my first year as an analyst, I sent a weekly report to leadership with an error in one formula. The sales numbers for one region were too high. I found it the next morning and told my manager right away. I sent a correction with a short note and checked the other reports for the same error. Then I built a simple check sheet that compares totals before each report goes out. I have not repeated that error since, and two coworkers now use the same check sheet."

A question about a mistake is close to the question about your weakness. This guide to the greatest weakness interview answer shows how to make both honest and useful.

Build Your Story Bank in One Evening

You do not need 30 separate stories. Build a bank of six to eight stories that cover many skills.

  1. List your main projects and moments from the last three to five years.
  2. For each one, write the situation, task, action, and result in short notes.
  3. Mark which skills each story shows: teamwork, leadership, conflict, failure, and so on.
  4. Make sure that each skill in the job post has at least one story.
  5. Include at least one story about a mistake or a failure.
  6. Practice each story aloud until it takes one to two minutes.
Story Skills it shows
[Project with a tight deadline] Pressure, prioritizing, teamwork
[Disagreement about a decision] Conflict, communication, influence
[Mistake you fixed] Failure, ownership, process improvement
[Project you led] Leadership, initiative, planning
[Difficult customer] Customer focus, calm under pressure
[New skill learned fast] Adaptability, learning

Fill in your own stories in the first column.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • A general answer. "I always communicate well with my team" is not a story.
  • A hypothetical answer. Do not say what you would do. Say what you did.
  • Too much background. The interviewer does not need the full history of the project.
  • No result. Always finish with what happened and what you learned.
  • Only "we". The interviewer needs to know your part.
  • A story that makes a coworker look bad. Describe the situation fairly.
  • A made-up story. Follow-up questions will show the gaps.

Practice Before the Interview

Ask a friend to read questions from the list above in random order. Answer each one with a story from your bank. Record yourself if you can, and check the length and the clarity.

Behavioral interview questions often appear together with other common interview questions, so prepare both types. With a story bank, each new question becomes a choice of which story to tell, not a test of memory.

title: How to Find Remote Jobs: A Practical Search Method That Works
description: How to find remote jobs: search with the right filters and terms, check location rules, adapt your resume for remote work, and avoid remote job scams.

faqs.q: Are remote jobs harder to get than office jobs?
faqs.a: Often, yes, because one remote post can attract applicants from a whole country. You improve your chances when you target roles that fit you closely and tailor each application.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a remote job in another state?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Many US remote jobs are open only in certain states, because of tax, payroll, and legal rules. Read the location line in the job post before you apply.

faqs.q: Do remote jobs pay less?
faqs.a: It varies. Some companies pay the same for a role everywhere, and some adjust pay by location. Ask the recruiter how the company sets pay for remote roles.

faqs.q: What skills do employers look for in remote workers?
faqs.a: Clear writing, reliable time management, and comfort with remote tools are common needs. Show them with examples on your resume and in your interview.

headings.text: Know the Types of Remote Jobs
How to Find Remote Jobs: 7 Search Methods
Check the Location Rules in Every Post
How to Spot Remote Job Scams

html:
To find remote jobs, search job boards with the "remote" filter and also with terms like "work from home", "distributed", and "anywhere in the US". Then check the location rules in each post, because many remote jobs are open only in certain states or time zones. Target companies that already work remotely, use your network for referrals, and tailor each application to show that you work well without an office. Avoid any "remote job" that asks you to pay money or share bank details before an offer.

Know the Types of Remote Jobs

The word "remote" means different things in different posts. Read the details before you apply.

Type What it usually means
Fully remote You can work from anywhere, often within one country
Remote within a region You must live in certain states or time zones
Remote first Most of the team is remote, but there may be an office
Hybrid You work from an office on some days each week
Temporary remote The role is remote now but may move to an office later
Remote with travel You work from home but travel for meetings or clients

Decide which types you accept before you start. This saves you from long interview processes for jobs that do not fit.

How to Find Remote Jobs: 7 Search Methods

1. Use Filters on Large Job Boards

Most large job boards have a remote filter. Use it, but do not trust it alone. Some posts that are marked remote are hybrid, and some fully remote jobs are not marked. Read each post.

2. Search With More Than One Term

Companies describe remote work in different ways. Search with each of these terms plus your job title:

  • "remote"
  • "work from home"
  • "distributed team"
  • "anywhere in the US"
  • "virtual"
  • "telecommute"

3. Use Remote-Focused Job Boards

Some job boards list only remote jobs. They can save you time, because you do not need to filter out office roles. Check that a board shows the company name and links to the company's own careers page.

4. Target Remote-First Companies

Companies that already run fully remote teams hire remotely all year. Make a list of 20 to 30 such companies in your field. Many of them say on their careers page that they are remote first or distributed. Check their careers pages each week.

5. Use Your Network

Ask former coworkers who work remotely how their company hires. Ask about open roles and referrals. A referral can be especially helpful for remote roles, because they may attract many applicants. This guide on how to ask for a referral has message templates.

6. Set Job Alerts

Create saved searches with your title, the word "remote", and your country or state. Turn on daily email alerts. Early applications are easier for a recruiter to see before the list gets long.

7. Look at Contract and Freelance Work

Some remote roles start as contracts. A contract can turn into a full-time role, and it gives you recent remote experience for your resume. Check the terms carefully, because contract work often has different taxes and benefits.

Check the Location Rules in Every Post

This is the step that most applicants skip. A remote job in the US is often limited to certain states. The employer must follow payroll, tax, and employment rules in each state where staff live.

Look for lines like these in the post:

  • "Remote, US only"
  • "Remote in [list of states]"
  • "Must work [time zone] hours"
  • "Must live within [distance] of [city]"

If you live outside the listed area, do not apply unless the post says that the list may change. Rules differ by country too, so a "remote" job in another country usually does not mean that you can work from anywhere in the world.

Make Your Application Remote-Ready

Remote employers often look for proof that you can work well on your own. Show it in your materials.

Your Resume

  • Add "Remote" next to past remote roles, for example "Data Analyst, [Company] (Remote)".
  • Mention remote tools that you use, such as video meeting software, chat tools, and project management tools.
  • Add results that show independent work and clear communication.

Then tailor your resume to the job description for each role.

Your Cover Letter

Add one or two sentences about how you work remotely. Use a specific example.

I have worked remotely for [number] years with a team across [number] time zones. At [Company], I [result], and I kept the project on track with written weekly updates and short video check-ins. I am comfortable working on my own and I write clearly, which matters on a team like yours at [Company].

Your Interview

Expect questions such as "How do you stay organized when you work from home?" and "How do you communicate with a team you do not see every day?" Prepare a short story for each one. Test your camera, microphone, and internet connection before every video interview.

How to Spot Remote Job Scams

Fake remote jobs are a real risk, because remote work is in demand and the whole process can happen online. Watch for these warning signs:

  • The employer asks you to pay for training, equipment, or a starter kit.
  • They send you a check and ask you to send part of the money back.
  • The interview happens only by text chat or instant messaging.
  • The offer comes very fast, with no real interview.
  • They ask for your bank details or your Social Security number before a written offer.
  • The email comes from a free email address, not the company's domain.
  • The pay is much higher than normal for the work.

If you are not sure, find the company's official website on your own and contact them through it. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) also publishes advice on job scams on its consumer website.

Keep Your Search Organized

Remote searches often involve many applications to companies in different places. Track each one with the company, the role, the location rules, the date, and the next step. If you search while you still have a job, this guide on how to look for a job while employed shows how to keep the search private and steady.

Checklist Before You Apply

  • The post is fully remote, or the type of remote work fits you.
  • You live in an allowed state, country, or time zone.
  • The company is real, and the post links to its own careers page.
  • Your resume shows remote experience or independent work.
  • Your cover letter has one specific example of how you work remotely.
  • Nobody asked you for money or bank details.

Learning how to find remote jobs takes a little more care than an office search. Use several search terms, check the location rules, and apply to fewer roles with stronger applications.

title: Internship Cover Letter: How to Write One, With a Full Example
description: Write an internship cover letter with no full-time experience. Get a 5-part structure, a fill-in template, a full example, and a final checklist.

faqs.q: Should I include my GPA in an internship cover letter?
faqs.a: Include your GPA if the posting asks for it or if it is strong for your field. If it is not strong, leave it out of the letter and let your coursework and projects carry the case.

faqs.q: Can I use the same internship cover letter for every application?
faqs.a: You can reuse the structure and some proof lines. Change the opening, the reason you want this company, and the skills you match, because those parts must fit each posting.

faqs.q: Is it OK to send an internship cover letter as the body of an email?
faqs.a: Yes, if the posting tells you to apply by email. Put a short version in the email body and attach the full letter as a PDF unless the instructions say otherwise.

faqs.q: How do I write an internship cover letter for a company that has no open posting?
faqs.a: Address the letter to a team lead or the campus recruiter, say which kind of internship you want and when you are available, and ask if they expect openings for that term.

headings.text: What an Internship Cover Letter Must Do
How to Write an Internship Cover Letter in 5 Parts
What to Write When You Have Little Experience

html:
An internship cover letter is a one-page letter that tells an employer two things: why you want this internship, and why you can do the work. Use your classes, projects, part-time jobs, clubs, and volunteer work as proof. Keep it to about 250 to 350 words, name the internship and the term, and match two or three skills to the posting.

Most internship applicants have the same problem: the resume looks thin. The cover letter is where you fix that. It gives you room to explain one project in detail. It also shows that you read the posting and that you will be easy to work with.

What an Internship Cover Letter Must Do

A hiring manager who reads an internship cover letter does not expect years of results. They want answers to a few simple questions:

  • Do you know what this internship is and what the team does?
  • Can you do the basic tasks in the posting, or learn them fast?
  • Did you finish things before, such as a project, a job, or a club role?
  • Are you available for the dates and hours of the program?
  • Will you be reliable and easy to work with?

Every paragraph in your letter should answer one or more of these questions. If a sentence does not, cut it.

How to Write an Internship Cover Letter in 5 Parts

1. The header and greeting

Put your name, email, phone number, and city at the top. Add a LinkedIn or portfolio link if it shows relevant work. Then address a real person if you can find one. Check the posting, the company careers page, and LinkedIn for the internship coordinator or team lead. If you cannot find a name, "Dear [Team Name] Hiring Team" is fine. For more options, read how to address a cover letter.

2. The opening paragraph

Name the internship, the term, and your school and year. Then give one specific reason you want this internship at this company. A specific reason is a product you use, a project the team published, or a skill the posting names that matches your studies.

Example opening lines:

  • "I am a junior in marketing at [University], and I am applying for the [Season Year] Marketing Internship at [Company]."
  • "Your posting asks for someone who can clean and chart data in Excel. I did that every week this year for my research lab."

3. The proof paragraph

This is the most important part. Pick one or two experiences and describe them with facts: what you did, what tools you used, and what happened. Class projects count. A part-time job counts. A club role counts.

Weak: "I am a hard worker with strong communication skills."

Strong: "As treasurer of the [Club Name], I tracked a budget of [amount] in Google Sheets and sent a monthly report to 40 members."

Use numbers only when they are true. A small, real number is better than a big, vague claim.

4. The fit paragraph

Connect your skills to two or three requirements in the posting. Use the same words that the posting uses, if they are true for you. This also helps if the company uses an applicant tracking system, because many of these systems search for terms from the posting. Then say what you want to learn. Internships are training programs, and a clear learning goal shows that you will use the time well.

5. The close

Confirm your availability (dates, hours, and whether you can work on site, hybrid, or remote). Thank the reader and ask for a conversation. Sign with your full name.

Internship Cover Letter Template

Copy this template and replace every item in square brackets.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I am a [year] studying [major] at [University], and I am applying for the [Internship Title] for [Season Year] at [Company]. I want to join [Company] because [specific reason: a product, a project, or a team goal you read about].

In [class, job, or club], I [specific task] using [tool or skill]. The result was [what happened, with a true number if you have one]. That work taught me [skill from the posting], which your posting lists as a key part of the role.

Your posting also asks for [requirement 2] and [requirement 3]. I [one line of proof for requirement 2], and I [one line of proof for requirement 3]. During the internship, I want to learn [specific skill or area], and I am ready to take on the routine tasks that help the team.

I am available from [start date] to [end date] for [hours per week], and I can work [on site / hybrid / remote]. Thank you for your time. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can help [Team Name] this [season].

Sincerely, [Your Name]

Full Internship Cover Letter Example

Here is a complete example for a data analyst internship. The student and the company are fictional.

Dear Ms. Rivera,

I am a junior studying economics at Lakeview State University, and I am applying for the Summer 2028 Data Analyst Internship at Northpoint Foods. I use your store app every week, and I want to help the team that decides which offers customers see in it.

This year, I worked as a research assistant in the economics department. I cleaned survey data from 600 students in Excel, built pivot tables, and made charts for a faculty report. I learned to check every column for errors before I start the analysis, and I learned to explain a chart in two sentences.

Your posting asks for SQL and clear written communication. I completed an introductory SQL course this spring and used it in a class project to compare prices across 12 grocery chains. I also write a weekly summary for my lab, so I am used to short, clear reports. During the internship, I want to learn how a retail team tests offers and measures the results.

I am available from June 1 to August 14, full time, and I can work on site in Chicago. Thank you for your time. I would welcome a conversation about how I can help your analytics team this summer.

Sincerely, Jordan Lee

What to Write When You Have Little Experience

If you have no job and no big project yet, use what you have. These sources all count as proof:

Source What to show Example line
Class project A skill from the posting and a finished result "I built a budget model in Excel for a team of four."
Part-time job Reliability, customer contact, and responsibility "I trained two new staff members on the register."
Club or team Organization and teamwork "I planned three events and managed the sign-up list."
