Volunteer work Commitment and people skills "I tutored two middle school students every week for a year."
Personal project Initiative and a tool you learned alone "I built a small website to track my running times."

For more ideas, read our guide to a cover letter with no experience.

Common Internship Cover Letter Mistakes

  • You write about what the internship will do for you, and not about what you can do for the team.
  • You copy your resume line by line. The letter should add detail, not repeat.
  • You use the wrong company name. This happens when you reuse a letter. Read every name twice.
  • You write more than one page. Most internship letters need three or four short paragraphs. See how long a cover letter should be for word counts.
  • You forget your availability. Programs have fixed dates, so state yours.
  • You use general praise such as "your company is a leader in the industry." Give a specific reason instead.

Final Checklist Before You Send

  • The letter names the internship title, the term, and your school.
  • The opening gives one specific reason for this company.
  • One paragraph describes a real project or job with facts.
  • You match two or three requirements from the posting, in the posting's words.
  • You state your dates, hours, and work location.
  • The letter is one page and between 250 and 350 words.
  • You saved the file as a PDF with your name in the file name, unless the posting asks for another format.
  • You read the letter out loud once to find errors.

If you apply to many internships, a tool can save time on the first draft. CoverBetter writes a first draft from your resume and the job post, and you then edit the facts and the reasons so they are yours.

Schools, countries, and companies can have different rules for internship applications. Always follow the instructions in the posting or from your career center first.

title: How to Compare Job Offers: A Side-by-Side Method That Works
description: Learn how to compare job offers on total pay, benefits, growth, and daily life. Use the scorecard, the questions to ask, and the decision steps.

faqs.q: How long can I take to decide between two job offers?
faqs.a: Many employers expect an answer within a few days to a week. Ask for a specific deadline when you receive the offer, and ask politely for more time if you need it.

faqs.q: Should I tell a company that I have another offer?
faqs.a: You can, if it is true and you would accept their offer on better terms. Say it plainly and do not invent details, because employers sometimes ask to see the other offer.

faqs.q: Is a signing bonus worth more than a higher base salary?
faqs.a: Usually a higher base salary is worth more over time, because raises and bonuses often build on it. A signing bonus is paid once and can have a repayment rule if you leave early.

faqs.q: How do I compare a remote job offer with an in-office offer?
faqs.a: Put a dollar value on the commute, the work clothes, and the meals you save, and a time value on the hours you get back. Then compare that with any pay difference between the two offers.

headings.text: Step 2: Get Every Offer in Writing
Step 3: Compare the Money Side by Side
Step 4: Score the Things That Are Not Money
Questions to Ask Before You Decide
Step 6: Make the Decision and Close Both Doors Well
Common Mistakes When You Compare Job Offers

html:
To compare job offers, put each offer in one table and compare the same items. These include base pay, bonus, equity, benefits, time off, schedule, location, the role, the manager, and growth. Turn every money item into a yearly dollar amount. Then score the items that are not money against the priorities you write down before you look at the numbers. The best offer is the one that wins on the items that matter most to you, not the one with the biggest salary.

Two offers at the same time feel like good news, and they are. But they also create pressure, because each employer wants an answer soon. A clear method helps you decide fast and with less regret.

Step 1: Write Your Priorities First

Before you open the offer letters again, write down what you need from your next job. Do this first, so the biggest number does not decide for you.

Answer these questions on paper:

  • What is the lowest yearly pay that covers your costs and savings goals?
  • Do you need health insurance for a partner or children?
  • How many days a week can you commute, and how far?
  • What do you want to learn in the next two years?
  • What kind of manager helps you do your best work?
  • How much risk can you accept (for example, a new startup or a role with a large commission)?

Then rank your top five items. You will use this ranking in Step 4.

Step 2: Get Every Offer in Writing

You cannot compare job offers well with verbal numbers. Ask each employer for a written offer that includes:

  • Job title and start date
  • Base salary and pay schedule
  • Bonus target and how it is paid
  • Equity grant, vesting schedule, and type (for example, stock options or restricted stock units)
  • Signing bonus and any repayment rule
  • Benefits summary (health, dental, vision, retirement plan, and match)
  • Paid time off and holidays
  • Work location and remote or hybrid policy

If a detail is missing, ask for it. A simple email works: "Thank you for the offer. Before I decide, could you send the benefits summary and the details of the retirement match?"

Step 3: Compare the Money Side by Side

Turn every money item into a yearly number. This is the core of how to compare job offers fairly. Use a table like this one.

Item Offer A Offer B
Base salary [amount] [amount]
Target bonus (yearly) [amount] [amount]
Equity (yearly value of the vesting) [amount] [amount]
Signing bonus (spread over the years you expect to stay) [amount] [amount]
Retirement match (yearly) [amount] [amount]
Your health insurance cost (yearly) [minus amount] [minus amount]
Commute cost (yearly) [minus amount] [minus amount]
Total yearly value [total] [total]

A few rules make the numbers more honest:

  • Count a bonus at its target only if the company paid it in past years. Ask: "How much of the target bonus did people in this role receive last year?"
  • Treat equity in a private company as uncertain. It can be worth a lot, or nothing. Many people count it at a discount or at zero for the main comparison.
  • Compare health plans by your likely total cost: the premium, the deductible, and the out-of-pocket maximum. A cheap premium with a high deductible can cost more if you see a doctor often.
  • Check the cost of living if the jobs are in different cities. Housing is often the biggest difference.

Taxes, equity, and retirement plans have complex rules. If a large part of an offer is equity, talk to a tax professional before you decide.

Step 4: Score the Things That Are Not Money

Money is only part of the decision. Many people leave jobs because of the manager, the hours, or a lack of growth. Score each offer from 1 to 5 on the items you ranked in Step 1.

Factor Weight (1 to 5) Offer A score Offer B score
The work you will do every day [weight] [score] [score]
Your manager [weight] [score] [score]
Growth and learning [weight] [score] [score]
Schedule and flexibility [weight] [score] [score]
Team and culture [weight] [score] [score]
Job security [weight] [score] [score]

Multiply each score by its weight, then add the results. The total does not make the decision for you. But it shows you where each offer is strong and where it is weak.

Questions to Ask Before You Decide

If you do not have enough facts to score an item, ask. Employers expect questions at the offer stage. These questions get useful answers:

  • "What would a successful first six months look like in this role?"
  • "How do people in this role usually grow? Can you give an example?"
  • "How are raises decided, and how often?"
  • "What are the normal working hours for this team, and how often do people work late?"
  • "Can I talk with someone who would be my peer on the team?"
  • "Has the team changed much in the past year?"

Also look at the company from the outside. Read recent news about the company. Check reviews from current and past employees, and read them for patterns, not single stories.

Step 5: Negotiate Before You Choose

A second offer often gives you room to ask for more. If you prefer Offer A but Offer B pays more, ask Offer A to close the gap. Be honest and specific.

Hi [Recruiter Name],

Thank you again for the offer for the [Job Title] role. I am excited about [Company] and the work on [team or project]. I have another offer with a base salary of [amount]. [Company] is my first choice. If you can move the base salary to [amount], I am ready to accept this week.

Best regards, [Your Name]

Only say you will accept if you mean it. For more on how to ask, read our guide on how to negotiate salary.

Step 6: Make the Decision and Close Both Doors Well

Look at your money table and your score table together. Then ask yourself two last questions:

  • Which job would you regret turning down in a year?
  • Which job fits the life you want right now, not only the career you want later?

When you choose, accept the offer in writing first. Then decline the other offer quickly and politely, so the company can move to its next candidate. Thank them by name and keep the message short. You may want to work with these people later.

Common Mistakes When You Compare Job Offers

  • You compare only the base salary and ignore benefits, bonus, and commute costs.
  • You count private company equity as if it were cash.
  • You decide before you have every detail in writing.
  • You accept one offer verbally and then keep negotiating with the other company.
  • You ignore the manager. Ask to meet the person you will report to if you have not.
  • You let a short deadline force a decision. Ask for a few more days if you need them.

Offer rules and benefits differ by country and by state, so check the local rules that apply to your offer.

title: Informational Interview Questions: 40 to Ask, Plus How to Ask
description: Get 40 informational interview questions by topic, a request message template, a 20-minute plan for the call, and a thank-you note you can copy.

faqs.q: How long should an informational interview last?
faqs.a: Ask for 15 to 20 minutes and keep to that time. If the other person wants to talk longer, let them choose to continue.

faqs.q: Can I ask for a job in an informational interview?
faqs.a: Do not ask for a job directly. Ask for advice and information. If the conversation goes well, you can ask at the end if they know of any openings or anyone else you should talk to.

faqs.q: What should I wear to an informational interview?
faqs.a: Dress one step more formal than the person's usual work clothes. On a video call, a clean, simple top and a quiet background are enough.

faqs.q: What if the person does not reply to my request?
faqs.a: Send one short follow-up after about a week. If there is still no reply, thank them in your mind and ask someone else.

headings.text: How to Ask for an Informational Interview
What to Do After the Interview

html:
Good informational interview questions ask about the other person's real work and advice, not about a job opening. Ask how they got into their role and what a normal week looks like. Then ask which skills matter most, what they wish they knew earlier, and who else you should talk to. Prepare 8 to 10 questions for a 20-minute conversation, and choose the 5 or 6 that fit best when the call starts.

An informational interview is a short conversation with someone who does the job, works at the company, or is in the field that interests you. You are not applying for anything. You are collecting facts and advice that you cannot find online. Often, you also make a new professional contact.

How to Ask for an Informational Interview

Keep the request short and specific. Say who you are, why you chose this person, and what you want: a short call at a time that suits them. Make it easy to say yes.

Hi [First Name],

I am a [your role or status] interested in [field or role]. I read your [post, article, or profile] about [specific topic], and I would value your advice. Would you be open to a 20-minute call in the next two weeks? I can work around your schedule. I want to learn how you got into [field] and what skills matter most in your role.

Thank you, [Your Name]

If you send this on LinkedIn, cut it to fit the connection note limit. Our guide on how to message a recruiter has more tips for short messages that get replies.

Informational Interview Questions by Topic

You do not need all 40. Pick the questions that fit your goal and the person.

Questions about their path

  1. How did you get into this field?
  2. What did you do before this role?
  3. What made you choose this company?
  4. Was there a turning point in your career? What happened?
  5. If you started again today, what would you do differently?
  6. What do you wish you knew in your first year?

Questions about the work

  1. What does a normal week look like for you?
  2. Which parts of your job take the most time?
  3. What do you enjoy most about the work?
  4. What is the hardest part of the job?
  5. Which tools or software do you use every day?
  6. Who do you work with most, inside and outside your team?
  7. How does your team measure success?
  8. What problems is your team trying to solve this year?

Questions about skills and hiring

  1. Which skills matter most for success in this role?
  2. Which skills are hard to find in candidates?
  3. What do strong new hires do in their first few months?
  4. What experience would make a candidate look ready for this kind of role?
  5. Are certifications or degrees important in this field, or does experience count more?
  6. How do people in this field usually find their jobs?
  7. What makes an application or resume strong for this type of role?
  8. What mistakes do you see people make when they try to enter this field?

Questions about the company and culture

  1. How would you describe the culture on your team?
  2. How do people here get feedback?
  3. How do people usually grow or move up here?
  4. How has the company changed since you joined?
  5. What kind of person does well here? What kind of person has a hard time?
  6. How do teams here work with remote or hybrid colleagues?

Questions about the field

  1. Which changes in this field do you expect over the next few years?
  2. Which companies do interesting work in this field?
  3. Which publications, newsletters, or groups do you follow?
  4. Are there events or associations that you recommend?
  5. Which roles are close to yours that I should also look at?

Questions about your own plan

  1. Based on my background, what gaps should I close first?
  2. Is there a type of project I could do now to build relevant experience?
  3. How would you describe my background to someone in your field?
  4. What would you do in my position?
  5. Do I sound realistic about my timeline?

Closing questions

  1. Who else do you recommend I talk to?
  2. Is there anything I did not ask that I should know?

A 20-Minute Plan for the Conversation

A plan helps you respect the other person's time and still get the most useful answers.

Time What to do
Minutes 0 to 2 Thank them. Give a 30-second summary of your background and your goal.
Minutes 2 to 8 Ask about their path and their work (2 or 3 questions).
Minutes 8 to 15 Ask about skills, hiring, and the company (2 or 3 questions).
Minutes 15 to 18 Ask for advice about your plan (1 or 2 questions).
Minutes 18 to 20 Ask who else to talk to. Thank them and end on time.

Watch the clock. At minute 18, say, "I want to respect your time. I have one last question." If they want to keep talking, they will tell you.

How to Prepare

  • Read the person's LinkedIn profile, recent posts, and any articles they wrote.
  • Read the company website and recent news.
  • Write your 30-second summary: who you are, what you do now, and what you want to learn.
  • Choose your 8 to 10 questions and put the most important ones first.
  • Prepare a short answer if they ask, "How can I help you?" Have one specific request ready, such as a name of another person to talk to.
  • Test your video link and audio if the call is online.

Questions to Avoid

Some questions waste the time or make the other person uncomfortable:

  • Questions you could answer with a quick search, such as "What does your company do?"
  • "Can you get me a job?" or "Are you hiring?" at the start of the call.
  • Questions about their salary. You can ask about pay ranges for the role in general if the conversation is open, but use care.
  • Questions about private company information.
  • Questions that criticize their employer or their choices.

What to Do After the Interview

Send a thank-you message the same day or the next day. Mention one specific piece of advice and what you will do with it.

Hi [First Name],

Thank you for your time today. Your advice about [specific advice] was very helpful. This week, I will [action you will take]. I will also reach out to [Name they recommended], as you suggested.

I will let you know how it goes.

Best, [Your Name]

Then keep the contact alive. Send a short update in a month or two, when you act on their advice or when you get a result. People like to know that their help made a difference.

If you later see an opening at their company, you can ask if they would refer you. Our guide on how to ask for a referral shows how to do that without pressure.

Common Informational Interview Mistakes

  • You talk more than you listen. Aim for the other person to talk most of the time.
  • You go over the time you asked for.
  • You read your questions like a survey and do not follow up on interesting answers.
  • You forget to ask who else you should talk to.
  • You do not send a thank-you message.
  • You disappear after one conversation and only return when you need something.

In some industries and countries, people call these "coffee chats" or "career conversations." The method is the same.

title: Video Interview Tips: Setup, Body Language, and a Day-Of Checklist
description: Practical video interview tips: test your tech, set up light and sound, look at the camera, handle problems calmly, and use the day-of checklist.

faqs.q: Should I use my phone or my computer for a video interview?
faqs.a: Use a computer if you can, because the screen is bigger and the camera is steadier. If you must use a phone, put it on a stand at eye level and turn on Do Not Disturb.

faqs.q: Is it OK to use notes during a video interview?
faqs.a: Short notes are usually fine, such as a few key words near the camera. Do not read full answers, because the interviewer can see your eyes move.

faqs.q: What should I do if the interviewer is late to the call?
faqs.a: Wait in the call for about 10 minutes. Then send a short email to the recruiter or interviewer to say you are in the meeting and ready, and ask if they want to reschedule.

faqs.q: How do one-way recorded video interviews work?
faqs.a: In a one-way interview, you see a question on screen and record your answer within a time limit, with no live interviewer. Practice with a timer, because you often get only one or two tries.

headings.text: Set Up Your Camera, Light, and Sound
Video Interview Tips for Body Language
How to Answer Questions on Video
What to Do When Something Goes Wrong

html:
The most useful video interview tips are simple. Test your technology the day before, and sit facing a light source. Put the camera at eye level, use headphones with a microphone, and look at the camera when you speak. Join the call five minutes early. Keep your answers a little shorter than in person, and have a backup plan if your internet fails.

A video interview is still an interview. The questions and the hiring decision are the same as in person. But the camera changes how you come across, and small technical problems can break your focus. Prepare for the setup as carefully as you prepare for the questions.

Before the Day: Test Everything

Do a full test at least one day before the interview, at the same time of day and in the same room.

  • Install the meeting app the employer uses (for example, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, or Google Meet) and update it.
  • Open the invitation link and confirm that it works.
  • Check your display name. Use your real first and last name.
  • Test your camera, microphone, and speakers inside the app, not only in your system settings.
  • Record a short test call and watch it. Look at your light, your background, and your sound.
  • Check your internet speed. If your connection is weak, use a cable or sit near your router.
  • Charge your laptop and keep the charger plugged in during the call.

If the employer uses a platform you do not know, ask the recruiter for a test link or any instructions.

Set Up Your Camera, Light, and Sound

Camera

Put the camera at eye level. Stack books under your laptop if you need to. Sit so that the frame shows your head and the top of your shoulders, with a little space above your head. A camera that looks up at you from a desk is the most common problem, and it is easy to fix.

Light

Face a window or a lamp. Light from in front of you makes your face clear. Light from behind you (for example, a window behind your chair) makes your face dark. If the light is uneven, put a lamp behind your laptop and point it at a wall in front of you.

Sound

Sound matters more than video. An interviewer can work with a slightly blurry picture, but not with an echo or noise. Use wired headphones with a microphone or a headset if you can. Choose a room with soft surfaces, such as a bedroom, because they reduce echo. Close windows and tell other people in your home when the call starts.

Background

Choose a plain, tidy background. A wall, a bookshelf, or a neat room is fine. Remove anything personal or distracting. A blur effect is usually acceptable, but some virtual backgrounds make your edges flicker. Test it first.

Video Interview Tips for Body Language

On camera, the interviewer sees only your face and shoulders. That makes small habits more visible.

  • Look at the camera when you speak, not at the interviewer's face on screen. This looks like eye contact to them. Put a small sticker near the camera as a reminder.
  • Look at the screen when you listen, so you can see their reactions.
  • Sit up straight and lean forward a little. It shows interest.
  • Nod and smile while you listen. On video, the interviewer cannot hear small sounds like "mm-hm" if your microphone suppresses noise.
  • Keep your hands in the frame sometimes when you explain something. Natural gestures help.
  • Do not look at a second screen or your phone during the call.

How to Answer Questions on Video

Video calls have a small delay. People often talk over each other because of it. Use these habits to keep the conversation smooth:

  • Pause for one second after the interviewer stops before you answer.
  • Keep answers shorter than in person. Aim for one to two minutes for most answers.
  • Structure each answer so that it is easy to follow. For behavioral questions, the STAR method works well.
  • End each answer clearly, so the interviewer knows you have finished. For example: "That is how I handled it."
  • If you did not hear the full question, ask: "Sorry, the sound cut out. Could you repeat the last part?"

Prepare answers to the questions that come up in most interviews, especially "tell me about yourself." A clear first answer helps you relax for the rest of the call.

What to Do When Something Goes Wrong

Technical problems happen. Interviewers know this. How you handle the problem matters more than the problem.

Problem What to do
Your video freezes Turn off your video for a moment and keep talking. Say what happened.
The sound cuts out Say, "I think I lost you for a moment. Could you repeat that?"
The call drops Rejoin the same link at once. If it fails, email the interviewer and offer to continue by phone.
A person or pet comes into the room Apologize briefly, mute if needed, and continue. Do not over-explain.
Loud noise outside Mute while the interviewer speaks. Mention it once if it continues.

Before the call, write down the interviewer's email and phone number, or the recruiter's. Then you can contact them at once if the call fails.

What to Wear

Dress as you would for an in-person interview at the same company, at least from the waist up. Wear the full outfit, so you are not surprised if you have to stand. Choose solid colors. Thin stripes and small patterns can flicker on camera. Avoid colors that match your background.

Day-Of Checklist

  • Restart your computer one hour before the call.
  • Close all other apps and browser tabs. Turn off notifications.
  • Put your phone on silent and out of reach.
  • Have water, a pen, and paper on the desk.
  • Put the job post, your resume, and your questions for the interviewer in one window you can see quickly.
  • Check your light and camera position one last time.
  • Join the call five minutes early.
  • Smile when the interviewer joins and say their name.

One-Way Recorded Interviews

Some employers use one-way video interviews. You record answers to written questions, and someone reviews the videos later. The same setup tips apply. In addition:

  • Read the instructions about time limits and retakes before you start.
  • Do a practice question if the platform offers one.
  • Speak to the camera as if a person is there.
  • Use the full answer time only if you need it. A clear, short answer is fine.

After the Video Interview

Write down the questions you were asked and your notes about the role while they are fresh. Then send a short thank-you email within 24 hours. Our guide to the thank-you email after an interview has templates.

Some employers have their own rules for video interviews, such as a required platform or camera on for the whole call. Always follow the instructions in the invitation.

title: Fake Job Postings and Job Scams: How to Spot Them and Stay Safe
description: Learn to spot fake job postings and job scams: the red flags, how to check a company, what to never share, and what to do if you were targeted.
keyword: fake job postings and job scams

faqs.q: Do real employers ever ask you to pay for training or equipment?
faqs.a: Real employers in the US do not usually ask new hires to pay for training, equipment, or a starter kit before they start. If a job asks you to pay or to buy something first, treat it as a likely scam.

faqs.q: Is it safe to give my Social Security number on a job application?
faqs.a: Do not give it on a first application or to anyone you have not confirmed. Employers usually need it after you accept an offer, for payroll and tax forms, through their official HR system.

faqs.q: Can a job scam happen on a well-known job board?
faqs.a: Yes. Scammers post fake jobs on popular job boards and on LinkedIn. Always confirm the job on the company's own careers page, and report the posting to the site if it looks fake.

faqs.q: What should I do if a scammer has my personal information?
faqs.a: Act fast. Contact your bank, change passwords you shared, and use the US government site IdentityTheft.gov to make a recovery plan if your identity information was exposed.

headings.text: The Most Common Types of Job Scams
Red Flags in Fake Job Postings
Red Flags During the Hiring Process
How to Check If a Job Is Real
What You Should Never Share Early
What to Do If You Think You Were Scammed

html:
Fake job postings and job scams try to get your money or your personal information by offering a job that does not exist. The clearest warning signs are an offer without a real interview and a request to pay for anything. Others are a check you must deposit and send back, and contact only through text or chat apps. Before you share personal details, confirm the job on the company's official careers page and contact the company through its official website.

Job scams target people who want work fast, and that is most job seekers at some point. Scammers copy real company names, real logos, and real job titles. Some create fake recruiter profiles. The good news: most scams follow the same few patterns, and you can learn to see them.

The Most Common Types of Job Scams

Scam type How it works What they want
Fake check scam They send you a check for "equipment" and ask you to send part of the money to a vendor. The check bounces later. Your money
Pay to start They ask for a fee for training, background checks, or a starter kit. Your money
Identity theft They ask for your Social Security number, bank details, or a copy of your ID before any real hiring process. Your identity
Reshipping You receive packages at home and send them to another address. The goods are often stolen. Your address and your help with a crime
Fake recruiter A "recruiter" offers a job and then asks for fees or personal data. Money or data
Task or "click" jobs You do simple online tasks, and then you must deposit money to "release" your earnings. Your money

The details change, but the goal is the same. A scam either takes money from you or takes information it can use later.

Red Flags in Fake Job Postings

Look for these signs in the posting itself:

  • The pay is very high for simple work or for no experience.
  • The description is vague. It does not say what you will do each day.
  • The posting has many spelling and grammar errors.
  • The company name is missing, or you cannot find the company online.
  • The contact email uses a free email service (for example, a Gmail or Yahoo address) instead of a company domain.
  • The posting says "no interview needed" or "start today."
  • The job asks you to apply through a chat app or by text message.

One sign alone does not prove a scam. Small companies sometimes write short posts. But two or three signs together are a strong reason to stop and check.

Red Flags During the Hiring Process

Many job scams start with a normal-looking posting. The warning signs appear later:

  • You get an offer after a short text chat, with no phone or video interview.
  • The "interview" happens only by chat, and the interviewer avoids a call.
  • They ask for your Social Security number, bank account, or ID photo before an offer in writing.
  • They send you a check and ask you to buy equipment from their "approved vendor."
  • They ask you to pay for anything: training, software, a background check, or a kit.
  • They pressure you to act fast or say the offer ends today.
  • The recruiter's email domain is slightly different from the company's real domain (for example, an extra letter or a different ending).
  • They ask you to move the conversation off the job site to a private app.

The fake check scam is especially common. Your bank may make the money available before the check fully clears. When the check bounces, the bank can take the money back from your account, and you lose what you sent.

How to Check If a Job Is Real

Use these steps before you share any personal details:

  1. Go to the company's official website by typing the address yourself. Do not use links in the message.
  2. Find the careers page. Check that the same job is listed there.
  3. Look up the recruiter on LinkedIn. Check how long the profile has existed, their work history, and their connections at the company.
  4. Compare the email domain with the domain of the company website.
  5. Call or email the company through the contact details on its official website. Ask them to confirm the recruiter and the job.
  6. Search the company name with words like "scam" or "fake recruiter."
  7. Ask for a phone or video interview with a named person. Real employers expect this.

If any step fails, stop. A real employer will understand a careful question. A scammer will push you to skip the checks.

What You Should Never Share Early

In a real hiring process, some information comes only after you accept a written offer, and only through the company's official HR system.

Information When a real employer usually asks for it
Social Security number After an offer, for tax and payroll forms (some employers ask earlier for a background check, with your written consent)
Bank account details After you start, for direct deposit
Copy of your ID or passport After an offer, for employment eligibility forms
Date of birth Usually after an offer, for benefits or background checks
Any payment from you Almost never

Rules about when an employer may ask for this information differ by state and by country. If you are unsure, ask the employer why they need it and how they will protect it.

Protect Yourself While You Search

  • Use a separate email address for job applications.
  • Remove your home address and date of birth from your resume. A city and state are enough.
  • Keep a record of every company you applied to, so you can recognize an unexpected "offer." A job application tracker helps.
  • Do not deposit a check from an employer you have not met and confirmed.
  • Do not pay money to get a job.
  • Turn on two-factor login for your email and job site accounts.

Remote jobs are a common target, because scammers can skip in-person meetings. Our guide on how to find remote jobs lists safer places to look.

What to Do If You Think You Were Scammed

Act quickly. Speed can limit the damage.

  1. Stop all contact with the scammer.
  2. If you sent money, contact your bank or the payment app at once and ask if they can stop or reverse the payment.
  3. If you shared your Social Security number or ID, go to IdentityTheft.gov to report it and get a recovery plan.
  4. Change passwords for any accounts you shared or used with the scammer.
  5. Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
  6. If the scam happened online, you can also report it to the FBI at IC3.gov.
  7. Report the fake posting or profile to the job board or to LinkedIn.
  8. Save every message, email, and payment record.

You did not fail because a scammer targeted you. These schemes are designed to look real. A report helps protect other job seekers, so make one even if you lost nothing.

Outside the US, report job scams to your national consumer protection agency or the police.

title: How Long Should a Resume Be? One Page or Two, by Career Stage
description: How long should a resume be? See the right length for your career stage, what to cut when you have too much, and when two pages is the better choice.
keyword: how long should a resume be

faqs.q: Is a three-page resume ever OK?
faqs.a: For most private-sector jobs in the US, no. Three pages or more are usually only right for academic CVs, some senior executive roles, and some government applications that ask for full detail.

faqs.q: Should my resume be one page if I am changing careers?
faqs.a: Often yes. A career changer usually has older experience that does not relate to the new field, so a focused one-page resume shows the relevant skills more clearly.

faqs.q: Does a longer resume help with applicant tracking systems?
faqs.a: Not by itself. These systems often match terms from the job post, so relevant words matter more than length. A two-page resume full of unrelated details does not help.

faqs.q: Should I make the font smaller to fit my resume on one page?
faqs.a: Do not go below about 10 point for body text, and keep normal margins. If the text only fits with tiny type, cut content instead.

headings.text: How Long Should a Resume Be at Each Career Stage?
When One Page Is the Right Choice
When Two Pages Is the Right Choice
What to Cut When Your Resume Is Too Long
How to Make Each Line Shorter
Formatting Rules That Keep the Length Honest

html:
A resume should be one page if you have less than about 10 years of relevant experience. Use two pages if you have more experience that relates to the job. Most US resumes should not be longer than two pages. The real rule is relevance: every line must help the reader decide that you fit this job. When you are unsure, choose the shorter version and keep only your strongest, most recent proof.

Resume length causes a lot of worry, but the answer is simpler than it looks. A hiring manager wants to find your fit quickly. Length only matters because extra lines make that harder.

How Long Should a Resume Be at Each Career Stage?

Use this table as a starting point. Then adjust for your field and the job.

Career stage Usual length What to focus on
Student or new graduate 1 page Education, internships, projects, part-time jobs, skills
1 to 5 years of experience 1 page Recent roles, results, and skills from the job post
5 to 10 years of experience 1 page, sometimes 2 Last 2 or 3 roles in detail, older roles short
10 or more years of experience 2 pages Last 10 to 15 years in detail, leadership, and scope
Senior executive 2 pages, sometimes more Results at company level, board or leadership work
Academic or research role As long as needed (a CV) Publications, grants, teaching, conferences

These are norms, not laws. A designer with a strong portfolio link might keep one page at any stage. A software engineer with 12 years and many relevant projects might need two.

When One Page Is the Right Choice

Choose one page in these cases:

  • You have less than about 10 years of work experience.
  • You are changing careers, and most of your past work is in another field.
  • You apply for an entry-level or junior role.
  • Your older jobs are similar, and they repeat the same skills.
  • The posting or the recruiter asks for one page.

A one-page resume forces you to choose. That is good. When you choose your best five or six results, the reader sees them at once.

When Two Pages Is the Right Choice

Choose two pages in these cases:

  • You have 10 or more years of experience that relates to the job.
  • You manage people, budgets, or large projects, and you need room for scope and results.
  • Your field values technical detail, such as engineering, IT, or healthcare, and the details match the post.
  • You have certifications, licenses, or security clearances that the job requires.

If you use two pages, fill at least half of the second page. A second page with three lines looks like a formatting mistake. Put your name and page number on the second page, in case someone prints it.

What to Cut When Your Resume Is Too Long

If your resume is too long, cut in this order. Start with the content that helps the reader least.

  1. Remove the objective statement. Replace it with a short summary only if it adds value. See our resume summary examples.
  2. Remove "References available upon request." Employers assume this.
  3. Cut jobs older than about 15 years, or list them in one line each with no bullets.
  4. Cut bullet points that describe duties instead of results.
  5. Merge similar bullet points into one.
  6. Remove skills that everyone in your field has (for example, "Microsoft Word" for an office role).
  7. Remove your full street address. A city and state are enough.
  8. Cut hobbies and interests unless they relate to the job.
  9. Shorten your education section if you have work experience. Remove high school, coursework, and GPA unless they help.
  10. Remove bullet points that do not relate to this job post.

The last step is the most powerful. When you tailor your resume to each job, the length often solves itself. Our guide on how to tailor your resume to a job description shows the method.

How to Make Each Line Shorter

Many resumes are long because each bullet point is long. Use this pattern: action verb, what you did, and the result.

Before: "Was responsible for the management of the company's social media accounts, which included the creation of content and the scheduling of posts on a daily basis."

After: "Managed 4 company social media accounts and scheduled daily posts."

More tips:

  • Start every bullet with a verb. Delete "Responsible for."
  • Remove words like "successfully," "various," and "a number of."
  • Use numerals for numbers (for example, "4" and not "four").
  • Keep most bullets to one line, and never more than two.
  • Use three to five bullets for recent roles and one or two for older roles.

Formatting Rules That Keep the Length Honest

Do not use formatting tricks to squeeze a long resume onto one page. Tiny text and narrow margins make your resume hard to read.

  • Use a body font size of 10 to 12 points.
  • Keep margins of about 0.5 to 1 inch.
  • Use clear headings and white space between sections.
  • Use one simple column for the main content. Some applicant tracking systems read complex layouts in the wrong order, and this varies by system.
  • Save as PDF unless the employer asks for Word.

If the text fits only with tiny type, the resume is too long. Cut content instead.

Special Cases

Employment gaps

Length does not hide a gap. Short, clear dates and a one-line explanation work better than extra detail. Read our guide on how to handle an employment gap on a resume.

Federal, academic, and international applications

US federal job applications often have their own resume rules, and these can change. Academic jobs usually ask for a CV, which lists all publications and can be many pages. In the UK, Europe, and many other countries, "CV" means a resume, and a two-page CV is common. Always follow the instructions in the posting.

Recruiter requests

If a recruiter asks for a specific length or format, follow the request. Recruiters know what their clients want to see.

A Quick Length Check

Before you send your resume, answer these questions:

  • Does every bullet relate to this job post?
  • Is your most relevant experience on the top half of page one?
  • Did you cut jobs older than about 15 years or shorten them to one line?
  • Is the font 10 points or larger?
  • If you have two pages, is the second page at least half full?
  • Can a reader find your current title, your top skills, and two strong results in a short scan?

If you answer yes to all of these, your resume is the right length, whether it is one page or two.

title: How to Decline a Job Offer Politely: Email Templates and Examples
description: Learn how to decline a job offer by email or phone without burning bridges. Get 5 templates for common reasons, what to say, and what to leave out.
keyword: how to decline a job offer

faqs.q: Can I decline a job offer after I accepted it?
faqs.a: Yes, but do it as early as possible, by phone and then in writing. Apologize, keep the reason short, and check your offer letter or contract for any terms about withdrawal or repayment of a signing bonus.

faqs.q: Should I decline a job offer by phone or email?
faqs.a: Email is fine for most offers. Call first if you had many conversations with the hiring manager or the recruiter worked hard for you, and then send a short email to confirm.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a reason when I decline a job offer?
faqs.a: No. A short, general reason is polite, such as "I accepted another role that is a better fit right now." You do not need to share the other company's name or salary.

faqs.q: Can I apply to the same company again after I decline an offer?
faqs.a: Usually yes, especially if you declined politely and quickly. Many people later join companies whose offers they once declined.

headings.text: How to Decline a Job Offer in 6 Steps
What to Include and What to Leave Out
How to Decline a Job Offer by Phone
How to Decline After You Already Accepted

html:
To decline a job offer, reply quickly and thank the person by name. Say clearly that you will not accept, give a short reason if you want, and leave the door open for the future. Send it by email, or call first and then confirm by email. Keep it to four or five sentences. Do not criticize the company or go into detail about another offer.

Declining an offer feels awkward, but it is a normal part of hiring. Recruiters and hiring managers hear "no" often. What they remember is how you said it. A fast, polite answer keeps your reputation strong and lets the company move to its next candidate.

How to Decline a Job Offer in 6 Steps

  1. Decide for sure. Do not decline until you are certain. If you have another offer, accept that one in writing first.
  2. Reply quickly. Answer within one or two business days of your decision. Do not let the deadline pass in silence.
  3. Choose the channel. Email works for most cases. Call first if you had a close relationship with the hiring manager or recruiter.
  4. Thank them. Mention their time and something specific from the process.
  5. State the decision clearly. Use words like "I have decided not to accept the offer." Do not leave room for doubt.
  6. Close warmly. Say you hope to stay in touch, if you mean it.

What to Include and What to Leave Out

Include Leave out
Thanks for the offer and their time Long explanations
A clear decision in the first or second sentence Criticism of the company, the pay, or the people
A short, general reason (optional) The other company's name and salary (unless you want to share)
A wish to stay in touch Promises you do not mean, such as "I will definitely apply again"
Your full name and the job title Any negotiation, if you have decided

If you still want the job but the pay is too low, do not decline yet. Negotiate first. Our guide on how to negotiate salary shows how.

Job Offer Decline Email Templates

Replace every item in square brackets. Use the subject line "Job Offer: [Job Title], [Your Name]" so the email is easy to find.

Template 1: You accepted another offer

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Thank you for offering me the [Job Title] position at [Company]. I enjoyed meeting the team and learning about [specific project or goal].

After careful thought, I have accepted another position that is a better fit for my goals right now. This was a hard decision, because I was impressed by [specific thing you liked].

I hope we can stay in touch, and I wish you and the team the best with [project or goal].

Sincerely, [Your Name]

Template 2: The role is not the right fit

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Thank you for the offer for the [Job Title] role. I appreciate the time you and the team spent with me.

After thinking about the role in detail, I have decided not to accept. I want a position with more focus on [area, such as client work or data analysis]. I do not think this role is the right fit for me now.

I enjoyed our conversations and hope our paths cross again.

Best regards, [Your Name]

Template 3: The pay or benefits do not work

Use this only after you tried to negotiate and the company could not move.

Dear [Recruiter Name],

Thank you for the offer for the [Job Title] position and for your help during the process. I also appreciate that you checked if the team could adjust the salary.

I understand that [Company] cannot change the offer at this time. Because of my financial needs, I must decline the offer. I enjoyed meeting the team, and I would be glad to talk again if a role with a different range opens in the future.

Thank you again, [Your Name]

Template 4: You are staying in your current job

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Thank you very much for the offer to join [Company] as [Job Title]. I enjoyed learning about the team and [specific project].

After a lot of thought, I have decided to stay in my current role for now. I am grateful for your time and for the chance to learn about your work.

I hope we can stay connected.

Kind regards, [Your Name]

Template 5: Personal reasons

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

Thank you for the offer for the [Job Title] role. Because of personal circumstances, I am not able to accept a new position at this time.

I am sorry that I cannot join the team, and I appreciate your time and understanding. I hope to stay in touch.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

You do not need to explain personal reasons. "Personal circumstances" is enough.

How to Decline a Job Offer by Phone

A short call can be more personal. Plan what you will say, and keep it under two minutes.

A simple script:

"Hi [Name], thank you for taking my call. I want to thank you again for the offer for the [Job Title] role. I thought about it carefully, and I have decided not to accept. [Short reason.] I really enjoyed meeting you and the team, and I hope we can stay in touch."

If they ask if anything could change your mind, answer honestly. If nothing would change it, say: "Thank you, but my decision is final." After the call, send a short email that confirms the decision in writing.

How to Decline After You Already Accepted

This is harder, but it happens. Act fast, because the company may have stopped talking to other candidates.

  • Call the hiring manager or recruiter first, then send an email.
  • Apologize clearly and do not blame the company.
  • Keep the reason short.
  • Return any equipment or documents they sent you.
  • Check your offer letter or contract for terms about signing bonuses, relocation payments, or notice. If you are unsure about your obligations, check the contract or ask a qualified advisor.

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I am sorry to tell you that I must withdraw my acceptance of the [Job Title] position. [Short reason, such as "Since I accepted, my circumstances changed, and I cannot start this role."] I know this causes problems for the team, and I apologize. Thank you for your understanding and for the time you invested in me.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

Mistakes to Avoid

  • You wait until the deadline, or you do not answer at all.
  • You decline in a text message, unless the recruiter used text for the whole process.
  • You give a long list of reasons.
  • You say something negative about the company, the team, or the interview.
  • You use another offer as pressure when you have already decided to decline.
  • You forget to tell the recruiter, if a recruiter managed the process.

Before You Send

Check that your decision is final, that you named the correct job title and company, and that you spelled the person's name correctly. If you are still choosing between two offers, use our method for how to compare job offers before you reply.

Customs differ in some countries and industries. In some cultures, a phone call is expected for any offer decision, so follow local practice when you know it.

title: Hidden Job Market: How to Find Jobs That Are Never Posted
description: The hidden job market is the jobs filled before or without a public posting. Learn where these roles come from and a weekly plan to reach them.

faqs.q: How big is the hidden job market?
faqs.a: Nobody can measure it exactly, because unposted jobs leave no public record. You will see many percentages online, but most do not come from a clear, current source, so treat them with care.

faqs.q: Is the hidden job market only for senior people?
faqs.a: No. Entry-level and mid-level roles also get filled through referrals, former interns, and contractors. Senior roles are more often filled through executive recruiters and personal networks.

faqs.q: Should I stop applying to posted jobs to focus on the hidden job market?
faqs.a: No. Do both. Apply to good posted jobs, and spend part of each week on contacts and companies, because the two methods support each other.

faqs.q: What if I do not have a professional network yet?
faqs.a: Start with people you already know, such as former classmates, former coworkers, and alumni of your school. Then add new contacts through informational interviews and professional groups.

headings.text: How to Reach the Hidden Job Market: A 6-Step Plan
Other Ways Into the Hidden Job Market

html:
The hidden job market is the set of jobs that employers fill without a public job posting, or before the posting gets much attention. These roles go to people the company already knows: referrals, former employees, contractors, and candidates who contacted the company first. To reach the hidden job market, choose target companies and build relationships with people who work there. Then ask for advice and referrals before a job is posted.

The term sounds mysterious, but the idea is simple. Hiring takes time and money. When a manager needs someone, they often ask, "Do we know anyone?" before they write a posting. If your name comes to mind at that moment, you compete with few people or with no one.

Where Hidden Jobs Come From

Not every hidden job is a secret. Many roles become "hidden" for ordinary reasons:

  • A manager plans a new role and asks the team for names before HR writes the posting.
  • An employee gives notice, and the manager calls a former colleague.
  • A team turns a contractor or intern into a full-time employee.
  • A company creates a role for a strong person it met, even without an open position.
  • An employer posts the job only on its own careers page or in a small industry group.
  • A recruiter fills the role from their own contacts before posting it widely.
  • A posting goes up, but a referred candidate is already far along in the process.

Many companies also must post some jobs publicly, because of their own policies or because of legal rules for certain employers. The rules vary by employer and location. So a posting can exist even when the company already has a strong internal candidate.

How to Reach the Hidden Job Market: A 6-Step Plan

Step 1: Choose 15 to 25 target companies

You cannot build relationships with every employer. Choose companies where you want to work and where your skills fit. Include a mix of large and small companies, because small companies often hire without formal postings.

For each company, write down:

  • What they do and which teams match your skills
  • Recent news (funding, new products, new offices, new leaders)
  • People you know there, or people in your extended network

Step 2: Map your network

Write a list of everyone you know who could know someone at your target companies. Include former coworkers, former managers, classmates, alumni from your school, friends, neighbors, and people from clubs or volunteer groups. Then use LinkedIn to see who is connected to your targets.

Most hidden jobs come through second-degree connections: the friend of a friend, or a former coworker's new teammate. You do not need a big network. You need a network that you use.

Step 3: Ask for conversations, not jobs

Contact people for short conversations about their work and their company. People help more when you ask for advice. Use our guide to informational interview questions to prepare.

Hi [First Name],

I am a [your role] with experience in [skill or area], and [Company] is one of the companies I admire most. I would value your view of what it is like to work on [team or area]. Would you have 15 minutes for a call in the next few weeks?

Thank you, [Your Name]

Step 4: Stay visible to the right people

One conversation is rarely enough. Keep in touch with useful updates every few weeks or months:

  • Share an article that relates to something they mentioned.
  • Tell them when you acted on their advice.
  • Congratulate them on news, such as a promotion or a product launch.
  • Comment with real thought on their posts.

When a role opens, the manager remembers the people they heard from recently.

Step 5: Ask for a referral when the time is right

When you learn about an opening, or when someone says, "We might hire for that soon," ask clearly. Make it easy: send your resume and a few lines they can forward. Our guide on how to ask for a referral gives templates.

Step 6: Contact hiring managers directly

If you have a strong match, you can write to the manager of the team you want to join. Keep the message short and focused on their needs.

Hi [Hiring Manager Name],

I saw that [Company] [recent news, such as launched a new product or opened an office in a city]. Teams in that stage often need [skill you offer]. In my current role at [Current Company], I [one specific result].

If you expect to add people to your team, I would like to talk. My resume is attached.

Best regards, [Your Name]

Do not send the same message to many managers at one company. Choose the one person whose team fits you best.

Other Ways Into the Hidden Job Market

Channel How it helps What to do
Recruiters They fill roles that are never posted publicly. Connect with recruiters who specialize in your field. See how to message a recruiter.
Professional associations Members often share openings first. Join one active group. Go to meetings and volunteer.
Alumni networks Alumni are often willing to help people from their school. Use your school's alumni directory and LinkedIn alumni search.
Contract and freelance work Short projects can turn into full-time roles. Accept project work at companies you want to join.
Industry events You meet people before they need to hire. Go with a goal: two real conversations per event.
Online communities Members share leads in Slack groups, forums, and newsletters. Contribute help first, then ask.

A Weekly Routine That Works

A plan you keep is better than a plan that looks big. Here is a simple routine for a full-time search. Reduce the numbers if you are employed.

  • Monday: Research two target companies and find two people to contact.
  • Tuesday: Send three or four short networking messages.
  • Wednesday: Hold one or two conversations.
  • Thursday: Send follow-ups and thank-you notes. Update your tracker.
  • Friday: Apply to the best posted jobs you found this week.

Track every contact with the date, the topic, and the next step. A simple spreadsheet is enough.

Mistakes That Close the Door

  • You ask for a job in your first message to a stranger.
  • You send long messages with your full life story.
  • You contact people only when you need something.
  • You forget to thank people who helped you.
  • You ignore posted jobs completely and wait for hidden ones.
  • You do not tell your network what kind of job you want. Be specific: the role, the industry, and the location.

The hidden job market takes more time than clicking "Apply." But each conversation teaches you about real roles, and each new contact can lead to the next one. Over weeks, those small steps add up.

In some countries and industries, networking customs differ, for example in how direct a first message can be. Adjust your tone to local practice.

title: Phone Screen Interview Tips: What to Expect and How to Pass
description: Phone screen interview tips: common questions with sample answers, how to talk about salary, a prep checklist, and what to do after the call.

faqs.q: How long does a phone screen interview usually last?
faqs.a: Most phone screens last 15 to 30 minutes. Some technical screens with a hiring manager can last 45 minutes or longer, so ask about the length when you schedule.

faqs.q: Who usually does the phone screen?
faqs.a: Often a recruiter or someone from HR. At smaller companies, the hiring manager may do the first call.

faqs.q: What if I miss the call from the recruiter?
faqs.a: Call or email back as soon as you can. Apologize briefly, confirm your interest, and offer two or three times when you are available.

faqs.q: Should I send a thank-you email after a phone screen?
faqs.a: Yes, a short one. Thank the person, mention one thing you learned about the role, and confirm your interest in the next step.

headings.text: What the Screener Wants to Learn
Phone Screen Interview Tips: Before the Call
Common Phone Screen Questions and Sample Answers
How to Sound Good on the Phone

html:
The best phone screen interview tips are simple. Research the company and role, prepare a 60-second summary of your background, and know your salary range. Have two questions ready, and take the call in a quiet place with your resume in front of you. A phone screen is a short call, often with a recruiter, to check basic fit before the real interviews. Your goal is to sound clear, interested, and qualified, and to move to the next round.

A phone screen is not a deep test of your skills. The screener usually checks a few things. Does your experience match the resume? Does your salary range fit the budget? Can you work the required schedule and location, and do you communicate well? If you prepare for those points, you remove most of the risk.

What the Screener Wants to Learn

What they check Example question What a good answer shows
Basic fit "Walk me through your background." Your experience matches the role.
Motivation "Why are you interested in this role?" You read the posting and know the company.
Logistics "Are you open to working on site three days a week?" No surprises later.
Pay "What are your salary expectations?" Your range fits their budget.
Timing "When could you start?" Your timeline fits their plan.
Communication Every question You answer clearly and briefly.

Phone Screen Interview Tips: Before the Call

Research the company and the role

Spend 20 to 30 minutes on research. Read the job post twice. Read the company's About page and recent news. Write down two or three facts you can mention, such as a product, a goal, or a recent change.

Prepare your short background summary

You will almost always hear some version of "Tell me about yourself." Prepare a 60 to 90 second answer: your current role, one or two relevant results, and why this job is the next step. Our guide to "tell me about yourself" has a full structure.

Know your numbers

Decide your salary range before the call. Research the market rate for the role and location. Many screeners ask about pay early, and some US states and cities require employers to share a pay range in the posting or on request. Our guide on how to answer the salary expectations question has sample answers.

Set up your space

  • Charge your phone and use a place with a strong signal.
  • Choose a quiet room. Close the door and silence other devices.
  • Put your resume, the job post, and your notes in front of you.
  • Have water, a pen, and paper ready.
  • If the call is on a video app with no camera, test the audio first.

One big advantage of a phone screen: the screener cannot see your notes. Use that. Keep a one-page sheet with your summary, your key results, and your questions.

Common Phone Screen Questions and Sample Answers

"Walk me through your background."

"I have five years in customer support, the last two as a team lead at a software company. I manage a team of six, and this year we cut our average response time by about a third. I am looking for a role where I can work more on support operations and processes, which is why this role caught my attention."

"Why are you interested in this role?"

"Your posting focuses on building the support process for a growing team. That is the part of my current job I enjoy most. I also use your product's mobile app, so I know the customer side already."

"Why are you looking to leave your current job?"

Keep it positive and short. "I have learned a lot in my current role. I want a bigger part in process design, and my current company does not have that kind of role right now."

"What are your salary expectations?"

"Based on my research for this kind of role in [City], I am looking for a range of [amount] to [amount]. I am flexible depending on the full package. Can you share the budgeted range for this position?"

"When can you start?"

"I need to give my current employer [notice period, often two weeks in the US] notice. So I could start about [number] weeks after an offer."

"Do you have any questions for me?"

Always say yes. Ask one or two questions about the role and the process. See the list below.

Questions to Ask the Screener

The screener knows the process best. Ask questions they can answer.

  • "What does the rest of the interview process look like?"
  • "What does a successful first few months look like in this role?"
  • "What is the most important skill for this role, in the hiring manager's view?"
  • "Why is this role open now?"
  • "What is the budgeted salary range for this position?"
  • "When do you expect to make a decision for the next round?"

Save deeper questions about team culture and strategy for the hiring manager. Our list of questions to ask in an interview has more.

How to Sound Good on the Phone

The screener only hears your voice. Small habits make a big difference.

  • Stand up or sit up straight. Your voice sounds more energetic.
  • Smile when you speak. People can hear it.
  • Speak a little slower than normal.
  • Use the screener's name once or twice.
  • Pause before you answer hard questions. A two-second pause is fine.
  • Keep most answers under two minutes. If they want more, they will ask.
  • Do not eat, chew gum, or type loudly during the call.

If the Call Surprises You

Sometimes a recruiter calls without warning and asks, "Do you have a few minutes to talk?" If you are not ready, say so politely:

Hi [Recruiter Name], thank you for calling. I am very interested in the [Job Title] role. I am not in a good place to talk right now. Could we schedule a call for [two specific times]?

A short delay is much better than a rushed, noisy call.

Phone Screen Prep Checklist

  • I read the job post twice and marked the top five requirements.
  • I wrote down three facts about the company.
  • I practiced my 60 to 90 second background summary out loud.
  • I prepared two short stories with results that match the posting.
  • I know my salary range and my earliest start date.
  • I know my answer about location, remote work, and schedule.
  • I wrote two or three questions for the screener.
  • I have my resume and notes in front of me.
  • My phone is charged, and I am in a quiet place.

After the Phone Screen

Within a few hours, send a short thank-you email:

Hi [Screener Name],

Thank you for your time today. I enjoyed learning more about the [Job Title] role and [one specific thing you learned]. I am very interested in moving forward, and I look forward to the next step.

Best regards, [Your Name]

Then write down what you learned: the process, the timeline, the salary range, and the names of the people you will meet. If you do not hear back by the date they gave you, send a polite follow-up.

Pay transparency rules and common notice periods differ by state and country, so check the rules where the job is located.

title: Ghost Jobs: How to Spot Fake Openings and Protect Your Time
description: Ghost jobs are postings with no real plan to hire soon. Learn why companies post them, the warning signs, and how to check a job before you apply.

faqs.q: Are ghost jobs illegal?
faqs.a: In most of the US, a posting with no plan to hire soon is not illegal by itself. Some places have proposed or passed rules about job posting disclosures, so the situation can change by location.

faqs.q: Is a ghost job the same as a job scam?
faqs.a: No. A ghost job usually comes from a real company that is not actively hiring. A job scam comes from someone who wants your money or personal data, often while pretending to be a real company.

faqs.q: Should I stop applying to jobs that might be ghost jobs?
faqs.a: Do not stop completely, because you cannot be sure. Spend less time on doubtful postings, send a quick application only if it is a strong match, and put your main effort into postings that pass your checks.

faqs.q: How long is too long for a job posting to stay open?
faqs.a: There is no single rule. Some roles are hard to fill and stay open for months. A posting is more doubtful when it stays open a long time and also shows other warning signs, such as no responses and a vague description.

headings.text: How to Check a Job Before You Apply
Ghost Jobs Compared With Job Scams
What to Do If You Think You Applied to a Ghost Job
Keep Your Effort Where It Pays Off

html:
Ghost jobs are job postings for roles that the company does not plan to fill soon, or at all. A company may leave an old posting online, collect resumes for later, or post to look like it is growing. To spot ghost jobs, check how old the posting is and whether it appears on the company's own careers page. Also check if the company is hiring for that team, and if a real person replies when you ask.

Ghost jobs waste your most limited resource: time. A tailored application can take an hour or more. When you send that work to a job that is not real, you get silence and start to doubt yourself. The problem is usually the posting, not you.

Why Companies Post Ghost Jobs

Most ghost jobs do not come from bad intent. Common reasons include:

  • The company filled the role, but nobody removed the posting.
  • The company froze the hiring budget after it posted the job.
  • The company wants a pool of resumes for future openings.
  • An internal candidate already has the job, but the policy requires an external posting.
  • A recruiting agency posts a general role to collect candidates for several clients.
  • The company wants to look like it is growing, to customers, investors, or its own employees.
  • A manager wants to see who is available before deciding to hire.

From the outside, you often cannot tell which reason applies. That is why you check the signs and limit how much time you invest.

Warning Signs of Ghost Jobs

No single sign proves that a posting is a ghost job. Look for several signs together.

Sign Why it matters How to check
The posting is many weeks or months old Old postings are more likely to be filled or frozen. Look at the posted date. Note that some sites refresh dates when a job is reposted.
The same job is reposted again and again The company may collect resumes without a plan to hire. Search the exact title and company. Check if it reappears every few weeks.
It is not on the company's careers page The posting may be old or copied by another site. Search the company's own careers page.
The description is vague Real roles usually have clear tasks and a team. Look for a team name, a manager title, and specific duties.
No salary range or location detail Real, budgeted roles often have more details, though this varies. Compare with the company's other postings.
The company had recent layoffs or a hiring freeze New hiring may be on hold. Search recent news about the company.
Many applicants and no replies Signs of a role that nobody is reviewing. Ask people who work there, or check if anyone got an interview.
"Always accepting applications" This often means a talent pool, not a current opening. Read the posting text closely.

Some job sites show the date that a posting first appeared, while others show the last update. Treat dates as a clue, not as proof.

How to Check a Job Before You Apply

Use these steps for any role where you plan to write a custom application. They take 10 to 15 minutes.

  1. Find the posting on the company's official careers page. If it is not there, be careful.
  2. Check the dates. Search for the title to see if older copies of the same posting exist.
  3. Look at the team on LinkedIn. Find people with related titles and check if the team is growing or shrinking.
  4. Read recent news about the company, such as layoffs, funding, or a new office.
  5. Find the recruiter or hiring manager. If you can, send a short message to ask if the role is active.

Hi [Recruiter Name],

I am interested in the [Job Title] role posted on [date or site]. Before I apply, can you confirm that the role is still open and actively hiring? I have [one-line summary of your fit], and I want to make sure my application reaches the right team.

Thank you, [Your Name]

If the recruiter replies and confirms the role, you now have a contact. If nobody replies, you have learned something too.

How to Protect Your Time

You cannot avoid every ghost job. But you can reduce how much time you lose.

Use two levels of effort

  • Full effort: a tailored resume and cover letter. Use this for roles that pass your checks and fit you well.
  • Quick effort: a short application with your standard resume. Use this for good matches where you have doubts about the posting.

Apply early

Fresh postings are more likely to be real and active. Set job alerts so you can apply within the first few days. This also helps with real jobs, because some employers review applications as they arrive.

Do not rely only on postings

Many real roles are filled through contacts, sometimes before a posting goes up. Spend part of each week on networking. Our guide to the hidden job market explains how.

Track everything

Keep a record of where and when you applied, and whether anyone replied. After a few weeks, you will see patterns: companies that never reply and sites that send you to old postings.

Ghost Jobs Compared With Job Scams

Ghost jobs and job scams are different problems, but some signs overlap.

Ghost job Job scam
Who posts it Usually a real company A scammer, often pretending to be a real company
What you lose Time and energy Money, personal data, or both
Typical signs Old posting, no reply, vague role Requests for payment, fast offers, chat-only contact
What to do Limit your effort and move on Stop contact and report it

If a posting asks you for money or for your bank details early, treat it as a possible scam, not a ghost job. Read our guide to fake job postings and job scams for the full checklist.

What to Do If You Think You Applied to a Ghost Job

  • Follow up once, about one or two weeks after you apply. A short message to the recruiter is enough. See our guide on how to follow up on a job application.
  • If there is no reply, mark the application as closed in your tracker and move on.
  • Keep the tailored material. You can reuse much of it for similar roles.
  • Do not take the silence personally. When a posting is not real, no application could succeed.

Keep Your Effort Where It Pays Off

Ghost jobs are frustrating, but they are a known part of the job search now. The best answer is a simple system. Check before you invest, apply early, and use two levels of effort. Build contacts who can tell you about real openings.

Rules about job posting disclosures differ by state, province, and country, and some places are changing them. Check local rules if you want to know what employers must disclose where you live.

title: Two Weeks Notice Letter: Templates, Examples, and What to Include
description: Write a two weeks notice letter in minutes. Get what to include, 4 templates for common cases, an email version, and the steps to resign well.

faqs.q: Is two weeks notice required by law in the US?
faqs.a: In most US jobs, two weeks notice is a custom, not a legal rule, because most employment is at will. Your contract, a union agreement, or company policy can require a different notice period, so check them.

faqs.q: Can my employer end my job right after I give notice?
faqs.a: In many at-will jobs, yes, an employer can decide to end your employment before your last day. Some employers pay out the notice period, but practices vary, so be ready for either result.

faqs.q: Do I count weekends in two weeks notice?
faqs.a: Two weeks usually means 10 business days, or 14 calendar days. State your exact last working day in the letter so there is no confusion.

faqs.q: Should I give more than two weeks notice?
faqs.a: Give more if your contract requires it, if you hold a senior role, or if you have a good relationship and want to help with a long handover. Do not give much more unless you are confident your employer will treat it well.

headings.text: What to Include in a Two Weeks Notice Letter
How to Have the Resignation Conversation
What Happens After You Give Notice

html:
A two weeks notice letter is a short, formal letter that tells your employer you are resigning. It states your last working day, usually two weeks from the date you give it. Include the date, your manager's name, a clear sentence that you resign, and your exact last day. Add a brief thank-you and an offer to help with the handover. Keep it to one short page, and do not explain your reasons in detail.

The letter is a record for HR, not a conversation. The conversation happens first, with your manager, in person or on a video call. The letter then confirms what you said, in writing.

What to Include in a Two Weeks Notice Letter

Part What to write Required?
Date The date you give the letter Yes
Greeting Your manager's name Yes
Resignation sentence "I am resigning from my position as [Job Title]." Yes
Last working day The exact date Yes
Thank-you One or two sentences Recommended
Handover offer How you will help during the transition Recommended
Contact details Personal email for after you leave Optional
Signature Your full name Yes

Leave out complaints, details about your new job, and long explanations. HR may keep this letter in your file for years.

Steps to Resign Well

  1. Sign your new offer first. Do not resign until you have a written offer and any conditions (such as a background check) are complete.
  2. Check your contract and the employee handbook. Look for the required notice period, rules about unused vacation, and any agreements about bonuses, equipment, or confidentiality.
  3. Tell your manager first, in a private conversation. Your manager should not hear it from a coworker or from HR.
  4. Give the letter right after the conversation, by email or on paper, and copy HR if that is your company's practice.
  5. Make a handover plan. List your open tasks, deadlines, contacts, and files.
  6. Work fully until your last day. People remember how you leave.
  7. Return company equipment, and ask HR about your final paycheck and benefits.

Rules on final pay, unused vacation, and benefits differ by state and by employer. Check your company policy and your state's labor department website for the rules that apply to you.

Two Weeks Notice Letter Templates

Replace every item in square brackets. For the email version, use a subject line like "Resignation: [Your Name]."

Template 1: Standard two weeks notice letter

[Date]

Dear [Manager Name],

Please accept this letter as formal notice that I am resigning from my position as [Job Title] at [Company]. My last working day will be [Date].

Thank you for the opportunities I had during my time here. I learned a lot from you and the team, especially about [specific skill or area].

During the next two weeks, I will do my best to finish my current work and hand over my tasks. Please let me know how I can help make the transition smooth.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

Template 2: Short and simple

Use this when you want to keep the letter neutral.

[Date]

Dear [Manager Name],

I am writing to give notice that I am resigning from my position as [Job Title]. My last day will be [Date].

I will help with the handover of my work before I leave.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

Template 3: Warm, for a good relationship

[Date]

Dear [Manager Name],

This letter confirms my resignation from my position as [Job Title] at [Company]. My last working day will be [Date].

This was not an easy decision. I am grateful for your support over the past [number] years, and for the chance to work on [project or achievement]. I will miss working with this team.

Before I leave, I will document my open projects, train [Name or "my replacement"] on [key tasks], and make sure all deadlines are covered. I would like to stay in touch, and you can reach me at [personal email].

With thanks, [Your Name]

Template 4: Notice period longer than two weeks

[Date]

Dear [Manager Name],

Please accept this letter as my formal resignation from my position as [Job Title]. As required by my contract, I am giving [number] weeks of notice, and my last working day will be [Date].
