Thank you for the support and the opportunities during my time at [Company]. I will work with you to plan a complete handover of my responsibilities before I leave.

Sincerely, [Your Name]

How to Have the Resignation Conversation

Plan what you will say before you meet your manager. Keep it short and calm.

A simple script:

"Thank you for meeting with me. I want to tell you that I have accepted a position at another company, and I am resigning. My last day will be [Date]. I have really valued working with you, and I want to make the handover as easy as possible for the team. I will send you my letter today."

Your manager may ask questions. Prepare for these:

  • "Where are you going?" You can share it or say, "I prefer to keep that private for now."
  • "Why are you leaving?" Give one short, positive reason, such as "I want to grow in [area]."
  • "Is there anything that would make you stay?"

How to Handle a Counteroffer

Some employers make a counteroffer: more pay, a new title, or other changes. Think before you answer. Ask yourself why you started to look for a new job. If the reasons were not only about money, a raise may not fix them.

If you want to decline the counteroffer, say: "Thank you, I appreciate the offer. I have made my decision, and I will keep my last day as [Date]." If you are unsure, our method for how to compare job offers can help you compare the counteroffer with the new job.

Common Mistakes

  • You resign before you have a signed offer.
  • You send the letter before you talk to your manager.
  • You forget to state an exact last day.
  • You write complaints or criticism in the letter.
  • You tell coworkers before your manager.
  • You stop working hard during the notice period.
  • You delete files or take company information with you. Leave everything that belongs to the company.

If you are still searching and not ready to resign, read our guide on how to manage a job search while employed.

What Happens After You Give Notice

Your employer may ask you to work the full notice period, a shorter period, or none of it. Some companies end access to systems on the same day. Prepare for that: before your meeting, save any personal files and personal contacts from your work devices, as long as company policy allows it. Do not copy company data.

Ask HR about your final paycheck, unused paid time off, retirement accounts, and health insurance continuation. In the US, many employers that offer group health insurance must offer COBRA continuation coverage. The rules depend on the employer and your situation, so ask HR for the details.

Notice customs and legal rules differ outside the US. In many countries, contracts or national law set the notice period, and it can be one month or longer.

title: Job Search Burnout: Signs, Causes, and How to Recover
description: Job search burnout is real. Learn the signs, why it happens, and a practical weekly plan to keep searching without running out of energy.

faqs.q: Is it OK to take a break from job searching?
faqs.a: Yes. A planned break of a few days to a week can help you return with better focus. Before you stop, write down the date you will start again and the first task you will do.

faqs.q: How many hours a day should I spend on my job search?
faqs.a: There is no single right number. Many people do better with a fixed block of a few focused hours each day than with long, open-ended days, and people who are employed often use much less time.

faqs.q: How do I explain to family that my job search is hard?
faqs.a: Tell them what you are doing each week and what kind of support helps you, such as fewer questions about results and more help with practical tasks. Specific requests work better than general complaints.

faqs.q: When should I talk to a professional about burnout?
faqs.a: Talk to a doctor or a licensed mental health professional if you feel hopeless, cannot sleep or eat normally, or the feelings last for weeks. If you think about harming yourself, contact a crisis line at once.

headings.text: Why the Job Search Causes Burnout
How to Recover From Job Search Burnout

html:
Job search burnout is the deep tiredness, low motivation, and loss of hope that can build up during a long job search. It comes from repeated rejection, silence from employers, uncertainty, and long hours of work with no clear reward. To recover, set fixed work hours for your search and measure the actions you control instead of the results. Take planned breaks, and get support from other people.

A job search is hard work, but it rarely feels like work, because you get no paycheck and little feedback. Many applications get no answer. Over weeks and months, that silence wears you down. If you feel burned out, it does not mean you are weak or lazy. It means you have used a lot of energy on a process that gives little back.

This guide gives practical steps. It is not medical advice. If your feelings are serious or last a long time, talk to a doctor or a licensed mental health professional.

Signs of Job Search Burnout

You may have job search burnout if several of these are true for you:

  • You dread opening your email or job sites.
  • You put off applications you once wrote quickly.
  • You feel tired even after a full night of sleep.
  • You apply to jobs without reading the posting closely, just to "get numbers."
  • You feel angry or hopeless after each rejection.
  • You avoid friends because they ask about your search.
  • You doubt your skills, even though your past work was good.
  • You work on the search all day but finish little.

Why the Job Search Causes Burnout

Knowing the causes helps you choose the right fix.

Cause What it feels like Main fix
No feedback Silence after most applications Measure your actions, not replies
No structure The search fills every hour of the day Set fixed hours and stop at a set time
Repeated rejection Each "no" feels personal Separate your value from the result
Too many low-fit applications High effort, low return Apply to fewer, better-matched roles
Isolation You do the search alone Talk to people every week
Money stress Pressure grows each month Make a money plan and look at it weekly

How to Recover From Job Search Burnout

1. Set working hours for your search

Treat the search like a part-time or full-time job, with a start time and a stop time. When the time ends, close the laptop. Do not check job sites in bed or late at night. Fixed hours protect your rest and make your work time more focused.

2. Measure what you control

You cannot control when an employer replies. You can control your actions. Set weekly goals for actions, for example:

  • Send 5 tailored applications.
  • Have 2 networking conversations.
  • Practice interview answers for 1 hour.
  • Learn 1 new skill item for 2 hours.

At the end of the week, check your actions. If you did them, the week was a success, even with no replies. A job search plan helps you set these goals.

3. Apply to fewer jobs, better

Many burned-out job seekers apply to everything. That often gives more rejections and less energy. Choose roles where you match most of the requirements, and spend more time on each one. Our guide on how many jobs you should apply to explains how to find your balance.

4. Take planned breaks

Plan one full day each week with no job search at all. After a hard rejection, such as after a final interview, take the rest of the day off if you can. A longer planned break of a few days can also help. Write down when you will restart, so the break does not turn into avoidance.

5. Talk to people

Isolation makes burnout worse. Schedule contact with people every week:

  • A friend who does not ask about your search
  • A job search group or an accountability partner
  • A former coworker who can remind you of your strengths
  • A career counselor, if you can access one (many schools and public workforce centers offer free help)

6. Protect your body

Small habits affect your energy more than you expect. Keep a regular sleep time. Go outside each day, even for a short walk. Eat regular meals. These steps do not solve the job search, but they give you energy for it.

7. Reframe rejection

Most rejections are about fit, timing, budget, or many other candidates. They are not a judgment of your value. After each rejection, ask one question: "Is there one thing I can learn from this?" If the answer is no, let it go and move on.

A Sustainable Weekly Plan

Here is an example plan for a full-time search. Adjust it to your situation. If you are employed, use about a third of these hours.

Day Morning (2 to 3 hours) Afternoon (1 to 2 hours)
Monday Find and choose roles for the week Networking messages
Tuesday Tailored applications Skill practice or a course
Wednesday Tailored applications Networking calls
Thursday Interview practice Follow-ups and tracker update
Friday Applications Review the week and plan the next one
Saturday Free Free
Sunday Free Free

A job application tracker helps you see your progress in one place, which can lift your mood on hard weeks.

Make the Repetitive Work Lighter

Repetitive tasks drain energy fast. Make them smaller:

  • Keep a "master" resume with all your results, and copy the relevant lines for each application.
  • Save answers to common application questions in one document.
  • Use job alerts instead of searching from zero each day.
  • Use a tool to write first drafts. For example, CoverBetter writes a first draft of a cover letter from your resume and the job post, and you edit it.
  • Batch similar tasks. Write all your follow-up emails at one time.

Write Down Your Wins

Burnout hides your progress. Keep a short list of wins and read it each Friday. A win can be small:

  • A recruiter replied.
  • You got a first interview.
  • You learned a new tool.
  • You finished all your planned actions for the week.
  • Someone agreed to an informational interview.

When to Get Professional Help

Burnout and depression can look similar. Contact a doctor or a licensed mental health professional if:

  • Low mood lasts for most days over two weeks or more.
  • You cannot sleep, or you sleep much more than usual.
  • You lose interest in things you used to enjoy.
  • You feel hopeless about the future.

If you have thoughts about harming yourself, get help now. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. In other countries, contact your local emergency number or a local crisis line.

title: What to Do After Being Laid Off: A Step-by-Step Checklist
description: What to do after being laid off: the first 48 hours, money and health insurance steps, how to explain it, and a plan to start your job search.
keyword: what to do after being laid off

faqs.q: Should I sign the severance agreement right away?
faqs.a: No. Read it carefully first. Agreements often include a release of legal claims and a deadline, and you may want an employment lawyer to review it before you sign.

faqs.q: Can I apply for unemployment if I got severance pay?
faqs.a: Often yes, but severance can affect when your benefits start or how much you receive, depending on your state. Apply and ask your state unemployment office how they treat severance.

faqs.q: How do I explain a layoff in an interview?
faqs.a: Say it in one or two sentences, without blame. For example: "My role was eliminated when the company cut the marketing team." Then move on to what you did well and why you want this job.

faqs.q: Should I take a break before I look for a new job?
faqs.a: A short break can help, especially after a stressful exit. Handle the time-sensitive tasks first, such as unemployment, health insurance, and the severance deadline, and then decide on the length of your break.

headings.text: What to Do After Being Laid Off: The First 48 Hours
Week One: Protect Your Money and Health Coverage
Week Two: Prepare Your Job Search
A Checklist for the First Month

html:
After being laid off, first get the facts in writing: your last day, final pay, severance terms, and benefits end date. In the first week, apply for unemployment benefits, choose your health insurance option, and make a basic budget. Save your work contacts and examples of your work if company policy allows it. Then rest briefly, update your resume and LinkedIn, tell your network, and start a structured job search.

A layoff is a business decision about a role or a budget. It is not a review of your work. Many skilled people lose their jobs in layoffs, and recruiters know this. The steps below help you protect your money, your health coverage, and your next opportunity, in a clear order.

What to Do After Being Laid Off: The First 48 Hours

You may feel shocked or angry. That is normal. In the first two days, focus on facts, not decisions.

  1. Ask for everything in writing: your last day, final paycheck date, severance offer, and when your benefits end.
  2. Do not sign anything on the spot. Ask how many days you have to review the severance agreement.
  3. Ask about unused paid time off, any bonus or commission you earned, and equity that has vested.
  4. Ask if the company offers outplacement services, such as career coaching.
  5. Ask if your manager or another leader will give you a reference.
  6. Save personal contact details for colleagues you want to stay in touch with.
  7. Save copies of your own documents, such as performance reviews and pay stubs, if company policy allows it. Do not copy confidential company data.

Questions to Ask HR

Topic Question
Final pay When will I receive my final paycheck, and what will it include?
Severance How much severance is offered, how is it paid, and what is the deadline to sign?
Paid time off Will unused vacation be paid out?
Health insurance When does my coverage end? When will I receive COBRA information?
Retirement plan What happens to my 401(k) and any company match?
Equity What happens to vested and unvested stock or options?
Reference How will the company confirm my employment to future employers?
Equipment How and when do I return company equipment?

Rules for final pay, paid time off, and severance differ by state and by employer. This guide is not legal advice. If the amounts are large or the agreement is complex, ask an employment lawyer to review it.

Week One: Protect Your Money and Health Coverage

Apply for unemployment benefits

Apply in the state where you worked, and apply soon. Many states do not pay for the time before you apply. Each state runs its own program with its own rules. The US Department of Labor has a page that links to state unemployment insurance programs.

Choose your health insurance

Find out exactly when your employer coverage ends. Then compare your options:

  • COBRA continuation coverage, if your employer offers it. It lets you keep the same plan, but you usually pay the full cost.
  • A plan through the Health Insurance Marketplace at HealthCare.gov or your state's marketplace. Losing job-based coverage usually gives you a special enrollment period, which has a time limit.
  • Coverage through a spouse's or partner's employer plan.
  • Medicaid, depending on your state and income.

Compare the total cost, not only the monthly premium. Check that your doctors and medicines are covered.

Make a basic budget

List your income sources: severance, final pay, unemployment benefits, savings, and any partner income. Then list your essential costs. Calculate how many months you can cover. This number reduces anxiety, because you can plan with a real deadline instead of a vague fear.

Pause or reduce costs you do not need. Contact lenders early if you expect trouble with payments, because some have hardship options.

Week Two: Prepare Your Job Search

Rest for a few days

If you can, take a few days to recover before you start applying. A layoff is stressful. A rested mind writes better applications and gives better interviews. If the stress lasts, read our guide on job search burnout.

Update your resume

Add your most recent role and your results while they are fresh. Write down the projects, numbers, and feedback you are proud of. Do not mention the layoff on your resume. Your dates and results are enough. If the search takes a while, our guide to an employment gap on a resume shows how to handle it.

Update LinkedIn

Update your headline and your "About" section. Use the "Open to Work" setting if it fits your situation. You can make it visible to recruiters only, or to everyone.

Tell your network

People cannot help you if they do not know you are looking. Send short, specific messages to former colleagues, managers, and friends in your field.

Hi [First Name],

I wanted to let you know that my role at [Company] was eliminated in a recent layoff. I am now looking for a new role as a [Target Job Title] in [industry or location]. In my last role, I [one specific result].

If you hear of an opening, or if you know someone I should talk to, I would really appreciate an introduction. Thank you!

[Your Name]

A public post on LinkedIn can also bring help from people you did not expect. Keep it positive: what you did, what you want next, and how people can help.

How to Explain the Layoff

You will be asked why you left. Prepare a short, honest answer and practice it until it feels natural.

Example answers:

  • "My position was eliminated when the company reduced the size of the operations team."
  • "The company closed our office, and my role was part of that change."
  • "After the merger, the company combined two teams, and my role was cut."

Then move to the future: "I am proud of what I did there, especially [result]. Now I want to [goal], which is why this role interests me."

Do not criticize your former employer. Do not over-explain. A layoff is a common event, and a calm answer shows maturity.

Build Your Job Search Plan

Once the urgent tasks are done, give your search a structure:

  • Define your target roles, industries, and locations.
  • Set weekly goals for applications, networking conversations, and interview practice.
  • Track every application in one place.
  • Keep a regular daily schedule with a start and stop time.

Our job search plan guide walks you through each step.

A Checklist for the First Month

  • I have my last day, final pay, severance terms, and benefits end date in writing.
  • I reviewed the severance agreement before signing, and I know the deadline.
  • I applied for unemployment benefits in my state.
  • I chose a health insurance option before my coverage ended.
  • I made a budget and know how many months I can cover.
  • I saved personal contacts and allowed personal documents.
  • I updated my resume and LinkedIn profile.
  • I told my network what kind of role I want.
  • I practiced my layoff explanation out loud.
  • I set a weekly job search plan.

Rules for unemployment, severance, and health coverage differ outside the US. In other countries, check your national government's employment and benefits websites.
